1.title: Checklist for delivering LIB faithfully
1.gist: A fidelity scorecard listing the structural steps a counselor should complete in every Living in Balance session, from room setup to the closing summary. It matters because the program's outcome results assume it is delivered as designed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Fidelity is the bridge between a study and your group. An evidence-based program only carries its evidence when the active ingredients actually show up; drift session by session quietly turns it into a different, untested intervention.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Checkbox fidelity measures adherence, not skill. A counselor can tick every box and still run a flat, lecture-heavy group. Researchers usually separate adherence (did you do it) from competence (how well), and the second predicts outcomes at least as much.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After your next session, score yourself honestly, then mark which skipped step you skipped on purpose and why. Deliberate adaptation is defensible; unnoticed drift is not.

ask: Which of these steps would you sacrifice first under a 45-minute count, and what does that reveal about what you believe is the active ingredient?
How would you tell the difference between adapting the program and abandoning it?

terms.d: How closely a program is delivered the way its developers designed and tested it.

2.title: Rating the quality of interaction
2.gist: The second half of the scorecard rates how the counselor relates to clients: warmth, nonjudgment, checking understanding, cultural relevance, MI and CBT use, and emotional safety at the end. It shifts the focus from what was covered to how it landed.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Common-factors research, associated with Wampold and others, broadly finds that alliance, empathy and counselor warmth account for a meaningful share of outcomes across therapies. Confrontational, judgmental styles in addiction work have generally performed worse, which is part of why MI spread.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Item 2 frames addiction as a compulsion that can overwhelm good intentions. That is a disease-leaning, low-blame stance that lowers shame, and shame is a strong driver of defensiveness and relapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Items 8 and 9 matter most in a facility: men return to a unit, not a home. A two-minute closing round on what stirred them up lets you catch someone who is triggered or raw before he walks back into a tense environment.

ask: Can a counselor be nonjudgmental about addiction while still holding someone accountable for harm done? Where is that line for you?
What would culturally relevant look like concretely for the groups you actually run?

terms.d: The working bond between counselor and client: agreement on goals, tasks, and a sense of mutual trust.

3.title: Session flow and opening relaxation
3.gist: The Quick Start Guide lays out the six-step session rhythm and scripts the optional opening relaxation: quiet sitting, muscle release, a calm image, and a silently repeated word. It sets a predictable structure for a 60 to 75 minute group.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The breathing-plus-repeated-word method closely resembles Herbert Benson's relaxation response, which he adapted from meditation traditions. The instruction not to worry about success echoes mindfulness teaching: noticing distraction and returning is the exercise, not a failure of it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Closed eyes can feel unsafe for men with trauma or in a housing unit with peers watching. Offer a soft gaze at the floor as an equal option, and keep your own eyes open so the room knows someone is holding watch.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A predictable structure lowers threat. For people whose lives have been chaotic, knowing what comes next frees attention for learning instead of scanning.

ask: What is the relaxation actually for here: arousal reduction, attention training, or a ritual that marks group time as different?
How might you measure whether the opening exercise changes participation later in the hour?

terms.d: A calm physiological state, the opposite of fight-or-flight, that can be cued by slow breathing and focused attention.

4.title: Running the core of the session
4.gist: Steps 3 through 6 cover the overview, working through readings and worksheets, optional video, role-play or visualization, and the closing summary. Most of the hour belongs to the facilitated content and discussion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Role-play is behavioral rehearsal, a core idea in Bandura's social learning theory: people acquire skills by watching, practicing, and getting feedback, not by hearing about them. Reading aloud alone rarely changes behavior.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Role-plays die when nobody volunteers. Lower the stakes: you play the difficult character first, keep scenes under two minutes, and let the observer group coach. Laughter is fine; it means people are engaged.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Reading information sections aloud can drift into a classroom lecture, which tends to engage literate members and lose others. Paraphrasing and pausing for examples usually keeps more of the room.

ask: If time forced you to cut either the reading or the role-play, which would you cut and what evidence supports that choice?
What makes a summary at the end actually consolidate learning rather than just repeat it?

5.title: Record of sessions delivered
5.gist: A log listing the twelve core LIB sessions with space to note the date each was run. It is the map of the whole core program and helps track that a group completes all twelve.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Read the titles as an arc: education and self-assessment first, then triggers and planning, then broader life domains like spirituality, sex, stress and emotions, closing with anger and relapse prevention. It moves from substance to whole life, which is the program's name in action.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Showing members the full list early gives them a sense of a finish line and of where the group is going, which can help with engagement in short-stay or open-enrollment settings.

ask: Why might the developers put spirituality and sexuality in the middle rather than at the end?
In open-enrollment groups, does the session order matter much, or is each session effectively standalone?

6.title: Opening Session 1: naming the problem
6.gist: Introduces the first session, which covers addiction terms, a self-assessment of severity, and the biology of addiction. Starting with shared vocabulary and a personal self-check frames everything that follows.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Starting with a self-assessment aligns with motivational approaches: when people evaluate themselves against criteria, the conclusion is theirs, which tends to stick better than a label handed to them by staff.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Mandated clients may approach a self-assessment strategically, under- or over-reporting depending on what they think it affects. Clarifying early what the results are and are not used for can make answers more honest.

ask: What does it change for a client to hear 'disorder' instead of 'addict' as the first word of treatment?
Why might biology be placed in the very first session?

7.title: What members are asked to face
7.gist: Lists the biology objectives and tells members they will need courage to look honestly at how substances harmed them and others, framing that insight as a route back to control. It also previews the glossary terms.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The promise here is that understanding leads to control. That is a cognitive premise, but insight alone is usually not enough; skills and environment change carry much of the load. Insight is the doorway, not the house.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking people to examine harm to others can trigger shame in a prison group. Distinguishing guilt (I did something bad) from shame (I am bad), a distinction June Tangney has researched, helps keep the honesty productive.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to pick one glossary word they think they already know and define it before reading. Comparing gives an instant, low-stakes discussion.

ask: Is 'taking back control' the right metaphor for someone whose daily life is controlled by an institution?
How do you invite honesty about harm without turning the group into a confession booth?

terms.d: Guilt focuses on a behavior and tends to motivate repair; shame focuses on the self and tends to motivate hiding.

8.title: Defining a substance use disorder
8.gist: Defines a substance use disorder as mood-altering drug use that harms a person's life, introduces the three drug classes, and opens Exercise 1 on how use damages lives. It anchors the program in consequences rather than quantity.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Defining the disorder by harm, not by how much someone uses, mirrors the DSM-5 approach. It sidesteps arguments about amounts and invites the more useful question: what has it cost you?

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The stimulant, depressant, hallucinogen scheme is a teaching simplification. Opioids, cannabis, and drugs with mixed effects do not fit neatly, so expect members with street knowledge to push back; welcome it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Exercise 1 asks about 'a person,' which is safe distance. Let them answer about others first, then ask which of those items they recognize from their own life.

ask: Where does harm-based diagnosis risk missing someone whose use has not caught up with them yet?
How would you explain to a skeptic why alcohol belongs on a list with heroin?

terms.d: Acting on the brain to change mood, perception, thinking, or behavior.

9.title: Addiction as a primary chronic disease
9.gist: Defines addiction as a primary, chronic, progressive condition shaped by genes, psychology and environment, compared to diabetes, and explains that it is not merely a symptom of another problem. This sets up why addiction needs its own treatment even when other issues improve.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The chronic disease model, championed in the US by figures like Nora Volkow and A. Thomas McLellan, argues addiction behaves like diabetes or hypertension: relapse rates are comparable, and it needs long-term management rather than one-time cure.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Critics such as Marc Lewis argue addiction is better seen as deep learning than disease, and many people recover without treatment, especially as they age out of heavy use. The disease frame reduces blame but can also reduce a person's sense that change is possible.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may hear 'lifelong disease' as a life sentence. Pair it with the diabetes point: managed diabetics live full lives. The message is management, not doom.

ask: If addiction is 'primary,' how do you make sense of someone who quits once their PTSD is treated?
Does the disease frame help or hurt accountability in a criminal justice setting?

terms.d: Long-lasting and recurring, needing ongoing management rather than a single cure.

10.title: When other problems and addiction collide
10.gist: Exercise 2 asks members to think about people whose psychological problems came before their addiction, and how each condition worsened the other. It introduces co-occurring disorders through others' stories before turning inward.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Co-occurring mental illness is common among people with substance use disorders, and higher still in justice-involved populations. Integrated treatment of both conditions at once is generally recommended over treating them in sequence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by drawing a two-way arrow on the board: depression leads to drinking, drinking deepens depression. Ask members to fill in their own loop. The cycle image often lands better than the abstract term 'co-occurring.'

ask: How does this worksheet sit with page 9's claim that addiction is primary? Can both be true?
How would you spot a member whose use is mostly self-medicating an untreated condition?

terms.d: Having a substance use disorder and another mental health condition at the same time.

11.title: Progression and three kinds of lost control
11.gist: Explains that untreated addiction tends to worsen and can kill, then breaks impaired control into three types: over amount, over stopping, and over behavior while intoxicated. These give members concrete handles for self-recognition.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Progression is the classic view, but longitudinal research shows many courses: some people worsen, some plateau, many reduce or stop on their own. Saying addiction usually worsens without help is fair; saying it always does overstates it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Loss of control over behavior links substance use directly to the offenses that brought many members to custody. Alcohol in particular lowers inhibition and narrows attention, which helps explain its strong tie to violence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which of the three kinds of lost control is easiest to admit and which hardest. Usually amount is easy; behavior, especially harm to others, is hard. That gap is worth naming gently.

ask: Why might the program spell out three distinct types rather than just say 'loss of control'?
What would 'control' look like for someone aiming at moderation rather than abstinence?

terms.d: Being unable to reliably limit how much, how often, or how one behaves when using.

12.title: Checking lost control and obsession
12.gist: Exercise 3 has members check which kinds of lost control apply to them; the page then describes preoccupation, and Exercise 4 asks for examples of out-of-control behavior. It moves from definitions to personal admission.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Preoccupation reflects how drugs hijack the brain's reward and salience systems: cues tied to the drug grab attention automatically. Robinson and Berridge's incentive-sensitization theory describes this as 'wanting' growing even when 'liking' fades.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Checkboxes are less exposing than writing. Debrief by asking for a show of hands per item, which normalizes the experience before anyone shares a story.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to estimate what share of their waking thoughts went to getting, using, hiding, or recovering during their heaviest period. The number often surprises them.

ask: Is preoccupation a cause of addiction, a symptom, or both?
How does incarceration change preoccupation: does absence quiet it or feed it?

terms.d: Persistent thinking about getting, using, or hiding a substance, crowding out other priorities.

13.title: Using despite harm, and denial
13.gist: Covers continued use despite consequences and defines denial as a largely unconscious defense that shields people from the reality of their addiction. It reframes denial as self-protection rather than deliberate lying.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Denial comes from psychoanalytic theory, systematized by Anna Freud. Cognitive science adds a related idea: motivated reasoning, where people evaluate evidence in ways that protect beliefs they need, often without awareness.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Older confrontational treatment tried to break denial head-on, and Miller and Rollnick argued this often increases resistance. In MI, what looks like denial is often treated as ambivalence and met with reflection rather than argument.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Never call a member 'in denial' in group; it hardens defenses. Instead ask what someone would have to accept if the problem were as serious as others think.

ask: If denial is unconscious, what can actually make it conscious?
Where do you see denial in people who do not use substances at all, including professionals?

terms.d: An automatic mental strategy that reduces anxiety by distorting or blocking awareness of painful facts.

14.title: Admitting denial, then the DSM self-check
14.gist: Exercise 5 asks members to check forms of denial they have used; Part 2 then introduces DSM-5 and its mild-to-severe scale and sets up a private self-assessment. It moves from defenses to structured self-evaluation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: DSM-5 merged the older 'abuse' and 'dependence' into one disorder rated by how many of eleven criteria apply: roughly two or three is mild, four or five moderate, six or more severe. A spectrum replaces the old yes-or-no label.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The note that sharing is optional is important in a facility where information can feel dangerous. Say it out loud, and mean it; privacy often buys more honesty than pressure does.

ask: What is gained and lost when addiction becomes a count of criteria?
Could a person be honest about denial while still being in it?

terms.d: The American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual, fifth edition, used to define mental disorders including substance use disorders.

15.title: Self-assessment: more, longer, more time
15.gist: Begins the DSM-style self-assessment with items on using more or longer than planned, failed attempts to cut down, and time spent getting, using and recovering. Members answer yes or no and give examples.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: These first items capture impaired control, one of four clusters the DSM-5 criteria fall into, alongside social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological signs like tolerance and withdrawal.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The 'provide examples' lines matter more than the checkbox. A yes with a vivid example becomes real to the person writing it; encourage one concrete memory per yes.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to total the hours in a typical using day spent getting, using, and coming down. Converting to hours per week makes the cost visible.

ask: Why might time spent be one of the most revealing criteria for people who say they 'functioned fine'?
How reliable is self-report on these items for someone facing legal consequences?

16.title: Self-assessment: cravings and life costs
16.gist: Continues the assessment with cravings, problems at home or work, continuing despite relationship damage, and dropping important activities. These items track how use crowds out the rest of life.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Behavioral economists describe addiction partly as narrowing of reinforcement: as the drug becomes the main source of reward, other rewards fade. Recovery then means rebuilding alternative rewards, not just removing the drug.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Item 7, giving up activities, invites a hopeful turn: ask what they used to enjoy before using took over. Those answers become material for later sessions on sober lifestyle.

ask: Craving was added as a criterion in DSM-5. Why might clinicians have wanted it there?
Which of these four items do you think best predicts relapse risk, and why?

terms.d: A strong desire or urge to use, often triggered by people, places, moods or objects linked to past use.

17.title: Self-assessment: danger, harm, tolerance
17.gist: Covers continuing despite danger, continuing despite physical or psychological harm, and tolerance. These items show use persisting even against clear self-interest.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Continuing despite known harm is the heart of the addiction puzzle. One explanation is delay discounting: people with addiction tend to weigh immediate rewards much more heavily than later costs.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw a scale with 'tonight' on one side and 'next year' on the other. Ask members to place what the drug offered and what it cost on each side. The time mismatch becomes visible.

ask: Is continuing to use despite danger irrational, or rational given how the person values the present moment?
Note that tolerance and withdrawal from a properly taken prescription do not count toward a disorder in DSM-5. Why might that exception exist?

terms.d: Needing more of a substance to get the same effect, or getting less effect from the same amount.

18.title: Withdrawal item and scoring the check
18.gist: Closes the self-assessment with the withdrawal item and explains that the items come from APA criteria, with four or five yeses pointing to a moderate disorder. More criteria generally means greater severity.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Criteria counts are crude: two people with five yeses can look very different, and the count says nothing about strengths, supports, or readiness. Severity guides intensity of care, but the RNR model would add risk and needs assessment before deciding what someone needs.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to score privately, then share only what surprised them. Surprise, not the number, is what opens discussion.

ask: What would a severity scale that also counted recovery capital look like?
Why does a moderate rating sometimes feel worse to a member than a severe one?

terms.d: The DSM-5 rating of mild, moderate or severe, based on how many criteria a person meets.

19.title: Owning the diagnosis; tolerance in practice
19.gist: Exercise 7 asks members whether they believe they meet at least a moderate disorder; the page then revisits time spent and tolerance, and Exercise 8 has them total daily hours and note rising doses. Self-diagnosis is the pivot point of Session 1.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking people to reach the conclusion themselves applies self-perception and MI principles: we believe what we hear ourselves say. A self-made judgment carries more weight than one delivered by staff.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some will answer no. Do not argue. Reflect it back and ask what would need to happen for the answer to be yes. Ambivalence spoken aloud is progress.

ask: How should you respond when someone with an obvious severe pattern checks no?
Is a yes on this page a sign of insight or of telling the counselor what he wants?

20.title: Mapping personal withdrawal experiences
20.gist: Defines withdrawal as the feelings and physical reactions on cutting down or stopping, varying by drug, and Exercise 9 asks what members experienced and whether they used to avoid it. It reveals use driven by escaping sickness rather than chasing a high.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Using to avoid withdrawal is negative reinforcement: the behavior is strengthened because it removes something painful. Koob's work on the 'dark side' of addiction argues this shift from chasing pleasure to escaping distress drives later stages.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Remind the group that withdrawal from alcohol and benzodiazepines can be medically dangerous, including seizures. That is useful safety information for reentry, where unplanned stopping can happen.

ask: When someone uses mainly to feel normal, what does that change about how you motivate them?
How might withdrawal memories act as a fear-based barrier to trying to quit?

terms.d: A behavior becomes more likely because it takes away something unpleasant, like withdrawal sickness.

21.title: How use pushes life aside
21.gist: Describes neglected duties at work, school and home, swapping old friends for using friends, and growing isolation, then Exercise 10 asks about working or parenting while high and how social life has suffered. It makes the social cost concrete.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Social network research suggests behaviors like drinking spread through networks. The swap from old friends to using friends is not just a symptom; the new network then holds the habit in place.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The parenting question is heavy for fathers in custody. Acknowledge it before anyone answers, and frame honesty here as an act of care for their kids, not an indictment.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw two circles: people around them before heavy use and during it. Who disappeared, who appeared? It sets up later sessions on sober support.

ask: Is isolation a cause of addiction, an effect, or both, and how would you test that?
How does a prison setting replicate the narrowed social world of active use?

22.title: Blaming problems vs. seeing causes; brain intro
22.gist: Exercise 11 asks members whether they blamed family problems for their use and now see that use caused those problems; Part 3 then introduces brain chemistry as the key to understanding dependence, tolerance and withdrawal.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The worksheet leans toward one answer: that drugs caused the family problems. Often causation runs both ways, and family conflict, trauma or violence can be real drivers. A good debrief allows both directions without letting either become an excuse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a reattribution exercise, a classic cognitive move: reconsidering what caused what changes how responsible and how capable a person feels.

ask: How do you help someone take ownership without denying that his family was genuinely hard?
Why place biology right after this most personal self-assessment?

23.title: Neurotransmitters and mood balance
23.gist: Explains neurotransmitters as chemical messengers whose levels being low, balanced, or high shape mood, energy and behavior, and notes that stress, pain, sleep, food and good events shift them. It lays the groundwork for how drugs hijack mood.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The too-low, balanced, too-high picture is a helpful teaching model but a big simplification. Mood depends on circuits, receptors and context, not just chemical levels; the old 'chemical imbalance' theory of depression is now considered overly simple.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Dopamine is often called the pleasure chemical, but neuroscientists such as Wolfram Schultz showed it signals prediction and wanting more than pleasure itself. That is why cues can trigger strong urges even when using no longer feels good.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the page's examples: winning a game, good news, sex. Then ask what natural highs members remember. It plants the idea that the brain can feel good without drugs.

ask: What is the risk of teaching clients a simplified brain story they may carry for life?
How do natural rewards differ from drug rewards in size and speed?

terms.d: A chemical that passes signals between nerve cells, such as dopamine, serotonin or GABA.

24.title: How drugs unbalance brain chemistry
24.gist: A short quiz confirms neurotransmitters affect thinking, feeling and behavior; the text then explains that one use causes a temporary imbalance while long-term use creates a continuous one, as the brain cuts its own production. This explains why quitting feels bad.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The body's tendency to counter a drug's effect is homeostasis, and Solomon's opponent-process theory describes it: each high triggers an opposing low that grows stronger with repetition, while the high weakens.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Use a seesaw image: the drug pushes one side down, and the brain loads the other side to stay level. Remove the drug and the seesaw slams the other way. That is withdrawal and early-recovery misery in one picture.

ask: If the brain adapts down, how long might it take to adapt back, and what does that imply for early recovery support?
How does the quiz's 'all of the above' answer reinforce the mind-body link the program wants?

terms.d: The body's drive to keep its internal systems stable, adjusting against outside changes.

25.title: Dependence is not the same as addiction
25.gist: Distinguishes physical dependence, the body adapting to a drug, from addiction, which adds compulsion and use despite harm, using the example of a hospital patient on painkillers. Exercise 13 asks if members have developed dependence.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: This distinction became central during the opioid crisis. Many pain patients are dependent but not addicted, and clinicians have debated how to treat both safely; abrupt tapering of dependent patients has been linked to harm.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Medications like methadone and buprenorphine maintain dependence while treating addiction. Many members carry stigma about medication treatment; this page gives you a foothold for explaining why that is not trading one addiction for another.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask: can you be addicted without being physically dependent? Cocaine and gambling are good examples that show compulsion does not require withdrawal.

ask: How does this distinction affect what you tell members about medication for opioid use disorder at release?
Which do members fear more, dependence or addiction, and why?

terms.d: The body's adaptation to a drug, so that stopping causes withdrawal; it can occur without addiction.

26.title: Withdrawal as the drug's mirror image
26.gist: Explains that withdrawal symptoms tend to be the opposite of the drug's effect, with depressants leaving anxiety and stimulants leaving depression and fatigue, and Exercise 14 asks members to list their own symptoms. It ties biology back to lived experience.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Make a two-column board: drug effect on the left, withdrawal on the right. Let members fill it from experience for alcohol, cocaine, heroin. They usually get it right, which builds confidence in the model.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Normalize the fear that comes with withdrawal. Members who felt they were going crazy often never told anyone. Hearing it is common removes some of its power.

ask: If withdrawal mirrors the drug, what does that predict about the emotional state of someone in early recovery?
Where does the mirror rule break down?

27.title: Tolerance, and its strange reverse
27.gist: Exercise 15 checks whether members noticed tolerance; the page then introduces reverse tolerance or kindling, where after an extreme reaction even small doses can trigger the same seizure or psychosis. It warns that the body does not always need more.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page blends two related ideas. In research, kindling usually refers to alcohol withdrawal seizures worsening after repeated detoxes, while sensitization describes stimulants producing stronger effects, including psychosis, with repeated use. Both are real; the label here is loose.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This page carries a safety message for reentry: after a break, the body does not respond like before. Link it to overdose risk after release, when lost opioid tolerance makes a former usual dose potentially deadly.

ask: How can tolerance and sensitization happen in the same person to different effects of the same drug?
Why might members dismiss this page as something that only happens to others?

terms.d: An increased response to a drug after repeated use, the opposite direction of tolerance.

28.title: A case of small dose, big reaction
28.gist: Gives the example of a man whose crack binge caused violent psychosis, and who had the same reaction to a small amount after three months clean; Exercise 16 asks whether members had a small dose hit unexpectedly hard.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Stimulant psychosis is well documented, and people who have had one episode appear more prone to another. Paranoia plus agitation is a dangerous mix, which is why this ties so closely to violent incidents.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect stories here, some involving violence or arrests. Keep the focus on what the body did, not the details of the offense, so the group stays a learning space rather than a war-story session.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask the group to rewrite the man's story with one decision changed. Where could he have stepped out? This previews relapse-prevention thinking.

ask: How do you handle war stories that glamorize use while still letting people be honest?
What does this case suggest about the assumption that 'a little won't hurt' after a long break?

29.title: Cross-tolerance and hidden substitution
29.gist: Defines primary and secondary drugs and explains cross-tolerance, where similar drugs like alcohol and Valium cover each other's withdrawal. It warns that quitting one while keeping another, like alcohol and marijuana, often leads back to both.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cross-tolerance is why benzodiazepines are used to manage alcohol withdrawal medically: they act on overlapping brain systems, especially GABA. The same overlap is what makes casual substitution risky.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that keeping marijuana will almost certainly lead back to alcohol is stronger than the evidence. Some studies find cannabis use can substitute for alcohol for some people, others find it raises relapse risk. Honest framing: it is a real risk worth tracking, not a certainty.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members see weed as not a real drug. Instead of arguing, ask them to test the idea: what happened to their drinking last time they cut weed, or the reverse?

ask: How would you respond to a member who argues harm reduction: switching to a less harmful drug is progress?
Where does the abstinence-from-everything stance fit with MOUD and harm-reduction approaches?

terms.d: Tolerance to one drug that carries over to another with similar effects.

30.title: Naming primary and secondary drugs
30.gist: Exercise 17 has members list their primary drug, secondary drug, and other regular drugs, with how long and when they use each. It builds a personal drug-use profile that later sessions draw on.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a basic functional profile. Asking when each drug is used reveals what job it does: sleep, confidence, coming down, social ease. Function, not chemistry, often explains substitution.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Add a column: what does this drug do for you? It turns a list into insight and shows which needs recovery must meet another way.

ask: What does someone's secondary drug tell you that his primary drug does not?
How would this profile help you match members to the right services at release?

31.title: Drug switching: the addiction moves, not ends
31.gist: Explains drug switching, where people use a completely different drug when the primary one is unavailable, such as alcohol for cocaine users, and concludes that recovery means stopping all psychoactive drugs. Exercise 18 asks what members use when their drug of choice is missing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Behavioral scientists see this as evidence that addiction is about the behavior and the need it meets, not one molecule. It parallels research on addiction substitution, where some people move from drugs to gambling or other compulsive behaviors.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The all-psychoactive-drugs rule is the traditional Minnesota Model stance. It is a clear line, but it can clash with medically prescribed psychiatric drugs or MOUD; members need to know the rule is about misuse, not refusing needed medication.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison often forces switching to whatever is available, like homemade alcohol or synthetic drugs. Ask what members used inside; it shows the pattern plainly.

ask: If the drug can change but the pattern stays, what is the pattern actually made of?
How would you explain to a member why his prescribed antidepressant does not break abstinence?

terms.d: Using a different drug, even one with opposite effects, when the preferred drug is unavailable.

32.title: The upper-downer cycle's hidden danger
32.gist: Describes the upper-downer cycle, where stimulants and depressants are used together and mask each other, letting people consume dangerous amounts; because cocaine wears off faster than alcohol, intoxication can suddenly hit. Exercise 19 asks if members have done this.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Alcohol and cocaine taken together form cocaethylene in the liver, a compound generally considered more toxic to the heart than cocaine alone. That adds a chemical reason to the masking danger on this page.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Today the cycle often runs with fentanyl and stimulants combined, sometimes unknowingly in the drug supply. The same masking logic applies, with higher overdose stakes.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw two curves on the board: cocaine fading fast, alcohol lasting. Mark the point where they cross. Members immediately see why someone feels fine, then is suddenly wasted behind the wheel.

ask: Why might a user experience the cycle as control rather than loss of control?
How does knowing about drug timing change advice you would give at release?

terms.d: How the body breaks down a drug; different drugs clear at different speeds.

33.title: Short-term effects versus the long tail
33.gist: Exercise 20 asks if members typically use in an upper-downer pattern; the page then distinguishes primary drug effects shortly after use from secondary effects of heavy or long use, like paranoia and sleep loss from cocaine or depression from alcohol.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is the core of the drug's bargain: the primary effect is what people use for, the secondary effect is often the very problem they started using to fix. The cure becomes the cause.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sleep deprivation alone can cause hallucinations and paranoia in healthy people, as sleep research has shown. Part of what looks like drug psychosis may be the sleepless binge itself.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to name the reason they first used, then the secondary effect they ended up with. Many will see the same feeling on both lists.

ask: What does the gap between primary and secondary effects suggest about why people persist?
How might you use this distinction in motivational interviewing?

terms.d: The delayed, often opposite effect of heavy or long-term drug use.

34.title: Secondary effects and session wrap-up
34.gist: Exercise 21 asks which secondary effects members have experienced, then the summary recaps Session 1: terms, self-assessment, and the biological reach of addiction. It closes the education-heavy opening session.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before closing, ask each member for one thing that changed how they see their own use. A single sentence each is enough and creates a concrete takeaway.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Session 1 is very information-dense. Retention research suggests people remember little of lectures without practice; the self-assessment parts likely carry more lasting weight than the definitions.

ask: If members only remember one idea from Session 1, which do you most want it to be?
How would you check a week later whether any of this stuck?

36.title: Role-play: stealing from a caring friend
36.gist: A role-play in which Min, actively drinking, takes money from her friend Tong, denies it, and pushes her away. It dramatizes compulsion, denial and the damage addiction does to the people who care.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Role-play builds perspective-taking. Playing Tong lets members feel what their families felt, which can produce empathy that lecture cannot. Playing Min lets them watch denial from the outside.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Swap roles halfway through. The member who played Min often becomes noticeably quieter as Tong. Ask what the switch felt like; that is the richest part of the debrief.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The characters' names and setting may feel distant to your members. Adapting names, place and amounts to familiar reentry details, while keeping the dynamics, usually increases buy-in.

ask: Which addiction features from Session 1 can you spot in Min's behavior?
What would a non-enabling, still-caring response from Tong look like?

38.title: Role-play: rebuilding broken trust
38.gist: A role-play between Maria, two weeks sober and asking for money for treatment, and Luiz, her husband, who doubts her after failed attempts. It explores trust, failed quit attempts, and what each partner must do.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Trust is rebuilt through behavior over time, not promises. This links to behavioral contracting ideas used in family therapy for addiction, such as Behavioral Couples Therapy.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The scene is a classic trust game: Luiz must decide under uncertainty. Game theory suggests trust grows through small repeated exchanges that are kept, which hints at practical solutions like paying the program directly.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members face this exact scene at release. Ask them to propose solutions that protect both partners, then ask who in their life holds Luiz's role.

ask: Should the burden of rebuilding trust be entirely on the person who used?
Note how the scene says marijuana and alcohol undermined her quitting. How does that tie back to cross-tolerance and switching?

40.title: Session 1 glossary, part one
40.gist: Collects the session's key definitions from addiction through primary drug effects, including cross-tolerance, denial, drug switching, neurotransmitters and physical dependence. It is a reference sheet for review.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The glossary calls addiction a biopsychosocial disorder, a model George Engel proposed in 1977 for medicine generally: illness emerges from biology, psychology and social context together, not any one alone.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run a quick glossary relay: read a definition aloud and have members shout the term, then ask someone to give a real-life example. Retrieval practice beats rereading for memory.

ask: Which glossary term do members most often misuse in everyday talk, and why does it matter?
Does the biopsychosocial label actually change treatment, or just how we describe it?

terms.d: The view that health problems arise from interacting biological, psychological and social factors.

41.title: Session 1 glossary, part two
41.gist: Finishes the glossary from psychoactive drugs through withdrawal, adding reverse tolerance, secondary effects, substance use disorder severity, tolerance and the upper-downer cycle. It notes severe disorders may be called addiction.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Language matters: research has found that clinicians rate a person described as a 'substance abuser' as more deserving of punishment than one described as having a 'substance use disorder.' John Kelly's work on this is often cited.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Invite members to say which terms they would use about themselves. Some prefer 'addict' as an honest label from twelve-step culture; others find it stigmatizing. Respect their choice.

ask: Should clients be free to call themselves addicts if the field is moving away from the word?
Which three terms here would you keep if you had to cut the glossary to three?

42.title: Session 2 opens: knowing the drugs
42.gist: Introduces Session 2, which surveys stimulants, psychedelics and hallucinogens, depressants, and how addictive substances affect the brain. It shifts from defining addiction to understanding specific substances.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Drug education alone has a weak track record for preventing use, as evaluations of programs like the original DARE showed. Its value in treatment is different: helping people interpret their own experience, not scaring them off.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Your members may know more street pharmacology than the manual. Position them as experts on experience and the text as a lens. It flips a potential power struggle into collaboration.

ask: What is the goal of drug education for people who already use heavily?
How do you handle a member whose experience contradicts the manual?

43.title: Stimulants: the seven common types
43.gist: Lists the objectives for depressants and the brain, asks members to examine how specific drugs affected them, and opens Part 1 by naming seven common stimulants, from cocaine and meth to caffeine and nicotine.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Putting caffeine and nicotine beside cocaine is deliberate. It shows that legality and social acceptance do not track pharmacology; nicotine in particular is highly addictive, and tobacco kills more people than illegal drugs combined.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to rank the seven by danger, then by how socially accepted they are. The mismatch makes a sharp discussion about why society draws lines where it does.

ask: What does the inclusion of legal stimulants do to members' sense of their own drug as uniquely bad or uniquely harmless?
How should you discuss prescribed stimulants for ADHD with members who have that diagnosis?

44.title: Stimulant effects climb with dose
44.gist: Explains that stimulants speed up the nervous system, with low doses bringing alertness, higher doses energy and anxiety, and very high doses agitation, paranoia and possible fatal overdose. A quick quiz confirms all these are possible.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a dose-response curve, and the Yerkes-Dodson idea fits it: some arousal improves performance, too much wrecks it. The drug moves people along that curve past its peak.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw an inverted U on the board. Ask members to place their typical use on it, and where they thought they were at the time.

ask: Why do people rarely stay at the low-dose end once they have felt the higher end?
How does appetite and sleep loss at any dose set up the later psychological problems?

terms.d: The relationship between how much of a drug is taken and how strong its effects are.

45.title: Same family, different force
45.gist: Exercise 2 asks which stimulants members used and what they sought; the text explains that stimulants share effects but differ in strength, duration and route, with smoking delivering the drug quickly to the brain, and notes that ingredients like pseudoephedrine are tracked because they make meth.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Speed of delivery shapes addictiveness: the faster a drug hits the brain, the stronger the rush and the stronger the learning. That is why crack and smoked meth tend to be more compulsive than slower forms.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page says smoking reaches the brain faster than injection. Both smoking and injecting are extremely fast routes, and pharmacologists do not fully agree on which is faster; the key point, that smoking is about as fast as it gets, stands.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The 'what effects were you looking for' question is gold. Write answers on the board; they reveal needs like confidence, energy, numbness, belonging.

ask: Why does route of use matter more than the drug's chemical name in predicting problems?
What do the effects members wanted tell you about what recovery must provide?

46.title: Legal stimulants can still overdose
46.gist: Warns that large doses of legal stimulants like caffeine pills can cause overdose-like problems, and that weak and strong stimulants converge at high doses. Exercise 3 asks how route changed effects and whether members ever megadosed a weaker stimulant.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Concentrated caffeine powders and pills have caused deaths, which led US regulators to act against bulk pure caffeine sales. The dose that is harmless in coffee becomes dangerous in concentrated form.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In facilities, members may misuse commissary caffeine, energy drinks or crushed medications. This page gives a neutral way to discuss that without accusing anyone.

ask: What does megadosing a weak drug reveal about what the person is really chasing?
How do you talk about legal substance misuse inside without sounding like you are policing?

47.title: What stimulants do to the body
47.gist: Describes stimulant physical effects such as restless repetitive activity, racing talk, shaking, a pounding fast heart, high blood pressure, dilated pupils, sweats and chills. Exercises 4 and 5 ask members about rapid heartbeat and uncontrollable activity.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Repetitive, pointless activity on stimulants has a name in research: stereotypy, documented in animal and human studies, and among meth users sometimes called 'punding,' like taking apart and reassembling objects for hours.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A pounding heart that feels like panic is worth linking to anxiety. Some members who later have panic attacks sober may fear they are dying or relapse to cope; naming the overlap now helps.

ask: Why might the body's alarm signals on stimulants fail to stop people from using more?
How could you use a member's memory of a racing heart in a motivational conversation?

terms.d: Repeating the same movement or action over and over without purpose, often seen with heavy stimulant use.

48.title: Stimulant moods: the rise and the crash
48.gist: Asks members about physical excitement, inner tension and medical effects they knew of, then explains that stimulants temporarily raise neurotransmitters and leave them below normal after stopping, producing depression and anxiety.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The crash after stimulants is partly why binges happen: using again is the fastest way out of the low. This is negative reinforcement wrapped around a positive one.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Sketch a mood line: baseline, spike, crash below baseline, slow return. Then show what happens when the next dose comes before baseline returns. The line drifts down over time.

ask: What does the crash mean for how quickly someone can feel good in early stimulant recovery?
How might anhedonia after stopping be mistaken for a permanent depression?

terms.d: Reduced ability to feel pleasure, common after stopping heavy stimulant use.

49.title: Altered mental states from stimulants
49.gist: Exercise 6 asks how stimulants affected mood and whether stopping brought depression; the page then lists the altered states stimulants can cause, intoxication, delirium, psychosis and withdrawal, starting with intoxication, whose strength depends on prior mood.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The point that the high depends on mood before use is important. It connects to expectancy and context effects: set and setting shape drug experience, not chemistry alone.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members whether the drug hit differently when they were happy versus miserable. Many notice they used most when feeling worst, which is exactly when the payoff felt biggest.

ask: If the high is relative to prior mood, who is most at risk of developing a strong attachment to stimulants?
How does this four-state frame help you assess someone arriving from the street?

50.title: Hypervigilance and borrowed personalities
50.gist: Describes stimulant intoxication as sensory overload and suspicious watchfulness, and notes temporary personality changes such as shy people turning aggressive or feeling invincible. Exercises 7 and 8 ask about altered states and times the drug did not lift mood.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Hypervigilance on stimulants looks much like trauma-related hypervigilance. For members with trauma histories, stimulants may amplify an already overactive threat system, which can help explain violent incidents.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The question about sexual behavior one would normally avoid touches risk, regret and sometimes coercion. Keep it general in group and offer individual follow-up.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name a trait the drug gave them, like confidence, then brainstorm one sober way to build a version of it. It turns loss into a goal.

ask: If the drug supplies a missing trait, what does that suggest about the root need?
How is 'feeling invincible' connected to criminal risk-taking?

51.title: Delirium, hallucinations, and illusions
51.gist: Asks about sensory overload and personality changes others noticed, then defines delirium as severe confusion from long or heavy stimulant use, and distinguishes hallucinations, perceptions of what is not there, from illusions, misreading something real.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Predictive processing theories in neuroscience see perception as the brain's best guess. Illusions are wrong guesses about real input; hallucinations are guesses running with little input. Drugs and sleep loss both loosen the brain's error checks.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The question about what others said about personality changes is powerful because it brings outside perspective inside the room. Invite one or two quotes from family members if people are willing.

ask: Why does the manual bother distinguishing illusion from hallucination for this population?
How would you tell stimulant delirium from a primary psychotic disorder in someone you are screening?

terms.d: An acute state of confusion and disorientation, often with fluctuating attention.
A misperception of something that really exists, like seeing a bush as a person.

52.title: Personal hallucinations and violence
52.gist: Exercise 9 asks whether members experienced stimulant hallucinations or illusions, what they were, and whether they became violent on stimulants. It links perception distortions to harmful behavior.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The violence question can feel like a confession of crimes. Remind the group about confidentiality limits before they answer, and accept a yes without details.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A drug explanation for violence can become an excuse. Debrief by holding both truths: the drug distorted perception, and the choice to use that drug, in that state, belonged to the person.

ask: How do you handle disclosures that touch on unresolved charges?
Where is the line between explaining violent behavior and excusing it?

53.title: Stimulant psychosis and paranoia
53.gist: Explains stimulant psychosis as a temporary break with reality, with paranoia, voices, visions and tactile hallucinations like crawling bugs, which can lead to lashing out. Exercise 10 asks whether members or people they know have had it.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Methamphetamine psychosis is well documented and usually clears with abstinence, but in a minority symptoms persist, and people with a prior episode are vulnerable to recurrence. 'Not permanent' is generally true but not guaranteed.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Tactile hallucinations of bugs are called formication. They often lead to skin picking and sores seen in heavy meth users, a visible sign of the internal state.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking about others first gives distance. Members who share about a friend are often describing themselves; let that be.

ask: What would you want correctional staff to know about stimulant psychosis on intake?
How might paranoia from stimulants persist as general distrust after use stops?

terms.d: The false sensation of insects crawling on or under the skin.
Unfounded belief that others intend harm or are plotting against you.

54.title: Stimulant withdrawal and its timeline
54.gist: Asks about crawling-skin sensations, then describes stimulant withdrawal: depleted neurotransmitters, depression, fatigue, irritability, sleep problems, sometimes suicidal thoughts, peaking around days three or four and easing over about two weeks.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Suicidal thoughts during stimulant withdrawal are a real risk. Make sure members know they pass, and that telling someone is safe. Know your facility's protocol before this page.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A known timeline is itself a coping tool. Uncertainty makes distress feel endless; knowing the peak and the decline lets people ride it out, much like urge-surfing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw the withdrawal curve with a peak at day three or four. Ask members to mark where they relapsed in past attempts. Many will mark the peak.

ask: Why might suicidal thinking in withdrawal be especially dangerous for someone just released?
How would you adapt this timeline message for someone in a long custody stay who is past it?

55.title: Later waves of craving and discomfort
55.gist: Notes that bursts of depression, agitation and craving can recur during the first three months, encourages members that they fade, and suggests meetings, meditation and exercise; Exercises 11 and 12 ask about personal symptoms.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Exercise has growing evidence for easing depression and possibly cravings in stimulant recovery, though studies vary in quality. It is a low-risk, high-upside suggestion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This mirrors Marlatt's relapse prevention idea that expecting setbacks reduces the shock when they come. A craving wave that is anticipated feels like weather, not failure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what worked inside to get through bad days. Facility-specific tools, like a yard workout or a letter-writing routine, are more usable than generic advice.

ask: What does it do to a person's confidence to believe 'I should be over this by now'?
Which of the three suggestions is most realistic for your members at reentry, and why?

56.title: Psychedelics and their five groups
56.gist: Asks how members coped with stimulant withdrawal, then opens Part 2 by naming five psychedelic groups, including LSD types, PCP, synthetic cannabinoids and marijuana, and stressing that their effects on thought and senses are unpredictable.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Lumping marijuana, synthetic cannabinoids and LSD together is a convenient category, but they differ greatly in risk. Synthetic cannabinoids, common in prisons, are often far more dangerous than cannabis, with seizures and psychosis reported.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psilocybin and MDMA are being studied as treatments for depression and PTSD in controlled settings. Members may have heard about it; distinguish supervised clinical research from street use.

ask: How do you discuss the psychedelic research news without endorsing street use?
Why might synthetic cannabinoids be so popular in correctional settings?

terms.d: Lab-made chemicals sprayed on plant material, sold as K2 or Spice, often more potent and unpredictable than marijuana.

57.title: Members' own psychedelic experiences
57.gist: Exercise 13 asks which psychedelics members have taken, what the experiences were like, and how they found the effects unpredictable. It invites personal reflection on drugs some see as harmless.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Psychedelic stories can become entertaining and glamorizing. Steer by asking what the experience cost or what went wrong, alongside what was appealing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write one word for the best trip and one for the worst. The contrast shows unpredictability without anyone needing to tell a long story.

ask: What drew people in your groups to psychedelics, escape or meaning-seeking?
How would you respond to someone who says a trip changed his life for the better?

58.title: Set, setting, and the bad trip
58.gist: Explains that dose, surroundings, past experience and expectations shape a psychedelic experience, and that fear can tip it into panic, though PCP can go badly regardless. A quiz confirms psychedelics distort senses, thinking, time and identity.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The terms 'set and setting' were popularized by Timothy Leary in the 1960s, but the idea is broader: expectancy and context shape every drug's effect, including alcohol, as balanced-placebo studies have shown.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Distortion of identity is a hallmark of psychedelics, sometimes called ego dissolution. It can feel profound or terrifying, which helps explain both mystical reports and lasting anxiety in some users.

ask: If mindset shapes the trip so much, what does that imply about context effects in your groups?
Why does the manual single out PCP as an exception?

terms.d: Mindset and environment, two factors that strongly shape a drug experience.

59.title: LSD, DMT, and mushrooms
59.gist: Exercise 15 asks what else might shape a trip and how psychedelics distort senses; the text explains that LSD resembles brain chemicals tied to senses, mood and sleep, and lists effects like distortion, higher heart rate, nausea and poorer coordination.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: LSD, psilocybin and DMT act mainly on serotonin receptors, especially the 5-HT2A type. Serotonin is the neurotransmitter the page alludes to without naming.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Classic psychedelics are generally considered to have low addiction potential compared with stimulants or opioids. Their main risks are dangerous behavior during the trip, panic, and triggering psychosis in vulnerable people.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may claim psychedelics are not addictive and therefore fine. Agree on the low addiction point, then ask about what happened around their use: other drugs, risky situations, impaired judgment.

ask: Does a drug need to be addictive to fit within a substance use treatment program?
How do you stay credible with members when the manual and current research differ in emphasis?

terms.d: A neurotransmitter involved in mood, perception, sleep and appetite; the main target of classic psychedelics.

60.title: What LSD does to perception and self
60.gist: A quiz confirms LSD distorts senses, mood and can cause panic; the text describes swirling visuals, warped time and space, and distorted self-image, from all-good to all-bad, and Exercise 17 asks how LSD scrambles sensory messages.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Seeing oneself as all good or all bad parallels splitting, a concept from psychodynamic theory and later DBT work with borderline personality. The drug produces temporarily what some people live with as a pattern.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members whether they have ever seen themselves as all bad while sober. Then ask what evidence would complicate that picture. A quiet cognitive restructuring moment, prompted by a drug page.

ask: What does LSD's effect on time and self suggest about how ordinary perception is constructed?
How can a single bad trip shape someone's relationship with fear years later?

61.title: Bad trips; the mescaline-ecstasy family
61.gist: Asks about bad trips, then introduces the mescaline family, from the peyote cactus to synthetic MDMA or ecstasy and similar drugs sold as ecstasy, noting they blend psychedelic and stimulant effects and belong to the amphetamine family.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Peyote has a long ceremonial history among Indigenous peoples of the Americas, and its religious use by members of the Native American Church is legally protected in the US. Context and culture change what a drug means.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Pills sold as ecstasy frequently contain other substances, from caffeine to synthetic cathinones and sometimes more dangerous adulterants. The page's note that other drugs are sold as ecstasy is an understatement in today's supply.

ask: How do you discuss ceremonial use of substances respectfully in a group that includes Indigenous members?
Why does the drug's chemical family matter to someone who just bought 'molly'?

terms.d: A synthetic amphetamine-related drug, known as ecstasy or molly, with stimulant and mild psychedelic effects.

62.title: Ecstasy: love drug to amphetamine
62.gist: Explains that low doses of mescaline-family drugs cause mild sensory changes and feelings of trust and love, while high or chronic doses act like amphetamines with high blood pressure, agitation and possible violence. Quizzes and Exercise 19 ask about personal use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: MDMA's warmth comes largely from a large release of serotonin and the bonding hormone oxytocin. The midweek low many users report likely reflects serotonin depletion afterward, a mirror of the high.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Ecstasy's dangers often come less from the drug alone than from heat, dehydration, overdrinking water, and mixing. Accurate harm information is more credible to young users than blanket scare messages.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The question about using it alone or with other drugs reveals polydrug use. Expect most to say with others, which reconnects to the upper-downer cycle.

ask: Why might a drug that produces trust be especially tempting for people raised in mistrust?
What makes harm-reduction information credible to someone who has used for years?

terms.d: A hormone linked to bonding and trust, released naturally during closeness and touch.

63.title: PCP: the drug that splits mind from body
63.gist: Asks about people who took too much ecstasy, then introduces PCP and ketamine as dissociative anesthetics that cut the mind off from the body and block pain, explaining reports of extreme strength and continued fighting despite injury.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The image of superhuman PCP users fed fear-driven policing narratives. The core truth is that pain blocking and terror prevent people from stopping; the 'superhuman' part is mostly myth, and has been used to justify force.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Ketamine, in a related family, is now used as an approved rapid-acting treatment for depression in a nasal form. One molecule can be medicine or danger depending on dose, setting and supervision.

ask: How do drug myths about violent users shape how justice-involved people are treated?
What is the difference between dissociation from trauma and drug-induced dissociation?

terms.d: A drug that blocks pain by disconnecting awareness from bodily sensation, like PCP or ketamine.

64.title: No safe dose of PCP
64.gist: Describes PCP's unpredictability, from mild euphoria and rubbery legs to sudden terror, psychosis and violence at the same dose, notes there is no safe dose and overdose can mean seizures or death, and that it lingers in fat cells. A quiz reviews these risks.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Unpredictability is itself a risk factor. Most drugs teach users their dose; PCP breaks that learning, so experience does not protect the user.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members may have used PCP unknowingly, since it can be laced into marijuana. Ask whether anyone had a reaction that seemed far stronger than the weed they thought they smoked.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members what 'unpredictable' means in their own using lives beyond PCP. Few drug users today know exactly what they are taking.

ask: What does PCP's inconsistency teach about the illusion of control in any drug use?
Why might extremely unpredictable drugs still attract people?

65.title: PCP reflection; spice and K2
65.gist: Exercise 21 asks about members' PCP experience and what mind-body disconnection does; the text then introduces synthetic cannabinoids like spice and K2, plant matter sprayed with varying chemicals, so users never know what they are taking.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Synthetic cannabinoids generally bind cannabinoid receptors much more strongly than THC, which helps explain their severe effects. Formulas change constantly, partly to stay ahead of bans.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Synthetic cannabinoids have been a major problem in many prisons, sometimes smuggled on paper. Members may have seen people collapse or seize. Let them share what they witnessed; it is often more persuasive than the text.

ask: What does mind-body disconnection have in common with how some members cope with stress sober?
Why does marketing these products as 'incense' or 'legal weed' matter for risk perception?

66.title: Spice's dangers; marijuana's mixed effects
66.gist: Lists severe synthetic cannabinoid effects, including psychosis, suicidal or homicidal thoughts, heart problems and seizures, then describes marijuana as psychedelic, depressant and mildly stimulant, partially cross-tolerant with alcohol, with low-dose effects like relaxation and appetite.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Cannabis use disorder is real; estimates suggest a meaningful minority of regular users develop it, and the risk is higher with daily use and early starting age. Cannabis withdrawal, with irritability and sleep problems, is recognized in DSM-5.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Members often know cannabis has medical uses. Acknowledging that honestly, while noting risks like psychosis in vulnerable people and dependence, keeps you credible.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The cross-tolerance with alcohol point helps explain a common pattern: men who quit drinking and smoke more weed, or vice versa. Ask who has seen this in themselves.

ask: How do changing marijuana laws shape your members' openness to this page?
Is it consistent to treat marijuana as a drug of concern when it is legal in many states?

terms.d: A recognized disorder where marijuana use becomes compulsive and causes harm.

67.title: Heavy marijuana and what it was for
67.gist: Notes that high doses of marijuana can cause LSD-like distortions, panic and paranoia, and that it is stored in fat and lingers for weeks; Exercise 23 asks about combining it with other drugs and what effect members wanted.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: High-potency cannabis has been linked in research, notably studies led by Marta Di Forti, to higher rates of psychosis, especially with daily use. Potency today is much higher than decades ago.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Fat-storage explains long detection windows in drug tests, which matters for supervision after release. It does not mean the person is still high weeks later; detection and impairment are different.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Clarify the difference between showing up on a test and being impaired. It is a practical issue for members on probation and earns trust.

ask: What effect most members wanted from marijuana, and does that need differ from what they wanted from alcohol?
How does long detection time affect how probation-bound members think about use?

68.title: Depressants and dangerous combinations
68.gist: Opens Part 3 on depressants, opioids and sedative-hypnotics, which slow thought and breathing, and explains additive effects, one plus one equals two, versus potentiation, where combinations like beer and Valium hit much harder and raise overdose risk.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Combining opioids with benzodiazepines or alcohol is a well-established overdose risk; US regulators added boxed warnings to opioid and benzodiazepine labels about using them together.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Write 1+1=2 and 1+1=4 on the board. Ask members which combinations they think fall in each column. Then reveal that most depressant mixes belong in the second.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This is lifesaving information at reentry. Mention naloxone and where to get it locally, framing it as protection for friends as much as self.

ask: Why might people underestimate potentiation even after a near overdose?
How does this page connect to the reverse tolerance warning in Session 1?

terms.d: When two drugs together produce a greater effect than the sum of each alone.

69.title: Tallying depressant use and its purpose
69.gist: Exercise 25 asks members which depressants and how much they used in a typical week, and what effect they sought. It builds a concrete consumption picture and surfaces the needs behind it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing actual weekly amounts is a form of self-monitoring, which in behavior therapy can itself reduce use by making the invisible visible.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to guess low. Ask them to think of one specific week, then count day by day. Concrete recall usually produces higher, more honest numbers.

ask: Why might people seek a depressant effect: relief, sleep, numbness, or something else?
What would you do with this weekly estimate in a treatment plan?

70.title: Opioids: pain, pleasure, and fentanyl
70.gist: Explains that opioids slow pain signals and calm anxiety, warns that synthetic fentanyl is far stronger than heroin and often sold as heroin, and describes low- and high-dose effects, nodding, pinpoint pupils, constipation and lowered sex drive.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page says fentanyl is about a thousand times stronger than heroin. Standard pharmacology references put fentanyl at roughly 50 to 100 times stronger than morphine and more potent than heroin by a smaller factor; the thousand figure is closer to fentanyl analogues like carfentanil. The warning stands, the number is off.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page notes high doses stop emotional as well as physical pain. Social pain and physical pain share some brain circuitry, and opioid systems are involved in both, which helps explain why people with trauma and loss are drawn to opioids.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Fentanyl has transformed the street supply since this kind of text was written. Ask members whether they knew what was in what they bought. Most did not, which leads naturally into naloxone and test strips.

ask: What does opioids' relief of emotional pain imply for treating trauma in your population?
How should you correct an outdated fact in the manual without undermining the material?

terms.d: A powerful synthetic opioid, now common in the illicit supply and a leading driver of overdose deaths.

71.title: Opioid quiz and combination use
71.gist: Exercise 26 checks that opioids relieve pain and anxiety, bring a pleasure surge and cause constipation; Exercise 27 asks whether members used opioids and with what other drugs.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Combinations with benzodiazepines or alcohol are where many overdoses happen. When members say yes to mixing, link it back to potentiation from two pages earlier without lecturing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to estimate how many people they know who have died of overdose. Write the total for the group on the board, silently. Let it sit for a moment before moving on.

ask: How do you hold space for grief over overdose deaths without derailing the session?
Why might pleasure be listed alongside constipation in the same quiz, and what does that do?

72.title: Opioids for pain; withdrawal like flu
72.gist: Asks whether members took opioids for pain and got high, then describes opioid withdrawal as a severe flu lasting about a week, longer for methadone, and states it is safer than sedative withdrawal because it rarely causes seizures.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Opioid withdrawal is rarely directly fatal, but 'will not result in death' is too strong. Deaths from dehydration during unmanaged withdrawal have occurred in jails, and the biggest danger comes after: lost tolerance makes overdose much more likely if use resumes.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Methadone and buprenorphine are now recognized as highly effective long-term treatments, not only weaning tools; maintenance is associated with substantially lower overdose death rates.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members first got opioids by prescription. Hearing that is common reduces shame and opens talk about how dependence started without bad intentions.

ask: What should every member know about tolerance before release?
How might the 'just a flu' framing lead people to underestimate withdrawal-driven relapse?

terms.d: A partial opioid agonist used to treat opioid use disorder, easing cravings and withdrawal with lower overdose risk.

73.title: Sedatives, sleeping pills, and GHB
73.gist: Defines sedatives as calming drugs like Valium and Xanax and hypnotics as sleeping pills, notes alcohol is both, describes slowed reactions and fatal high doses, and explains GHB, once sold as a supplement, and its use with Rohypnol in drug-facilitated sexual assault.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Benzodiazepines, alcohol and GHB act on the brain's main calming system, GABA. That shared target explains their cross-tolerance, their dangerous combinations, and why their withdrawal can be lethal.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The date-rape part can land differently for members who are survivors, or who have been accused. Keep it factual, note consent cannot exist when someone is drugged, and watch for reactions.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Driving impairment is a concrete harm here. Sedatives slow reaction time in ways people do not feel, a gap between subjective and objective impairment shown in driving studies.

ask: Why might Xanax be particularly popular among people with untreated anxiety in reentry?
How do you open a conversation about consent and substances without putting anyone on trial?

terms.d: The brain's main calming neurotransmitter, targeted by alcohol, benzodiazepines and GHB.

74.title: Which sedatives, and for what
74.gist: A quiz shows sedative-hypnotics include alcohol, prescription sedatives and GHB; Exercise 30 asks which ones members used and whether for sleep, calm, or to get high. It clarifies that alcohol sits in the same family as pills.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating sleep, calming and getting high identifies function. Using to sleep or calm down signals an unmet need, insomnia or anxiety, that needs a sober solution or relapse risk stays high.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to rate their sleep now on a 1 to 10 scale. Poor sleep is a known relapse risk; mention one practical tool like a fixed wake time.

ask: Why does it matter that members see alcohol in the same category as Xanax?
How would you address insomnia for someone who used for years to sleep?

75.title: Intoxication, paradoxical rage, blackouts
75.gist: Describes sedative intoxication, impaired judgment, memory and coordination, and doing things one normally would not, notes some people become aggressive instead of calm, and explains blackouts and brownouts, as well as fatal breathing suppression in overdose.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Blackouts happen because alcohol disrupts the hippocampus from forming new memories; the person can act and talk normally but not record it. Aaron White's research has made this widely known.

deeper.label: Critique
