deeper.text: The page's mention of brain swelling as the cause of memory gaps is a simplification. Long-term heavy drinking can cause brain shrinkage and thiamine-related memory disorders like Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome; blackouts are usually about acute memory encoding failure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Paradoxical aggression is directly relevant to many members' charges. Asking 'what did others tell you happened?' respects the memory gap while still opening reflection.

ask: How do you work with someone who cannot remember the offense he was convicted of?
What makes alcohol uniquely tied to violence compared with other sedatives?

terms.d: Memory loss for events during intoxication, caused by the brain failing to store new memories.

76.title: Aggression, memory gaps, deadly withdrawal
76.gist: Exercise 32 asks whether alcohol ever made members aggressive or caused memory gaps; the text then introduces sedative-hypnotic withdrawal as the most dangerous kind, with tolerance and withdrawal severity depending on dose and duration.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The GABA system adapts to constant sedation by becoming less responsive and boosting excitatory signals. Remove the drug and the brain is left over-excited, which is why seizures can occur.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members assume heroin withdrawal is worst because it looks worst. Correcting that matters at reentry: stopping heavy drinking or benzos abruptly without medical help can be deadly.

ask: Why does the most dangerous withdrawal often come from the most socially accepted drug?
How would you respond to a member planning to quit drinking cold turkey after release?

77.title: Stages of sedative withdrawal
77.gist: Describes sedative withdrawal in stages: early stimulant-like symptoms such as racing heart, sweating, tremors and insomnia one to four days after last use, then possible delirium, seizures and death without medication, and later bursts of anxiety and craving.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Severe alcohol withdrawal can include delirium tremens, a medical emergency. Medically supervised detox, usually with benzodiazepines on a taper, is the standard of care.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Prolonged withdrawal, with anxiety and craving bursts months later, is sometimes called post-acute withdrawal. The evidence base for its exact course is thinner than for acute withdrawal, but the experience is widely reported.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members list one person or place they would call if withdrawal symptoms started after release. A written plan is more likely to be used than a good intention.

ask: What practical barriers stop people leaving custody from reaching medical detox?
How might late withdrawal bursts be misread as proof that recovery is not working?

terms.d: A severe, potentially fatal alcohol withdrawal state with confusion, shaking, hallucinations and unstable vital signs.

78.title: Personal sedative withdrawal history
78.gist: Exercise 34 asks whether members have gone through withdrawal from sedative-hypnotics like alcohol and whether they used other drugs during it. It surfaces self-medication and switching under withdrawal.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members who detoxed alone in jail cells may carry fear or trauma from it. A simple acknowledgment that it should not have happened that way can build trust.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Using other drugs during withdrawal is street-level cross-tolerance from Session 1: people learn by experience which drugs ease which sickness. Naming that link shows their experience fits a model.

ask: How do past detox experiences shape someone's willingness to try quitting again?
What would trauma-informed withdrawal care look like in a jail?

79.title: Brain scans: ecstasy and serotonin
79.gist: Opens Part 4 on drugs and the brain and describes a scan comparing a drug-free brain with that of someone who used ecstasy several times and was clean three weeks, showing lower serotonin activity, the chemical tied to mood, memory, sleep and pain.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Ecstasy neurotoxicity research has been contested. One influential study on primates was retracted after a drug mix-up, and human findings are mixed; heavy repeated use likely affects serotonin systems, but dramatic claims from a few users are less certain.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Brain images are persuasive, sometimes more than they deserve. Psychology research has found that adding brain pictures can make explanations seem more convincing even when they add little.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the scans as a hopeful frame too: brains change with use, and they also change with abstinence. Plasticity works in both directions.

ask: Why might a brain image persuade members more than a verbal explanation?
What is the ethical line between motivating with scary images and misleading?

terms.d: The brain's ability to change its structure and function in response to experience, including recovery.

80.title: Damage that fades slowly with abstinence
80.gist: Shows the ecstasy scan and says repeated use is tied to sleep, mood, anxiety, memory and attention problems that may last up to two years, with brain function likely recovering over time but more use meaning more risk of lasting damage.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page's real message is about time horizons. If the brain needs months to recover, then the first weeks of sobriety are the worst sample of what sober life feels like. Judging recovery by week two is like judging a healed bone in its cast.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: It is hard to separate drug effects from pre-existing differences: people who use heavily may have had more mood or attention problems beforehand. Longitudinal studies help, but cause and effect remain partly uncertain.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write a note from themselves at six months clean to themselves at two weeks clean. What would future-self want present-self to know?

ask: How does the 'recovery takes long' message encourage some members and discourage others?
What other explanation besides drug damage could account for the scan difference?

81.title: Cocaine and the slowly recovering brain
81.gist: Describes brain scans showing reduced activity in a cocaine user after ten days clean and partial improvement after one hundred days, indicating drug-related brain changes that last months beyond quitting.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Scans like these come from PET imaging research, much of it associated with Nora Volkow and colleagues, showing reduced brain metabolism and dopamine receptor availability in people with cocaine addiction, with partial recovery over months of abstinence.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Reduced frontal activity matters because the prefrontal cortex supports planning and impulse control. Early recovery thus asks people to use self-control with a brain whose self-control machinery is still healing; structure and support fill the gap.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reframe: this is why external structure, routines and people, matters so much early on. It is not weakness to lean on others; it is borrowing frontal lobes.

ask: What does reduced frontal activity imply about relying on willpower in early recovery?
How would you use this page with someone who feels he should already be fine after three months?

terms.d: The front part of the brain involved in planning, judgment and controlling impulses.

82.title: Cues light up the craving brain
82.gist: Compares scans of a recovering cocaine user watching a nature video versus a cocaine video; the drug video activated the amygdala, showing that cravings from drug images have a biological basis and that small cues like sounds or smells could spark relapse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is classical conditioning, from Pavlov: cues repeatedly paired with a drug come to trigger the body's anticipation on their own. Research led by Anna Rose Childress was influential in imaging these cue-driven limbic responses in cocaine users.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Proust's madeleine scene in literature captures cue-triggered memory: a taste summons an entire past. Drug cues work similarly, but they summon desire, not just memory.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This page is the perfect bridge into Session 3 on triggers. Ask members which sights, sounds or smells instantly take them back. Music is often the first answer.

ask: If cues are learned, can they be unlearned, and what would that take?
How does a prison environment shape which cues a member will meet first at release?

terms.d: A brain region involved in emotion and emotional memory, active during cue-triggered craving.
Learning in which a neutral cue paired repeatedly with something meaningful comes to trigger a response on its own.

83.title: Brains need time; Session 2 wrap-up
83.gist: Admits science does not fully understand drug-related brain changes but stresses they are unhealthy and can last, urging complete abstinence so the brain can heal; the summary recaps Session 2's survey of drug classes and brain effects.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that even a short relapse could seriously injure the brain is stronger than the evidence for most drugs. The more defensible point is that relapse can restart cravings and set back recovery, and after abstinence carries real overdose risk.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The honest admission that scientists do not yet understand everything is a good model for members: uncertainty is not a reason to dismiss risk, nor to exaggerate it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close by asking each member which drug fact surprised him most this session. It turns a dense lecture into a personal takeaway.

ask: Is it ever justified to overstate risk in treatment to motivate abstinence?
How does the abstinence frame here fit with harm reduction for members who will not quit everything?

84.title: Role-play: two partners running out
84.gist: A role-play where Michael and Julie argue as their painkiller supply runs low, blaming and accusing each other, minimizing use, and Julie vowing it is the last time. It shows denial, craving-driven thinking and conflict in a using couple.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Their fight about fairness is really a fight about scarcity driven by craving. Scarcity research by Mullainathan and Shafir suggests scarcity narrows attention and crowds out other thinking, a frame that fits how craving takes over a relationship.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the group to call out each defense mechanism as it appears: minimizing, blaming, rationalizing. Then ask which of them each member uses most.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have the actors replay the scene where Julie means it this time. What would she actually do differently in the next hour?

ask: Why is 'this is the last time' so common and so rarely true?
How might painkillers that began as prescriptions shape these characters' sense of whether they have a real problem?

85.title: Session 3 opens: triggers and relapse
85.gist: Introduces Session 3 on triggers, cravings and relapse, with three parts: what triggers are, how a trigger leads to relapse in four steps, and how to stop that chain. It moves from education to practical relapse prevention.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Relapse prevention as a field owes much to Marlatt and Gordon's 1985 model, which treats relapse as a process with identifiable high-risk situations and coping choices, not a sudden moral failure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Frame this session as practical skill-building, not more confession. Members often perk up when they hear they will leave with tools.

ask: What changes for a member when relapse is seen as a chain of steps rather than one event?
Why might trigger work be more urgent for people about to be released than for those mid-sentence?

terms.d: A person, place, thing, feeling or situation linked to past use that can spark craving.

86.title: Why talk about craving at all
86.gist: Lists objectives for defusing triggers and interrupting drug thoughts, asks members to examine the people, places, feelings and things tied to use, and explains why the program discusses cravings despite fear that talking about them could provoke use.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Thought suppression research by Daniel Wegner showed that trying not to think about something can make it more intrusive, the famous white bear effect. Avoiding all craving talk may backfire; learning to handle the thoughts works better.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page treats drug thoughts and dreams as a normal part of recovery. Normalizing reduces the alarm, so a thought is just a thought rather than a sign of failure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If a member gets visibly triggered during this session, use it live: pause, name it, and walk through what he is noticing. That is the session's skill happening in real time.

ask: When might talking about drugs in group genuinely be harmful, and how would you tell?
What is the difference between normalizing cravings and treating them lightly?

terms.d: Trying to push a thought away, which often makes it come back stronger.

87.title: Mapping where and when you used
87.gist: Argues that understanding relapse helps prevent it, then Exercise 1 gives a long checklist of times, places, moods and situations, from payday and ATMs to dates, sex and holidays, for members to mark where they frequently used.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a functional analysis of use: identifying the antecedents that reliably precede it. Behavior therapists use this to target the highest-risk situations first.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The money-related items, payday, ATMs, check-cashing, are especially potent cues for many members. Point them out; managing cash at release is a concrete, plannable step.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After checking items, have members star the three most powerful. Those three become the backbone of their relapse prevention plan.

ask: Why might money be one of the strongest triggers of all?
Which items on this list would be hardest to avoid in a member's actual reentry neighborhood?

88.title: Using contexts versus sober ones
88.gist: Asks members to list other places and times they used, people they almost always used with, and, importantly, places, activities and people tied to not using. It maps both risk and protection.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The last two questions shift from risk to protective factors. Strengths-based approaches and the Good Lives Model argue recovery is built on what to move toward, not only what to avoid.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Spend more time on the sober lists than the using lists. Members often struggle to fill them, which itself is important information for planning.

ask: What does it mean if a member cannot name anyone he never used with?
How could you turn the sober list into a concrete reentry plan?

terms.d: Something in a person's life that lowers the chance of a problem, like a sober friend or stable job.

89.title: Associations: coffee, news, cigarette
89.gist: Explains that everyone who uses connects people, places and things with use, illustrated by the coffee, morning news and cigarette routine, where any part can trigger the urge; Exercise 2 asks members for their own examples.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Habit research, such as Wendy Wood's work, suggests much behavior runs on context cues rather than intentions. Changing the context, a new route, new morning ritual, can be more powerful than resolve.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members pick one daily routine they will have after release and redesign it so the old chain is broken: different time, place, or first action.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The cigarette example is safe and familiar. Start there, then ask for drug examples; momentum from the easy case helps.

ask: Why might routines in prison actually protect against some triggers but set people up for others at release?
How do you break a chain when you cannot avoid the cue, like the morning itself?

90.title: Internal, external, and sensory triggers
90.gist: Defines three trigger types that usually combine: internal feelings like insecurity, anger or boredom; external people, places, days and things; and sensory cues like music, lights, or powdered sugar resembling drugs. It gives members a vocabulary to sort their own cues.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Internal triggers are often the most dangerous because they travel with you. You can leave a bar, but not your loneliness. Marlatt and Gordon's research found negative emotional states were among the most common precipitants of relapse.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Boredom deserves special attention. Psychologists studying boredom describe it as a signal that current activity lacks meaning, which links triggers to purpose and later sessions on spirituality and balance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Sensory triggers can be surprising and even funny, like sugar or a bank's fluorescent light. Light humor here lowers defenses and makes it easier for members to admit odd triggers.

ask: Why might internal triggers be underreported compared with external ones?
How could a counselor accidentally become a trigger, through tone, a phrase, or topic?

terms.d: A feeling or mental state, like boredom or anger, that has become linked with using.

91.title: Naming personal triggers by type
91.gist: Exercise 3 asks members to name and describe their own internal, external and sensory triggers. It turns the three categories into a personal inventory for relapse planning.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often list external triggers easily and stall on internal ones. Prompt with: what were you feeling right before the last time you used? Most can answer that.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rate each trigger from 1 to 10 for strength. A ranked list is more useful for planning than an unranked one, and the top items deserve the most rehearsal.

ask: What is the risk of a trigger list that is too long to be useful?
How would you help a member who insists he has no triggers?

92.title: Four ways to deal with triggers
92.gist: Lays out four steps: identify triggers with help from others' feedback, avoid them where possible, interrupt the unavoidable ones like weekends with planned healthy activities, and talk about them so cravings do not build in secret.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Planning specific 'if this, then that' responses ahead of time, what Peter Gollwitzer calls implementation intentions, has been shown across many studies to make follow-through more likely than general goals.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Talking about cravings works partly through affect labeling: research by Matthew Lieberman and colleagues suggests putting feelings into words can dampen emotional reactivity.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Avoidance is a strong early tool but has limits. Many members return to the same neighborhoods and families, where avoidance is impossible; long-term recovery needs coping in the presence of triggers, not only distance.

ask: Which of the four steps do you think your members underuse most, and why?
How do you balance avoidance advice with the reality of returning to the same block?

terms.d: A specific plan in the form 'if X happens, I will do Y,' which makes action more automatic.

93.title: Planning against your strongest triggers
93.gist: Exercise 4 asks members to name their two strongest triggers and ways to avoid them, ways to interrupt unavoidable triggers, and ways to reduce triggers' power. It moves from inventory to action plan.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for specifics. 'Stay busy' is not a plan; 'Friday at 7 I go to the meeting at the church on my street with my brother' is. Ask who, what, when and where.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pair members to role-play one plan: one plays the trigger, like an old friend inviting them out, the other practices the response. Thirty seconds each, then switch.

ask: What makes a relapse plan feel real to someone versus just a worksheet?
How might the plan need to change between the first week out and the third month?

94.title: Four steps from trigger to use
94.gist: Explains that long-term users have especially strong trigger links and lays out a four-step chain, trigger, thought, craving, use, illustrated by Darlene, who meets her old dealer after cashing a check and ends up smoking crack at his house.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Darlene's decision to go to the dealer's house to get concert tickets is what Marlatt called a seemingly irrelevant decision: a small choice that looks innocent but steers straight toward a high-risk situation.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The chain shows why craving is not the starting point. By the time the body reacts, attention has narrowed. Neuroscience of craving suggests early interruption, before arousal builds, is far easier.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to tell their last relapse as a four-step chain. Most can, and seeing their own story fit the model is powerful and less shaming.

ask: Where on Darlene's chain would you intervene first, and why there?
How would the model need to change for someone whose main trigger is internal, like depression?

terms.d: A small, harmless-looking choice that gradually leads toward a high-risk situation for relapse.

95.title: Analyzing Darlene's triggers
95.gist: Exercise 5 asks members to identify Darlene's three main triggers, which she could have avoided, and how she might have interrupted those she could not. It practices trigger analysis on a safe, outside example.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Analyzing someone else first is easier than analyzing oneself, a pattern explained partly by the actor-observer asymmetry: we see others' situations more clearly than our own.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expected answers: the check-cashing store and cash, the old dealer, the concert memory and flirtation. Accept others, then ask which of Darlene's triggers they share.

ask: Why do people see others' relapse risks more clearly than their own?
What does Darlene's case suggest about handling money on release day?

96.title: Was Darlene thinking clearly?
96.gist: Asks members to imagine Darlene's thoughts as she approached her dealer and whether, nervous with sweaty palms, she could really think clearly about going for concert tickets. It highlights how craving distorts reasoning.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: George Loewenstein's idea of the hot-cold empathy gap fits: in a calm state, people underestimate how strongly a craving will sway them later. Darlene, calm earlier, likely never pictured herself at his door.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write the thought Darlene told herself, then a counter-thought she could have used. This is a mini cognitive restructuring exercise, the CBT core.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The concert tickets story is the cover story. Ask members what cover stories they used. The answers usually bring laughter of recognition.

ask: If people cannot think clearly once craving starts, what must happen before it starts?
How does the empathy gap affect how members plan for release while still in custody?

terms.d: The tendency, when calm, to underestimate how much strong states like craving will change our choices.

97.title: Defusing a trigger at step one
97.gist: Notes that most people wait until craving starts before acting, when it is hardest, and teaches defusing triggers early: avoid or immediately leave high-risk situations, and change routines around unavoidable ones like payday with planned, shared activities.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is stimulus control, a classic behavioral technique: change the environment so the behavior has fewer chances to start. It is often more effective than trying to resist an urge once it begins.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Leaving immediately assumes freedom of movement. Members on supervision, in shared housing, or depending on family who use may not easily leave. Plans need options that work when exit is not possible.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Keeping using friends and paraphernalia is the page's warning. Ask members what they still have or know of: a number in a phone, a stash spot. Planning to cut those is concrete work.

ask: Why do people keep paraphernalia or phone numbers even when they plan to quit?
What would stimulus control look like in a halfway house shared with active users?

terms.d: Changing your surroundings or routines to reduce exposure to cues that prompt a behavior.

98.title: Three ways to stop a drug thought
98.gist: Teaches interrupting step two, the thought, before it becomes craving, using a mental light switch image, snapping a wrist rubber band while saying no, and relaxation such as progressive muscle release, yoga or meditation. Members are urged to find the technique that fits them.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thought stopping and rubber-band snapping are older techniques with weak evidence, and suppression research suggests pushing thoughts away can make them rebound. Newer approaches favor noticing and riding out urges, as in Bowen and Marlatt's mindfulness-based relapse prevention and its urge-surfing practice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The muscle tensing and releasing described here is progressive muscle relaxation, developed by Edmund Jacobson. It works on the body side of craving, the sweaty palms and racing heart, rather than arguing with the thought.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Offer the switch as a cue to redirect, not a demand to erase the thought. Pair it with an action, as the page suggests: stand up, walk, shower. Changing the body often changes the mind faster.

ask: When is distraction helpful, and when does it just postpone a craving?
How would you explain urge-surfing to a member who wants the thought gone, not watched?

terms.d: Noticing a craving as a wave that rises, peaks and passes, without acting on it or fighting it.

99.title: Case study: Joe walks into a party
99.gist: Exercise 6 presents Joe, newly sober, who goes to a friend's party unaware of his nerves and meets familiar faces, loud music, low lights and pot smoke until his heart races. Members name his triggers and why he missed them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Joe did not notice his nervousness because he was busy. Low interoceptive awareness, poor reading of one's own body signals, makes internal triggers invisible until they are strong. Mindfulness practice aims partly to sharpen this awareness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Joe's case mixes all three trigger types: internal nerves, external friends and party, sensory music, lights and smell. Ask members to sort them aloud; it reviews the whole session in two minutes.

ask: Why is 'a friend I hadn't seen in a while' such a common gateway back to use?
What does Joe's busyness suggest about the risk of an overloaded first month out?

terms.d: Sensing the body's internal state, like heartbeat, tension or hunger.

100.title: Advising Joe; Session 3 wrap-up
100.gist: Asks what members would tell Joe to do at the party and how he could have prevented the situation, then summarizes Session 3: trigger types, the identify-avoid-interrupt-talk steps, the four-step chain to relapse, and techniques to stop it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Giving Joe advice is a quiet MI move: people often argue themselves into change when they coach someone else. Afterward ask whether they would follow their own advice at that party.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write a three-line exit script for a party like Joe's: what they say, where they go, whom they call. Rehearse one aloud before closing.

ask: Is the best advice for Joe to leave, or to never have gone, and what does each require?
How would you measure whether members leave Session 3 with a usable plan rather than just knowledge?

101.title: Visualization: the craving switch
101.gist: A guided visualization for practicing the mental switch: picture a detailed switch or dial, notice that ON brings nervousness and drug thoughts, turn it OFF and feel calmer and in charge. Members are encouraged to practice once or twice daily.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Mental imagery activates many of the same brain systems as perception, and imagery-based rehearsal is used in sport psychology and some therapies. Evidence for imagery specifically reducing drug cravings is promising but limited.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Imagery is double-edged: drug cravings themselves are often vivid images, as Kavanagh's elaborated intrusion theory of desire proposes. Competing with a calming image fights fire with a different fire.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to describe their switch out loud after the exercise. Rich detail, a brass dial or a cell light switch, suggests they actually built the image; vague answers mean more practice is needed.

ask: Why might daily practice matter more than the switch image itself?
How could the switch metaphor mislead someone into expecting cravings to vanish on command?

terms.d: Deliberately creating detailed mental images to shape feelings and prepare for future actions.

102.title: Session 4 opens: planning sobriety
102.gist: Introduces Session 4 on planning for sobriety, with three parts: sobriety and relapse as processes and decisions, warning signs and the parts of a full recovery program, and a review of relapse decisions and triggers.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Treating relapse as a process with warning signs echoes Terence Gorski's relapse warning sign work and Marlatt's model, both of which shifted relapse from sudden failure to something that can be seen coming.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members near release, this session is the bridge into reentry planning. Tie objectives to real dates, places and people they will face in their first week out.

ask: Why might the program teach planning after triggers instead of before?
What would a full program of recovery need to include for someone leaving prison with no housing?

103.title: Addiction as many small steps
103.gist: Lists Part 3 objectives and what members will be asked to examine, then opens Part 1 by recalling the trigger work and stating that addiction is a process of many small steps and decisions, fast for some and slow for others, not a single event.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle argued character is built from repeated actions: we become what we habitually do. Addiction and recovery both fit that ancient idea, one small act at a time.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Seeing addiction as a series of decisions restores agency without blame. Each step was a choice under pressure, which means each future step is also a choice that can go the other way.

ask: Does describing addiction as a decision process sit uneasily with the chronic disease model of Session 1, or can both hold?
What counts as a decision when much of behavior runs on habit?

104.title: Sobriety and relapse are processes too
104.gist: Exercise 1 asks how addiction was a process for members and what small steps led there; the text then explains sobriety as many small decisions away from use, and relapse as a series of decisions toward it, so awareness of decisions is the core of planning.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This mirrors Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change: change moves through stages and often cycles, rather than flipping once. A single vow is a moment; sobriety is a path through stages.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members who swore they would never use again and did often carry heavy shame. The process frame lets them see the vow was not the problem; the missing small steps were.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw a staircase with members: the bottom steps toward use, the top steps toward sobriety. Ask for one tiny step up they can take today, inside the facility.

ask: Why might 'I'm never using again' actually make relapse more likely for some people?
How small can a recovery decision be and still matter?

terms.d: A model describing change as moving through precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance.

105.title: Your small steps, both directions
105.gist: Exercise 2 asks members to name little steps that could lead them to relapse and the small steps that could build their sobriety. It personalizes the process view and starts the actual plan.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologist Karl Weick's idea of small wins suggests concrete, modest successes build momentum and confidence better than grand goals. Bandura would add that each small success raises self-efficacy.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for the relapse steps first, then flip each one into its sobriety mirror: 'keeping his number' becomes 'deleting his number.' Paired lists are easy to remember.

ask: Which is easier for your members to list, steps toward relapse or toward sobriety, and what does that tell you?
How could you follow up after release to see whether these small steps were taken?

terms.d: Confidence in one's ability to carry out a specific action, a key predictor of behavior change.

106.title: Tracing the small steps toward the bar
106.gist: Exercise 3 asks members to script an invitation to use and then trace the quiet steps that walk a sober person back to an old bar. It makes the idea of relapse as a slow chain of minor choices concrete and personal.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon called these 'apparently irrelevant decisions': choices that look harmless alone but steadily move someone toward a high-risk situation. Spotting them early is cheaper than resisting a craving at the bar door.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Question 1 flips perspective: members play the tempter. Debrief by asking which lines were most persuasive and why, then name the same lines as the voice their own addiction uses on them. Laughter here is useful; it shows they know the script cold.

ask: If relapse is decided long before the first drink, where does personal responsibility actually sit in the chain?
What are the 'apparently irrelevant decisions' in a prison day, where bars and old friends are not available?

terms.d: A small choice that seems unrelated to using but brings a person closer to a risky situation.

107.title: Warning signs before the slip
107.gist: Part 2 opens by framing warning signs as signals that part of a recovery plan needs reinforcing, then starts a self-check list (fear of failure, policing others, isolation, tunnel vision). Members begin locating their own early-alarm patterns.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This checklist echoes Terence Gorski's relapse-prevention work, which treats relapse as a progression of attitude and behavior changes that unfold before any use. The point is to catch drift while choices are still easy.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Self-report checklists invite people to tick what looks socially acceptable. In a correctional setting, members may under-check to look 'safe' to staff, so the list works better as a talking tool than as a measure.

ask: Why might zealously judging other people's sobriety be a danger sign rather than a strength?
How would you tell the difference between tunnel vision and an accurate complaint about real injustice in the system?

terms.d: Fixating on one bad area of life until it feels like the whole picture, breeding helplessness.

108.title: Mood, body, and follow-through signals
108.gist: The checklist continues with signs rooted in mood and daily functioning: low mood, poor planning, fantasy escapes, hopelessness, friction with supports, anger, eating and sleep problems. It shows relapse risk often shows up in the body and routine first.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sleep loss and poor eating impair the prefrontal systems that support impulse control, which is one reason HALT (hungry, angry, lonely, tired) became a recovery slogan. Biology and willpower are not separate tracks.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to rank the signs by which shows up first for them. Most people discover a personal sequence, such as bad sleep, then irritability, then skipping a meeting. A known sequence becomes a personal early-warning system.

ask: Which of these signs could just as easily signal depression or trauma that needs separate treatment rather than more willpower?
Why might creating conflict with supporters feel justifying, and what need does that justification serve?

terms.d: Recovery acronym for hungry, angry, lonely, tired: states that lower defenses against cravings.

109.title: The masks relapse wears
109.gist: The final warning signs focus on attitude and honesty: skipping meetings, the 'I don't care' front, self-pity, thoughts of using, lying, and resentment. It names defenses that hide fear and pain behind toughness or blame.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The 'I don't care' front fits what attachment researchers call deactivating strategies: shutting down the need for others to avoid rejection. In prison culture, that armor is often adaptive, which is why dropping it feels so risky.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Self-pity and system-blaming will surface loudly here. Avoid arguing about whether the system is fair; often it isn't. Reframe: 'Even if that's true, what does dwelling on it do to your odds of staying clean?' That keeps you out of a debate and on their goal.

ask: When does anger at the system count as a relapse warning sign, and when is it a reasonable response that deserves validation?
Why does secretly wishing to use a 'secondary' drug count as a warning sign for the primary addiction?

110.title: Others can see what you can't
110.gist: This page argues relapse is a process others often notice first, which is why feedback and sponsorship matter, then asks members about getting a sponsor. It also flags drifting away from recovery activities as a major warning sign.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies of Twelve Step involvement generally find that active engagement, such as having a sponsor and doing service, predicts better outcomes than attendance alone, though people who choose to engage may already be more motivated.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologists describe a 'bias blind spot': we readily see distortions in others but not ourselves. Outside observers are a practical correction, much as scientists rely on peer review.

ask: For someone leaving prison with a fragile network, what could fill the sponsor role if Twelve Step groups don't fit them?
How can a member tell honest feedback from someone simply trying to control them?

terms.d: An experienced Twelve Step member who guides a newer member through the steps and in crises.

111.title: Secrets versus a full program
111.gist: The page contrasts addiction's habit of secrecy with recovery's need for honest communication, then begins Exercise 6, a checklist of components of a full recovery program. Members mark which parts will be hardest for them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Secrecy keeps shame private, and shame tends to drive hiding and use. Disclosure to safe people breaks that loop, which is why honesty is framed as foundation, not virtue.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In a correctional setting, full openness has real costs: disclosures can reach staff, courts, or other residents. Help members distinguish honesty with safe supports from oversharing in unsafe places.

ask: Is lying to oneself the same process as lying to others, or something different in how it works?
Which list items on this page are about avoiding things, and which are about building things? What does that balance suggest?

terms.d: Interrupting a craving thought on purpose, often with a word or image, and redirecting attention.

112.title: Building a recovery menu
112.gist: The checklist finishes with steps toward family, medical, spiritual, recreational, vocational and medication supports, then asks which components feel easiest. The broad list shows recovery as rebuilding a whole life, not only abstaining.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recovery capital, a concept from Granfield and Cloud, describes the personal, social, and community resources that sustain recovery. This list is essentially a recovery-capital inventory.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Medication-assisted treatment may draw scorn from members who see it as 'not really clean.' Name that belief openly and note that MAT for opioid use disorder is backed by strong evidence and endorsed by major health agencies.

ask: Why might 'easiest' items on a checklist be worth questioning too?
Which of these supports actually exist for a person released next month, and which only on paper?

terms.d: Using approved medications such as buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone alongside counseling.
The internal and external resources a person can draw on to start and sustain recovery.

113.title: Naming the hard parts and the gap
113.gist: The worksheet asks which recovery components are hardest and which haven't been started yet, and what it would take to begin. It turns a list into a personal gap analysis and a first action step.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The question 'what will it take?' is a motivational interviewing move: it invites change talk in the member's own words, which tends to predict follow-through better than advice given to them.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member pick one unstarted item and shrink it to a step doable within 48 hours, such as asking one named person to be a crisis contact. Small, specific, time-bound steps beat vague resolutions.

ask: What separates a component someone hasn't done yet from one they don't truly intend to do?
How might the hardest items reveal a member's core relapse risk better than any assessment tool?

terms.d: A client's own statements favoring change, such as desire, ability, reasons, need, or commitment.

114.title: Two brains: alarm versus planner
114.gist: Part 3 defines triggers as cues linked to past use, stronger the more severe the addiction, and introduces a simple lower-brain/higher-brain model. Exercise 7 then asks members to name their strongest triggers.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Triggers work through classical conditioning: cues repeatedly paired with a drug come to provoke craving on their own, like Pavlov's bell. That is why a street corner or a song can hit as hard as the drug's smell.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The two-part brain is a teaching simplification. Emotion and reasoning are deeply intertwined, and Antonio Damasio's work suggests decisions need emotional input to work at all. Use the model as a metaphor, not anatomy.

ask: If conditioning built the triggers, what would 'unlearning' them look like, and why does extinction often fail outside the clinic?
Which of a member's triggers might be internal states rather than people or places, and why are those harder to avoid?

terms.d: A cue linked to past use that sparks thoughts of using or cravings.
Learning in which a neutral cue paired with a reward starts producing a response by itself.

115.title: When reason becomes the lawyer
115.gist: Members describe triggers that led to use, then the text explains how the drive for the drug can overpower logic, which then invents excuses. It sets up relapse decisions as reasoning hijacked to serve craving.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Jonathan Haidt's image of the rider and the elephant fits: reasoning often acts as a press secretary justifying where the emotional elephant already wants to go. The reasons are real thoughts, but they come after the pull.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In CBT terms these are permission-giving beliefs, a concept Beck and colleagues used in their cognitive therapy of substance abuse. Catching the permission thought is a key intervention point.

ask: If the logical brain can be recruited to justify use, how can a person ever trust their own reasoning during a craving?
Where else in criminal thinking do you see after-the-fact justification working the same way?

terms.d: A thought that grants permission to use, like 'I deserve it' or 'just once won't matter.'

116.title: The fantasy of controlled use
116.gist: Exercise 8 asks for a relapse decision that once made sense, and Exercise 9 explores how time sober can erase memories of loss of control, feeding fantasies of controlled use. Members check familiar statements like being back in control.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologists describe 'fading affect bias': painful memories lose emotional sting faster than pleasant ones. That helps people heal but also lets the misery of addiction fade while the highs stay vivid.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Whether any formerly dependent person can return to moderate use is still debated; some studies find a minority can, especially with milder problems, but it is risky and hard to predict for those with severe dependence.

ask: How should a counselor respond honestly to a member who cites research that some people do return to moderate drinking?
What memory tools could keep the costs of past use as vivid as the pleasures?

terms.d: The tendency for negative emotions tied to memories to fade faster than positive ones.

117.title: Session 4 wrap-up: relapse as process
117.gist: Members explain why controlled-use statements are relapse decisions, then the summary recaps the session: relapse is a process, warning signs exist, and a full program can be planned. It frames the work as courage plus a planning skill.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close by having each member say one warning sign they own and one plan component they will start. Spoken commitments in front of peers tend to stick better than silent ones, and peers can later hold each other to them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Prochaska and DiClemente place planning in the preparation stage of change. Members in contemplation may resist making plans; meeting them where they are matters more than finishing the worksheet.

ask: Is framing relapse as a decision process empowering, or could it deepen shame for people who relapse?
How would you check, weeks later, whether this session's planning actually changed behavior?

118.title: Role-play: Annette's Friday detour
118.gist: A role-play follows a woman early in recovery who, on payday Friday, chooses a pharmacy in her old using neighborhood and meets an old friend offering drinks and a joint. The group identifies triggers and better choices.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The cheaper-pharmacy excuse is a textbook apparently irrelevant decision, wrapped in a caring errand. Payday, boredom, and her own 'I'm better now' stack several risks at once, showing how triggers compound.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Annette says no twice, so members may call it a success. Push further: the second pause was the danger moment. Ask what would happen on a worse day, and replay the scene with the member choosing the closer pharmacy.

ask: Why might her mother's warning make her more likely to go, not less?
What would a version of this scene look like for a man coming home from prison with gate money?

terms.d: Acting out a scene to rehearse responses; behavioral rehearsal builds skills better than discussion alone.

119.title: Session 5 opener: legal isn't safe
119.gist: Session 5 introduces alcohol and tobacco, arguing their legality hides real danger, and notes tobacco kills more people than other drugs combined. It challenges the common belief that legal means harmless.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Major public health agencies consistently rank tobacco as the leading cause of preventable death in the United States, and alcohol also ranks among the top preventable causes. Legal status reflects history and politics more than pharmacology.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Prohibition in the 1920s and the drug war's later choices show how a society decides which substances are criminal. Many members have been punished for drugs less lethal than the ones sold on the corner store shelf.

ask: What does it mean for your members' sense of fairness that legal drugs cause more deaths than many of the illegal ones they were convicted for?
Why do people perceive risk based on legality rather than evidence?

120.title: Session 5 roadmap: alcohol and tobacco
120.gist: This overview lists Part 1 goals on alcohol's effects, progression, health damage, pregnancy, and mixing with other drugs, and Part 2 goals on nicotine dependence and reasons for smoking. It previews a four-question self-assessment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many in a prison group see smoking as their last allowed comfort, and tobacco talk can feel like an attack. Signal early that the goal is understanding, not confiscating anything.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Including tobacco reflects growing evidence that treating nicotine alongside other substances does not harm, and may help, recovery from those substances.

ask: Why might quitting smoking during treatment have been discouraged historically, and what changed the thinking?
Which objectives here are knowledge goals, and which actually require personal reflection?

121.title: CAGE: four quick screening questions
121.gist: Part 1 begins with the CAGE questionnaire by John Ewing, covering cutting down, annoyance at criticism, guilt, and morning eye-openers. Members answer the first questions and read plain explanations of what each asks.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: CAGE is brief and widely used, but it targets lifetime dependence and misses risky or binge drinking, and works less well in some groups. Tools like the AUDIT are often preferred today for broader screening.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In custody, members may answer to protect themselves. A screener is only as good as the honesty it meets, so frame it as private information for their own use.

ask: Why might asking about feeling a need to cut down be more revealing than asking whether someone tried?
What would a screening tool built for incarcerated adults need that CAGE lacks?

terms.d: Four-question alcohol screener: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener.
A brief test that flags who may need fuller assessment; it does not diagnose.

122.title: Scoring CAGE, then telling the story
122.gist: The last two CAGE items cover guilt and morning drinking, with a cutoff of two yes answers suggesting a likely problem. Exercise 2 then shifts from yes/no answers to concrete examples of cutting down.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The eye-opener item matters because a morning drink to calm shakes points to physical dependence and withdrawal relief, a sign of more advanced drinking than social guilt alone.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Moving from a score to stories is where insight happens. Someone who scores one may still tell a story that worries them; let the story, not the number, lead the conversation.

ask: What is lost and gained when a complex life gets compressed into a cutoff score of two?
How is guilt about drinking different from shame, and which one is more useful for change?

terms.d: A morning drink to ease shakes or a hangover, often signaling withdrawal.

123.title: Putting faces on the CAGE answers
123.gist: Members give specific examples of complaints about their drinking, guilt, and what they felt before morning drinks. It turns abstract answers into memorable personal evidence.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking what someone felt before an eye-opener surfaces the function of drinking, like dread or shakes. Functional analysis, a staple of behavioral therapy, asks what a behavior does for a person, not just whether it happens.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write one complaint in the exact voice of the person who said it, then answer back as their sober self. The exercise shifts criticism from attack to information.

ask: Why do concrete episodes motivate change more than general admissions like 'I drank too much'?
Whose complaints do members dismiss most easily, and what does that reveal about power in their relationships?

terms.d: Mapping what comes before and after a behavior to learn what need it serves.

124.title: Alcohol as a sedative-hypnotic
124.gist: This page classifies alcohol as a sedative-hypnotic that calms and induces sleep, and warns that its confidence boost is misleading, especially for driving. Exercise 3 asks how members used alcohol for calm or anxiety relief.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Alcohol enhances GABA, the brain's main inhibitory signal, like benzodiazepines do. That shared action is why mixing alcohol with benzos or opioids can dangerously suppress breathing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Self-medication theory, associated with Edward Khantzian, suggests people gravitate to drugs that relieve their particular pain, such as anxiety. Asking about anxiety relief opens that door.

ask: If alcohol truly relieves anxiety in the short run, what honest argument can you make against it to someone who is anxious every day?
Why does alcohol make people overestimate their abilities at the very moment they are impaired?

terms.d: A drug class that calms and causes sleep, including alcohol, benzodiazepines, and barbiturates.
The brain's main calming chemical messenger, boosted by alcohol.

125.title: False confidence and regret
125.gist: Members recall times they felt competent while drinking but were told otherwise, and things said or done while drinking that they regret. It links alcohol's effects to real-world consequences in their own lives.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Alcohol myopia theory, from Steele and Josephs, holds that alcohol narrows attention to the most immediate cues, so long-term consequences drop out of view. That explains much drunken regret.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Regret questions can touch offenses, including violence. Set ground rules about what to share given confidentiality limits, so members can reflect without self-incriminating.

ask: How might alcohol myopia help explain the link between drinking and many crimes members were involved in?
When does regret drive change, and when does it just feed the next drink?

terms.d: Narrowed attention under alcohol, which magnifies immediate cues and hides consequences.

126.title: Why alcoholism sneaks up slowly
126.gist: This page defines addiction as a progressive process and notes alcohol dependence usually develops more slowly than cocaine or heroin addiction, often unnoticed. It introduces four overlapping stages that may span two to twenty years.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Speed of delivery shapes addiction risk: smoking or injecting reaches the brain within seconds, tightly linking act and reward. Alcohol's slower rise means weaker conditioning per drink but a long, quiet buildup.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Progression is common but not universal. Large population surveys find many people with alcohol problems improve, some without treatment, so 'always gets worse' is an oversimplification.

ask: What does a slow progression mean for the role of family and friends as early detectors?
If many people recover without treatment, what does that imply about what treatment adds?

terms.d: Tending to worsen over time if not treated.

127.title: Four stages from tolerance to binges
127.gist: The stages run from tolerance to memory lapses, loss of control with mixing drugs, and prolonged binges in late-stage alcoholism. Exercise 4 begins by asking whether members needed more alcohol for the same effect.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This sequence echoes E. M. Jellinek's mid-twentieth-century phases of alcoholism, which also moved from tolerance through blackouts and loss of control to chronic binges. His model shaped the disease concept still used today.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Jellinek's phases were built largely on surveys of AA members, a select group. Later research found much more variety in how drinking problems develop, so stages describe a pattern, not a rule.

ask: Why might tolerance be misread as a sign of strength, as in 'I can hold my liquor'?
How does a stage model help or hurt someone who doesn't see themselves in stage four?

terms.d: Needing more of a drug to get the same effect.
A partial memory gap about events during drinking.

128.title: Blackouts and binges, personally
128.gist: Members answer whether they've had blackouts and binges, how they felt on realizing a blackout, and how long binges lasted. It brings the stage model down to lived experience.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A blackout is not passing out: the person stays awake and active but the brain stops forming new memories, as alcohol disrupts the hippocampus. Someone may drive or fight and recall nothing.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Blackout stories can include discovering what one did from others or from court records. Expect shame, and validate how frightening it is to not know one's own actions.

ask: What ethical and legal questions arise when someone cannot remember an act they committed during a blackout?
Why might the feelings after discovering a blackout be a strong motivation lever?

terms.d: A gap in memory while drinking, when the brain fails to record events despite being awake.

129.title: What heavy drinking does to the body
129.gist: This page lists alcohol-related disorders: cancers of mouth, throat and liver, fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis, nerve damage from vitamin B1 shortage, heart disease, and digestive damage. It dismantles the idea of alcohol as a weak drug.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Major health bodies classify alcohol as a known human carcinogen, and risk rises with dose; for some cancers, risk appears to rise even at moderate intake. Combined with tobacco, risks for mouth and throat cancers multiply.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Wernicke encephalopathy is a medical emergency from thiamine deficiency; untreated it can become Korsakoff syndrome, with lasting memory loss and confabulation. Early thiamine can prevent much of this.

ask: Why does health information alone rarely change drinking, and what makes it land when it does?
How might undiagnosed alcohol-related brain damage be mistaken for resistance or dishonesty in a group?

terms.d: Scarring of the liver that replaces healthy tissue and can cause liver failure.
Vitamin B1; heavy drinkers often lack it, risking brain damage.

130.title: Alcohol damage close to home
130.gist: Exercise 5 asks whether members ever saw alcohol as body-damaging and whether family members suffered alcohol-related illness. It links health facts to people they love.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Family history matters both ways: twin and adoption studies suggest genes account for a substantial share of alcohol-use-disorder risk, while growing up around heavy drinking shapes habits and beliefs too.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A relative's death from drinking may be a grief point. If someone goes quiet, slow down and acknowledge the loss before returning to the lesson.

ask: Why might watching a relative's decline make some people more cautious and others more fatalistic?
How would you talk about genetic risk without making it sound like destiny?

131.title: The indirect harms: poison, hunger, chemistry
131.gist: This page explains indirect alcohol damage: toxic breakdown products, empty calories that crowd out nutrition, and disrupted blood sugar and fats. A quick check question consolidates that alcohol harms nearly every system.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The liver converts alcohol to acetaldehyde, a toxic and cancer-linked compound, before breaking it down further. Heavy drinking keeps tissue bathed in it, which helps explain liver and throat damage.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Multiple-choice items with an 'all of the above' answer are easy to game. Use it as a launch: ask which harm surprised members most and which they had already felt in their own bodies.

ask: Why might hypoglycemia symptoms in a drinker be mistaken for intoxication or a psychiatric problem?
What does the empty-calories idea suggest about nutrition support in early recovery?

terms.d: A chemical produced when the body breaks a substance down.
Dangerously low blood sugar, causing weakness, confusion, and in severe cases coma.

132.title: Alcohol and the unborn child
132.gist: The page explains how drinking in pregnancy raises miscarriage risk and can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, stressing the vulnerable early weeks when many don't know they're pregnant. Exercise 7 checks understanding of the possible outcomes.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Health authorities state no amount of alcohol in pregnancy is known to be safe. FASD is a spectrum: many affected people have no distinctive facial features but live with learning, attention, and impulse-control problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: FASD is thought to be overrepresented in justice-involved populations, often undiagnosed. Some members may carry it themselves, which changes how instructions, memory, and consequences land.

ask: How might undiagnosed FASD in a group member be misread as defiance or criminal thinking?
How can this content be taught to men without making it feel like it's only women's responsibility?

terms.d: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: lifelong physical, learning, and behavioral effects of prenatal alcohol exposure.

133.title: Alcohol as the gateway back
133.gist: After a FASD check item, the page explains how many people use alcohol alongside or instead of their main drug, with unnoticed tolerance, and urges abstinence from all mood-altering substances. Alcohol is cast as a trigger that loosens judgment.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on whether people treated for drug problems can safely drink is mixed; some do, but drinking is often associated with higher relapse risk to the primary drug. The cautious recommendation reflects that risk.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Total abstinence is a strong goal but not the only one; harm reduction approaches accept stepwise change. For members who reject full abstinence, a rigid stance can end the conversation rather than reduce harm.

ask: Is 'California sober' a reasonable compromise or a relapse decision in disguise? What evidence would settle it?
Why might alcohol's legality make it the most likely first slip for someone leaving prison?

terms.d: Developing a problem with a new substance after stopping another, often from a shared reward pathway.

134.title: How drinking and drugs got linked
134.gist: Exercise 9 asks members how drinking got tied to their other drug use and how drinking might sway decisions to use. It personalizes the trigger link from the previous page.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pairing drugs, such as alcohol with cocaine, builds a combined cue: drinking itself then calls up the other drug. Alcohol plus cocaine also forms cocaethylene in the liver, a compound linked to added heart strain.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw a two-column chain: a typical night's first drink on the left, the moment they picked up the other drug on the right, and every step between. The gap usually shrinks with honesty.

ask: If alcohol both triggers cravings and lowers resistance, which effect would you target first in a relapse plan?
How do social settings, not just chemistry, bundle alcohol with other drugs?

terms.d: A compound formed when alcohol and cocaine are used together, more toxic to the heart.

135.title: Nicotine: the world's quiet drug
135.gist: Part 2 establishes nicotine as a drug acting on the autonomic and central nervous systems, both alerting and calming, and notes its harms emerge slowly. Its slow damage makes it seem manageable when it isn't.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Nicotine stimulates acetylcholine receptors and triggers dopamine release; inhaled, it reaches the brain within seconds. That speed and many daily doses make it a powerful conditioning machine.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The calming effect smokers feel is partly relief from mild withdrawal between cigarettes, a pattern sometimes called the deprivation reversal model. The cigarette often fixes the stress it created.

ask: If a smoker's calm is largely withdrawal relief, how would you explain that without sounding like you're dismissing their experience?
Why do delayed harms shape behavior so weakly compared with immediate rewards?

terms.d: The automatic control system for heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, and sweating.

136.title: Smoking as everyone's background habit
136.gist: Exercise 10 asks how widespread smoking makes quitting harder, how smoking might affect other addictions given high rates among alcoholics, and whether smoking triggers drug cravings. It frames tobacco as part of the recovery picture.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies suggest smoking cessation during addiction treatment is associated with better, not worse, abstinence from other substances, contrary to the old fear that quitting everything at once overwhelms people.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In facilities where tobacco is banned or traded as currency, smoking carries economic and social meaning. Ask what it means inside versus outside, and how release will change access.

ask: Why do smoking rates remain high among people with addictions and mental illness while dropping in the general public?
How would you test whether cigarettes cue cravings for a specific member's drug of choice?

137.title: Nicotine withdrawal you can name
137.gist: The page explains nicotine tolerance builds slowly but physical dependence comes fast, with withdrawal starting within a day or two and fading over weeks. Exercise 11's checklist reveals that common moods between cigarettes are withdrawal signs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Labeling irritability or restlessness as withdrawal rather than personality changes the story a smoker tells: the anger is chemistry and temporary, not a sign that something is wrong with them.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Nicotine replacement, varenicline, and bupropion each improve quit rates over placebo, and combining medication with counseling tends to work best.

ask: How might nicotine withdrawal be confused with anger problems or depression in a group setting?
What does a withdrawal checklist teach about how all addictions shape mood between doses?

terms.d: The body's adaptation to a drug so that stopping produces withdrawal.
Patches, gum, or lozenges that deliver nicotine without smoke to ease quitting.

138.title: The leading preventable killer
138.gist: This page makes the case that cigarettes are the top preventable cause of US deaths, citing the 2014 Surgeon General's report, and details lung cancer, emphysema, heart disease, artery damage, and stroke. It gives tobacco's slow harm a concrete face.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The 1964 Surgeon General's report was a turning point that officially tied smoking to lung cancer, after decades in which the tobacco industry funded doubt. That history is a lesson in how profit shapes what people believe is safe.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Big death counts can numb. Ask members to picture a full prison yard and multiply; or better, ask who they personally lost. Personal stories beat statistics for motivation.

ask: Why did it take so long for evidence of smoking's harm to change laws and behavior?
What parallels exist between tobacco industry tactics and how other drugs are marketed today?

terms.d: Lung damage that destroys air sacs, causing lasting shortness of breath.
Narrowed arteries in the limbs that reduce blood flow, sometimes leading to amputation.

139.title: Smoking's hidden costs, noticed
139.gist: The page adds pregnancy risks and harms like cataracts and impotence, then asks members what effects they've noticed and whom they know with smoking-related illness. It shifts from facts to personal observation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Impotence often lands harder with men than cancer statistics. Use it carefully and without mockery; it shows smoking threatens things people value now, not only in old age.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members list three things smoking costs them today: money, breath on stairs, smell, a trade in the unit. Present costs motivate more than future risks.

ask: Why do immediate, personal costs usually move people more than lethal but distant risks?
How could a counselor tell the difference between fear appeals that motivate and ones that make people shut down?

140.title: Why you smoke, part by part
140.gist: Exercise 13 opens a six-factor look at the reasons people smoke, starting with stimulation: does it wake you or keep you going. The idea is that any quit plan must address the specific reasons.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This mirrors the logic of functional analysis: if smoking serves stimulation, a replacement for energy is needed; if it serves calm, a different coping skill. One-size quit plans fail because they ignore function.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members guess their top factor before answering, then compare. Surprises are common, and they make the debrief richer than the scores.

ask: Could the same factor approach be applied to members' main drug of choice? What would it reveal?
What healthy activities could genuinely provide stimulation for someone in a correctional setting?

141.title: Replacing energy and busy hands
141.gist: Members brainstorm other ways to get energy, such as exercise, then consider how handling cigarettes satisfies them and what could occupy their hands instead. It treats smoking as a ritual of the body, not just a chemical.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Habit reversal training teaches people to swap a competing response for an unwanted behavior. A stress ball or pen works because the hands' ritual, repeated thousands of times, has become its own cue and reward.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members mime lighting and holding a cigarette in slow motion, noticing each movement. Making the automatic ritual conscious weakens its grip and shows which part they miss most.

ask: Why might a physical ritual outlast the chemical dependence it was built around?
What substitutes are realistic inside a facility, where many common options are restricted?

terms.d: A behavioral method that replaces an automatic habit with a deliberately chosen competing action.

142.title: Pleasure and its substitutes
142.gist: This section asks what pleasure smoking brings, whether it resembles other pleasures, and what harmless activities could provide pleasure instead. It treats pleasure seeking as legitimate while redirecting it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral activation and the community reinforcement approach both rest on the same insight: drugs are easier to give up when life holds competing rewards. Removing pleasure without replacing it invites relapse.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Epicurus argued the good life rests on simple, lasting pleasures such as friendship and calm, not intense ones that bring later pain. Members often recognize this wisdom once it's stated plainly.

ask: When members compare smoking pleasure to other pleasures, what does that suggest about what they're really seeking?
Why might people in early recovery struggle to feel pleasure at all, and how should a counselor prepare them?

terms.d: Reduced ability to feel pleasure, common in early recovery as the reward system rebalances.

143.title: Does smoking really calm you?
143.gist: Members identify stressful moments when they smoke, rate how well smoking actually reduces anxiety, and list healthier anxiety-reduction methods. The middle question quietly invites them to doubt a long-held belief.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies comparing smokers before and after quitting generally find anxiety and stress decrease over time after quitting, supporting the idea that smoking's calm is largely withdrawal relief.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking how effective smoking is, rather than telling them it isn't, is Socratic questioning. Let members argue both sides; the doubts they voice themselves carry more weight than yours.

ask: What would count as fair evidence, from a member's own life, that smoking does or doesn't reduce anxiety?
Which anxiety tools translate well from tobacco to other drugs in a relapse plan?

terms.d: Guided questions that help someone examine a belief and reach their own conclusion.

144.title: Mapping a tobacco craving
144.gist: This section asks members to describe their craving signs, what they normally do, and whether cravings return right after a cigarette. That last question hints at why cutting down is hard.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cravings that return soon after smoking reflect nicotine's short half-life, roughly a couple of hours, which drives frequent dosing. Each cigarette resets a short cycle of relief and craving.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach urge surfing, from Marlatt's mindfulness-based relapse prevention work: notice the craving as a wave, observe where it sits in the body, and ride it until it peaks and fades without acting on it.

ask: Why might cutting down actually intensify how much each remaining cigarette is valued?
What does the craving cycle of nicotine teach about cravings for longer-acting drugs?

terms.d: Observing a craving mindfully as a wave that rises and falls instead of acting on it.
Time for the body to clear half a dose of a drug.

145.title: When the cigarette is just habit
145.gist: Members list craving strategies, then ask whether smoking still satisfies or continues out of habit, and how to break automatic smoking. It distinguishes wanting from doing on autopilot.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Neuroscientists describe a shift with repetition from goal-directed action to habit, run more by the dorsal striatum, so behavior continues even when the reward has faded. This is why habits need changed cues, not just willpower.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Kent Berridge's incentive-salience theory separates 'wanting' from 'liking': drugs can increase wanting even as liking declines, which fits smokers who keep smoking without enjoying it.

ask: If a habit continues without satisfaction, what is actually being reinforced?
How could you redesign a member's daily routine so smoking cues simply stop appearing?

terms.d: The 'wanting' that makes drug cues grab attention, separate from actual enjoyment.

146.title: Quit smoking with everything else
146.gist: This page argues quitting smoking is part of recovery, citing research that quitting together with other drugs improves abstinence, and recommends relapse-prevention skills and medical help. The session summary recaps alcohol and tobacco learning.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Reviews of smoking cessation within addiction treatment suggest it does not harm, and may modestly help, outcomes for other substances. The effect is real but not dramatic, so present it honestly.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect the objection 'one thing at a time.' Acknowledge it, then reframe: cigarettes are cues for the main drug, so keeping them keeps a trigger in your pocket. Let members choose a timeline.

ask: Why did addiction programs long tolerate or even encourage smoking, and what does that reveal about clinical culture?
If skills transfer across addictions, which skill from this session is most universal?

147.title: Visualization: the mental off switch
147.gist: This handout guides a visualization of a detailed switch that turns tobacco cravings off, paired with a positive affirmation, building on Session 3's mental switch. Repeated practice makes it a quick tool usable anywhere.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Elaborated intrusion theory, from Kavanagh, Andrade and May, holds cravings are fueled by vivid mental imagery. Competing imagery can crowd out craving images, which supports why visualization may help; results vary across studies.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Positive affirmations can backfire for people with low self-esteem, research suggests, if the statement feels false. Invite members to write one that feels true to them rather than reciting the sample.

ask: Why would a vivid image fight a craving better than a firm decision not to smoke?
How could you adapt this switch for a member who finds closing their eyes in a group unsafe?

terms.d: Deliberately creating mental images to shape feelings and behavior.
A short positive statement repeated to build a helpful self-view.

148.title: Session 6 opener: spirituality in recovery
148.gist: Session 6 introduces spirituality, prayer, and a Higher Power, aiming to explore personal views, addiction's effect on spirituality, and many paths to it. It prepares members for a personal and potentially sensitive topic.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Carl Jung wrote to Bill W. that a craving for alcohol might mirror a spiritual thirst, a letter AA history often cites. The idea that addiction fills a gap of meaning runs through recovery culture.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Groups will include devout believers, atheists, and people hurt by religion. Announce early that no belief will be imposed, and treat disagreement as useful material.

ask: Is spirituality a mechanism of recovery, or a context that makes other mechanisms work?
How can a counselor present spirituality without crossing professional boundaries?

149.title: Spirituality isn't the same as religion
149.gist: The page clarifies members won't be asked to adopt beliefs, then argues addiction affects spiritual life and that spirituality concerns everyday living rather than religion. It notes Twelve Step groups center spirituality while other groups don't.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research links spiritual or religious involvement to better recovery outcomes in some studies, but effects vary and causation is hard to establish; meaning, community, and structure may account for part of it.

deeper.label: Critique
