deeper.text: Court-mandated Twelve Step attendance has been challenged in US courts on religious-freedom grounds, with several rulings finding mandates coercive. Offering secular choices like SMART Recovery respects that.

ask: How would you define spirituality so that an atheist member could still engage with it honestly?
What happens to the concept if 'spirituality' becomes so broad it means almost anything?

terms.d: A sense of connection to meaning, values, or something larger than oneself, with or without religion.

150.title: Defining your own spirituality
150.gist: Exercise 1 asks members what spirituality means to them, which spiritual goals they want in sobriety, and what spiritual qualities they admire in others. It lets each member define the concept in their own terms.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking about qualities admired in others is a values-clarification move, close to acceptance and commitment therapy's work on chosen values. Values guide behavior when feelings and cravings pull the other way.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some will answer only with religious language, others will leave it blank. Offer neutral prompts: what gives you peace, what you'd die for, who you're becoming.

ask: Do admired spiritual qualities like patience or humility tend to be the opposite of what addiction cultivated?
How would you measure spiritual growth without making it about church attendance?

terms.d: Identifying what matters most to a person so it can guide their choices.

151.title: Self-centeredness as a spiritual problem
151.gist: After asking about steps toward spiritual goals, the page frames self-centeredness as total self-reliance, the belief one can control use despite evidence. It notes this grows gradually, so spiritual recovery is gradual too.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This idea is the root of AA's First Step: admitting powerlessness undoes the illusion of total self-control. Philosophers would call it a paradox, since giving up control is presented as the way to gain it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: For people who have been controlled and powerless all their lives, including many incarcerated adults, being told to surrender can feel like more of the same. Empowerment-oriented framings may fit some members better.

ask: How do you reconcile 'self-reliance is the problem' with CBT's message that you can control your thoughts and choices?
Is self-centeredness in addiction a cause, a symptom, or both?

terms.d: Here, relying wholly on oneself and one's own control, beyond simple selfishness.

152.title: How using made you selfish
152.gist: Exercise 2 asks how members became selfish while using, how self-reliance alone can harm spiritually, and what they want to change about themselves. It moves from confession to a change target.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Addiction narrows priorities until securing the drug outranks people and duties, which the DSM captures as giving up important activities. Selfishness is partly what that narrowing looks like from outside.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Admitting selfishness can trigger shame spirals or tough-guy denial. Separate the person from the behavior: 'what did using make you into,' not 'what kind of person are you.'

ask: Is the selfishness of addiction a moral failure, a symptom, or both, and does the answer change how you treat it?
How does prison culture reward self-reliance, and what does that mean for this lesson?

153.title: Reaching beyond yourself to change
153.gist: Members consider obstacles to change and whether they tend to go it alone. The text explains that sober clarity reveals defects like arrogance and fear, and that change requires reaching outside oneself.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social support consistently predicts better recovery outcomes, and Project MATCH-era research by Longabaugh and colleagues found that having a network supportive of drinking hurt outcomes, while AA could help build a sober one.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Albert Bandura noted self-efficacy grows partly through others: watching peers succeed and hearing encouragement. Reaching outward is not weakness; it is how confidence is built.

ask: Is there a tension between asking for help and building self-efficacy, or do they reinforce each other?
Why might clear thinking in sobriety initially feel worse than being high?

154.title: Character defects and outside help
154.gist: The page lists many sources of spiritual help, from a person or group to God or a Higher Power, arguing reaching out matters more than where. Exercise 3 asks about one character defect and past reliance on outside help.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Twelve Step language calls flaws character defects, worked on in Steps 6 and 7. Psychology would frame many of the same patterns as learned coping strategies that once protected the person.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one defect and when it first helped them survive, such as distrust that kept them safe on the street. Seeing its old function makes it easier to retire.

ask: What is gained or lost by calling a pattern a 'defect' versus a 'survival strategy'?
Does it really not matter whom someone reaches out to? When might the source of help be harmful?

terms.d: Twelve Step term for a personality trait, like dishonesty or resentment, that harms recovery.

155.title: HOW: honesty, open-mindedness, willingness
155.gist: This page offers HOW as a practical spirituality: honesty about unmanageability and feelings, open-mindedness to new ideas, and willingness to do what recovery takes, including daily inventories. It makes an abstract topic concrete.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Open-mindedness echoes what psychologists call intellectual humility, the recognition that one's beliefs might be wrong. Research links it to better learning and less defensive reactions to disagreement.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: HOW suits CBI-style work too: honesty mirrors catching risky thoughts, open-mindedness mirrors trying new thinking, willingness mirrors practicing skills. Bridge the two curricula for members in both.

ask: Can someone be honest without being open-minded, and what does that look like in a group?
Is willingness something one chooses, or something that grows after small actions?

terms.d: A regular personal review of one's actions, strengths, and wrongs, as in Twelve Step Step 10.

156.title: Honesty's edge and willingness's reach
156.gist: Exercise 4 asks about a strong honesty experience, noting honesty can wound when misused, and about what willingness means and how far members will go. It contrasts willingness with willpower.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: 'Brutal honesty' can be aggression in disguise. Twelve Step Step 9 itself warns against amends that would harm others, a reminder that honesty needs judgment and care.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Willingness over willpower fits research questioning the idea of willpower as a limited fuel; the 'ego depletion' effect has largely failed to replicate. Structure and commitment matter more than raw grit.

ask: Where is the line between honest feedback and cruelty in a group of incarcerated men or women?
If willpower is unreliable, what actually carries someone through a hard moment?

terms.d: The contested theory that self-control draws on a limited resource that runs out.

157.title: Many roads: faith, forgiveness, service
157.gist: The page names many paths to spirituality, highlighting faith, forgiveness of self and others, and service and kindness. Exercise 5 asks which aspects matter most and how to make them central.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Helping others in recovery has been linked to better outcomes in studies by Maria Pagano and colleagues; service may protect sobriety partly by building purpose and connection.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Forgiveness research, such as Everett Worthington's work, separates deciding to forgive from emotional forgiveness, which takes longer. Self-forgiveness also differs from excusing oneself; it still owns the harm.

ask: How should self-forgiveness work for someone who seriously harmed a victim?
Is service to others possible in a prison unit, and what forms could it take?

terms.d: Releasing self-condemnation while still accepting responsibility for wrongdoing.

158.title: Choosing your own Higher Power
158.gist: Part 2 explains that because addiction overpowers, Twelve Step programs urge reliance on a self-defined Higher Power, which can be the group, community, nature, or God. Exercise 6 asks what the phrase means to members.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The phrase 'God as we understood Him' was added to the steps partly to welcome agnostics. Many nonbelievers use the acronym Group Of Drunks or simply the group's collective wisdom as their Higher Power.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members whose image of God is punishing, the advice that a Higher Power be loving matters. Explore what kind of power they picture; harsh images often mirror harsh caregivers.

ask: Does a Higher Power need to be real in a metaphysical sense to work psychologically?
What does a member's image of God reveal about their attachment history?

terms.d: A self-defined source of strength greater than oneself, used in Twelve Step recovery.

159.title: Comfort and discomfort with belief
159.gist: Members explore which parts of the Higher Power idea feel comfortable or uncomfortable and when in life they have wanted to believe. It gives permission for ambivalence.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking about both comfort and discomfort is a classic MI decisional-balance move. Ambivalence spoken aloud becomes workable; hidden ambivalence quietly drives dropout.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologists have found people often turn to faith in crisis, sometimes called religious coping. Ken Pargament distinguished positive coping, like seeking support, from negative, like feeling punished by God.

ask: Why might people want to believe most in times of crisis, and is that belief less valid?
How would you support a member whose wish to believe conflicts with their doubts?

terms.d: Using faith to handle stress, which can be helpful or harmful depending on its form.

160.title: Spiritual change usually comes slowly
160.gist: This page explains most spiritual experiences are gradual, often noticed by friends first, and can center on God, love, nature, or fellowship. Awareness of a Higher Power brings awareness of one's place among others.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience, described a slow 'educational variety' of spiritual change, a term AA's Big Book borrowed. Miller and C'de Baca later studied rare sudden 'quantum changes.'

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Much recovery happens gradually through accumulating small changes, which fits learning theory better than dramatic conversion. Waiting for a lightning bolt can be a way to delay acting.

ask: Why might friends notice spiritual growth before the person does?
Could expecting a dramatic spiritual awakening become a relapse risk if it never comes?

terms.d: A shift in awareness toward meaning and connection, sudden or, more often, gradual.

161.title: Belonging, love, and recovery
161.gist: Members reflect on whether awareness of a Higher Power has helped, how much community belonging matters, and what love has to do with recovery. It ties spirituality to connection with people.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Johann Hari popularized the line that the opposite of addiction is connection, drawing loosely on Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiments, where rats in rich social settings used less morphine. The studies are debated, but the theme resonates.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: 'Love' can make tough members squirm. Translate it into loyalty, respect, or who would visit them. Most will have a person in mind; start there.

ask: Can community harm recovery as well as help it, as with gangs or using circles?
What does it mean for recovery planning if belonging, not abstinence, is the deeper need?

terms.d: Bruce Alexander's experiments suggesting environment and social life shape drug use in rats.

162.title: Prayer and Step Eleven
162.gist: The page introduces prayer through Step Eleven, as contact with one's Higher Power alone or with others, and asks what this means to members. It stresses praying for guidance rather than for one's preferred outcomes.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Praying for guidance rather than outcomes shifts focus from controlling events to controlling one's response, which parallels acceptance in DBT and the Stoic split between what is and isn't in our power.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The gendered 'Him' and theistic language can alienate members; the text itself suggests swapping words. Meditation without belief may meet the same need for those who reject prayer.

ask: Is praying for knowledge of one's path psychologically different from praying for a result? How?
How might the instruction against praying for desired outcomes land with someone praying for their children or their case?

163.title: Do you pray, and why?
163.gist: Exercise 9 asks members whether and how they pray, why or why not, and whether prayer could help their recovery. It invites candor whatever the answer.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on prayer's direct healing effects, such as intercessory prayer trials, has been largely negative, but studies of personal prayer and meditation point to possible benefits for stress and coping.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Treat a 'no' as fully legitimate. Ask the nonbelievers what practice gives them a pause before acting; that answer is their version of this page.

ask: What psychological functions might prayer serve even for someone unsure anyone is listening?
How do you keep your own beliefs about prayer out of the facilitation?

164.title: Regular prayer, not only crisis
164.gist: Members consider why regular prayer is recommended over prayer only in trouble, then the summary recaps the session's exploration of spirituality, prayer, and a Higher Power. It frames spiritual practice as daily maintenance.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Practicing a skill when calm makes it available under stress, a principle shared by fire drills and stress inoculation training. A daily ritual builds the pathway a crisis will need.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Close with one minute of silence where each member chooses prayer, a breath count, or a memory of someone they love. Equal options keep the closing inclusive.

ask: Why do we tend to seek help only in crisis, in prayer and in counseling alike?
What daily practice could a skeptical member keep that does the same job as regular prayer?

165.title: Sample prayers, including Serenity
165.gist: This page offers a prayer for those unsure how to pray, focusing on love and freedom from anger and guilt, and the Serenity Prayer. It gives words to members who lack them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Serenity Prayer is generally credited to theologian Reinhold Niebuhr in the twentieth century, and AA adopted it in the 1940s. Its logic of sorting what can and can't be changed echoes Epictetus's Stoic teaching.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The Serenity Prayer works as a decision tool even for atheists: have members sort a current worry into 'accept' or 'change' columns. Inmates often find the 'accept' column painfully long; validate that.

ask: What does 'wisdom to know the difference' require in practice, and how do people get it?
Can acceptance become passivity in the face of real injustice?

terms.d: A short prayer asking for acceptance, courage, and wisdom; widely used in recovery.

166.title: The Prayer of St. Francis
166.gist: This page presents the Prayer of St. Francis, which asks to bring peace, love, and hope where their opposites exist, and to give rather than seek. It models a spirituality of service over self.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Despite its name, historians generally trace the prayer to early twentieth-century France, not to Francis of Assisi. Its spirit fits him, but the attribution shows how texts gather authority.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Seeking to understand before being understood reverses the self-centeredness the session described, and resembles the empathy at the heart of motivational interviewing.

ask: Is a prayer's value affected by learning it was not written by its namesake?
How might a prayer focused on giving help someone who has mostly taken from others?

168.title: Visualization: your spiritual future self
168.gist: This guided visualization contrasts the empty purpose of getting high with recovery's new meaning, asking members to picture their spiritual self now and as they want to become. It turns spiritual goals into a sense of purpose.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl, in Man's Search for Meaning, argued people can endure almost anything with a reason to live, drawn from his concentration camp experience. That message often reaches incarcerated people deeply.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Future-self research by Hal Hershfield suggests feeling connected to one's future self predicts more future-minded choices; vivid imagery of that self may strengthen the link.

ask: What makes a purpose meaningful enough to compete with the pull of a drug?
How would you guide this exercise for someone serving a long sentence with a distant release date?

terms.d: Frankl's therapy centered on finding meaning as the primary human drive.

169.title: Session 7 opener: sex and substances
169.gist: Session 7 introduces how substances affect sex, how sex can trigger use, and common sexual problems with tips for recovery. It signals a sensitive but recovery-relevant topic.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect jokes, bravado, and silence. Set norms up front: no sharing about others by name, no graphic detail, humor allowed but not at a member's expense. Trauma histories, including sexual abuse, are common in custody.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Sex and drugs both activate the brain's reward system, so pairing them creates strong conditioned links. Sex can become a cue for use, and use a precondition for sex.

ask: Why might sex be one of the least-discussed triggers in treatment despite being one of the strongest?
How do gender and prison culture shape what members will say about sex in a mixed or same-sex group?

170.title: Alcohol and sex: the small-dose story
170.gist: After objectives on sexual problems and recovery tips, Part 1 states drug use affects sex lives, then describes how small occasional amounts of alcohol lower shyness and anxiety, easing arousal and increasing interest. It sets up the contrast with heavy use.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Expectancy research, including studies by Alan Marlatt using placebo drinks, found people who believed they had drunk alcohol behaved more disinhibited, even when they had not. Beliefs about alcohol shape sexual behavior too.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Lower anxiety helps sex, but the same disinhibition erodes judgment about consent and protection. The page's honesty about benefits makes the later costs more credible.

ask: If much of alcohol's sexual effect comes from expectation, what does that suggest about sober intimacy?
Why might the text start by admitting alcohol's benefits?

terms.d: What a person believes a drug will do, which shapes how they feel and act.

171.title: Desire up, performance down
171.gist: The page notes alcohol can lower guilt about behaviors people avoid when sober, then explains heavy or chronic use causes sexual dysfunction in men and women. Exercises ask about using alcohol for sexual anxiety and before sex.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Shakespeare's porter in Macbeth said drink provokes the desire but takes away the performance, a line written centuries before modern research confirmed the same pattern.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The line about doing things normally found unpleasant may touch regretted sex, exchange sex, or assault. Name that support is available individually, and keep the group discussion general.

ask: How does lowering guilt with alcohol relate to consent and to later shame?
Why could sexual dysfunction motivate a man to quit more than liver warnings?

terms.d: Difficulty getting or keeping an erection; often linked to heavy drinking.

172.title: How other drugs reshape sex
172.gist: Members weigh how alcohol helped and hurt their sex lives, then the text explains effects vary by drug: opiates often lower interest, stimulants raise desire but impair performance, and supposed enhancers can backfire. Injected or smoked stimulants spark intense sexual interest before the crash.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Stimulants flood dopamine, intensifying desire and linking sex and drug tightly; this is why methamphetamine and cocaine relapse is often tied to sexual cues. Opioids suppress sex hormones, dulling desire.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: 'Chemsex,' the use of drugs like methamphetamine to prolong sex, has become a public health focus, linked to higher HIV and hepatitis risk. Members may know it by other names.

ask: Why might asking how alcohol helped be essential before asking how it hurt?
How would a relapse plan differ for someone whose drug use and sex are fused?

terms.d: Using drugs, often stimulants, specifically to enhance or prolong sex.

173.title: Stimulants, disinhibition, and sexual harm
173.gist: The page completes stimulant effects on sexual function, then warns that drugs altering thinking or raising aggression can lead to bizarre acts or sexual violence. Check items confirm that drug effects depend on drug, dose, and route.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Alcohol is the substance most often involved in sexual assault, research consistently shows, through both perpetrator disinhibition and victim incapacitation. Intoxication never excuses an assault, legally or morally.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members may hold sex-offense charges or victim histories. Keep the tone factual, avoid jokes about violence, and know your facility's protocol if a disclosure comes up.

ask: Why does intoxication reduce blame for some acts in people's minds but should not for sexual violence?
How might a member's offense history change how they hear this page?

terms.d: Reduced restraint on impulses, so people act in ways they normally would not.

174.title: Drugs as a mask against intimacy
174.gist: This page argues substances hide the true self and block intimacy, flatten healthy sexual tension, and erode desire over time, though desire usually returns in recovery. Members check whether drugs dulled excitement for them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Attachment theory, from Bowlby onward, frames intimacy as the risk of being seen and depended on. Drugs can serve as a stand-in attachment object, safer than a person because it never rejects.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Healthy sexual tension sits on the same arousal curve as performance anxiety, an idea parallel to the Yerkes-Dodson pattern: some arousal sharpens experience, too much overwhelms it.

ask: What makes a drug feel safer than a partner for someone with a history of betrayal?
How would you explain to a member that awkward sober sex is part of recovery, not a sign of failure?

terms.d: Closeness built on honest self-disclosure, trust, and mutual care.

175.title: Using to get past sexual fear
175.gist: The page explains people use substances to lower inhibitions shaped by shame, unwanted experiences, or abuse, and points to therapy and medication as lasting help. Exercise 6 asks about fears of intimacy and using to cope.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Childhood sexual abuse is strongly associated with later substance use problems, especially among women in treatment and in custody. Integrated trauma-informed models like Seeking Safety, developed by Lisa Najavits, address both together.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This page can open trauma. Avoid probing for details in group; offer individual follow-up and grounding skills if someone becomes distressed.

ask: What would a trauma-informed version of this exercise ask instead of yes/no questions?
When does lowering inhibitions with a drug cross into avoiding healing?

terms.d: Practice that assumes trauma may be present and avoids retraumatizing people.

176.title: Sexual changes in early recovery
176.gist: Members note any changes in sexual interest during recovery and whether they feel low desire or used substances to raise it. It normalizes the shifts sobriety brings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: After stopping some drugs, especially opioids, hormone and reward systems take time to recover, so desire may dip, then surge. Knowing this is temporary prevents panic and relapse.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The phrase 'less desire than you should' assumes a normal amount. Desire varies widely between people; the useful question is whether it causes distress or conflict.

ask: Who sets the standard for how much desire someone 'should' have?
How might a surge of desire in early recovery be its own relapse risk?

177.title: When sex becomes a craving cue
177.gist: The page explains sex and stimulants hit similar pleasure circuits, so sex during use can trigger cravings. It advises avoiding high-risk sex early, waiting before new relationships, and eventually learning sex without cravings.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The common recovery advice to avoid new romantic relationships in the first year, often heard in Twelve Step circles, is folk wisdom more than tested rule, but it reflects real risk from intense emotion and new cues.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Men leaving prison often see sex as the first reward of freedom. Don't forbid; ask them to plan it: with whom, sober, and what they'll do if a craving shows up.

ask: Is it realistic to ask someone just released to postpone sex? What would a harm-reduction version of this advice look like?
How does pairing drugs and sex compare with pairing drugs and music or certain places?

178.title: Rewiring sex in an existing relationship
178.gist: For people already in a relationship, the page recommends honesty with a partner about cravings and asking for help, using intimacy to break the drug-sex link. Exercise 8 asks members to name that link and what to work on.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Couples-based treatment, such as behavioral couples therapy studied by Timothy O'Farrell and William Fals-Stewart, has generally outperformed individual treatment alone for some drinkers with a committed partner.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draft one sentence they could say to a partner about cravings. Rehearsing the words makes the conversation more likely to happen after release.

ask: What risks does disclosing cravings to a partner carry, and how do you weigh them?
If the partner still uses, what does that do to this advice?

terms.d: Treatment involving a partner to support sobriety and improve the relationship.

179.title: Where sexual problems come from
179.gist: Part 2 explains substances cause many sexual problems, which people then treat with more substances, and sorts causes into relationship, psychological, physical, and medication-related. It introduces sex therapy as a common, effective option.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Masters and Johnson pioneered modern sex therapy, including sensate focus, a stepwise touch exercise that reduces performance pressure. Many current approaches still build on it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The loop of a sexual problem leading to more drug use is negative reinforcement: the drug relieves distress, which strengthens use while worsening the original problem.

ask: Why might psychological causes of sexual problems be easier to fix than people assume?
How does the cycle of using to fix drug-caused problems apply beyond sex?

terms.d: A sex therapy exercise of gradual, pressure-free touch to rebuild comfort and arousal.
A behavior strengthened because it removes something unpleasant.

180.title: What makes sexual problems speakable
180.gist: Exercise 9 asks what would make it easier or harder to talk about a sexual problem, then the text begins sexual problems affecting both genders, starting with pain during intercourse. It addresses the stigma barrier first.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members' answers here describe what they need from you: privacy, matter-of-fact tone, a counselor of a certain gender. Treat the exercise as feedback on how to run the rest of the session.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Medical studies suggest many patients never raise sexual concerns unless a clinician asks first. Normalizing the topic is a clinical skill in itself.

ask: What does a person's comfort talking about sex reveal about their comfort with vulnerability in general?
How would your own discomfort shape what members disclose?

181.title: Low desire and ejaculation problems
181.gist: This page covers lack of arousal and desire, often from emotions, relationship conflict, substances, or medications, then premature and inhibited ejaculation in men. Most are described as treatable.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Arousal depends on the parasympathetic 'rest' system, while anger, fear, and anxiety engage the sympathetic 'fight or flight' system. That's why emotional states can shut down physical response.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The claim that frequent premature ejaculation is still probably psychological is dated; current views see mixed biological and psychological causes, though counseling and behavioral methods do often help.

ask: Why do antidepressants, a common treatment, sometimes undermine sexual function, and what dilemma does that create in recovery?
How could not responding to one partner but responding to another be diagnostic?

terms.d: The body's calming branch, needed for relaxation and sexual arousal.

182.title: Impotence and the trigger loop
182.gist: Exercise 10 asks how ejaculation problems could trigger use, then the page explains impotence is common and usually psychological, but also linked to medical conditions, substances, and many medications. A true/false item confirms drugs and stress both cause problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Erectile problems can be an early warning sign of cardiovascular disease, because penile arteries are small and narrow early. A sexual complaint may be worth a heart check.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Men may use bravado here. The trigger question works best framed as 'a guy you know': members can then describe shame-to-using loops without owning them yet.

ask: How does shame about sexual performance connect to masculinity norms in prison culture?
Why might a man prefer to blame drugs over admitting stress or depression?

183.title: Women's sexual problems and their causes
183.gist: The page covers pain near the surface or deep in the pelvis, vaginismus, and lack of orgasm in women, linking causes to infections, medical disorders, inhibition, trauma, drug use, and medications. Medical evaluation is recommended for lasting pain.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Women in the justice system report high rates of sexual trauma and untreated reproductive health problems, so medical referral is often part of recovery, not a side issue.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In a men's group, this page is a chance to build empathy and accurate knowledge about partners. Ask what they were taught about women's bodies and where they learned it.

ask: Why might women's sexual pain be underdiagnosed or dismissed in health care?
How could trauma-informed care change the way a doctor approaches vaginismus?

terms.d: Involuntary tightening of vaginal muscles that makes penetration painful or impossible.

184.title: Returning feelings and falling fast
184.gist: Members consider how women's sexual problems could trigger use and answer true/false checks, then the text warns that feelings, including sexual desire, return strongly in early recovery. Many mistake this surge for falling in love.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Early romance floods reward circuits much like a drug does, as Helen Fisher's brain-imaging studies of new love suggested. Swapping a drug for an intense new relationship can simply move the dependence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members describe an intimacy-first pattern: someone who met them at release becomes everything. Ask what happened the last time a new relationship ended in early recovery.

ask: How can someone tell real emotional intimacy from a relationship acting as a replacement high?
Why might a first-ever sober experience of intimacy feel so overwhelming?

terms.d: Using an intense new relationship to fill the role a drug once played.

185.title: Sex as a way to avoid pain
185.gist: The page explains people in early recovery face their pain and the pain they caused, and may use sex to escape it, though healing requires feeling and talking. Exercise 13 asks about using sex to avoid feelings and choosing between abstaining or relapsing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is experiential avoidance, a core concept in acceptance and commitment therapy: efforts to escape unwanted feelings tend to keep them alive. Any escape, sex included, can postpone the work.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The forced choice of abstaining for months or relapsing is a false dilemma for many; sex within a stable sober relationship need not threaten recovery. Use the question to probe priorities, not as a rule.

ask: Is every pleasurable escape in early recovery avoidance, or can some be healthy coping?
How would you respond to a member who says sex is the only thing keeping him sane?

terms.d: Trying to escape or suppress unwanted thoughts and feelings, often making them worse.

186.title: Balancing intimacy and independence
186.gist: This page frames healthy relationships as a recovery task, balancing feelings, dependence and independence, leading and following, closeness and distance. Exercise 14 starts by asking who matters most in members' lives.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Family systems theorist Murray Bowen called this balance differentiation: staying connected to others while keeping a clear self. Low differentiation shows as either fusion or cutoff, both common in addiction.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Listing important people inside a facility can be painful: some will have no one, or only people who still use. Have them include people they want to rebuild ties with.

ask: Why might people from chaotic homes swing between enmeshment and isolation?
How could 'accepting social responsibilities' be framed so it doesn't sound like a parole condition?

terms.d: Bowen's term for staying emotionally connected while keeping one's own identity.

187.title: Strengths, weaknesses, and a relationship goal
187.gist: Members list their strengths and weaknesses in intimate relationships, name their most important relationship goal, and outline steps toward it. It converts the session into a personal plan.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Turn each weakness into a 'when-then' plan, such as: when I feel jealous, then I'll say so before checking her phone. Peter Gollwitzer's research on implementation intentions shows these if-then plans boost follow-through.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Strengths are often harder to name than weaknesses for this population. Ask peers to name one strength for each member; outside eyes break the shame filter.

ask: Why do goals about relationships often get stated as goals about another person's behavior, and how would you redirect that?
Which relationship weaknesses also show up as criminal thinking patterns?

terms.d: An if-then plan linking a specific situation to a specific response.

188.title: Session 7 wrap-up: sex and recovery
188.gist: The summary recaps how sex and substance use become linked, how drugs affect intimacy, and how sexual problems can lead to self-medication. It acknowledges the courage this personal material took.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Close by asking each member for one word describing how the session felt. It lets discomfort be named without detail, and alerts you to anyone needing individual follow-up.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Public health frames sexual health as part of overall well-being, not only disease avoidance. Recovery programs that ignore sex leave out a major relapse pathway.

ask: What did this session leave out that matters for incarcerated adults, such as consent, STI testing, or LGBTQ members?
How would you evaluate whether this session changed anyone's risk behavior?

189.title: Role-play: the old flame invitation
189.gist: A role-play pairs someone two months sober, who admits sexual attention drew them to drugs, with a lonely old using partner who invites them over after work. It rehearses a situation where attraction and drugs pull together.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The 'just catching up' belief is a classic rationalization; the scene stacks loneliness, attraction, an old neighborhood, and drugs at the friend's home. Several triggers at once make a decision harder later.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Assign the using role to a member with strong persuasion skills; the realism matters. Debrief what tactics worked on the person in recovery and replay with a better ending.

ask: Why is the friend's loneliness as important to the scene as their drug use?
How should a person in recovery decide when to say no to someone they care about?

190.title: Debriefing the role-play
190.gist: The suggested questions ask how important it is to tell others you quit, whether attraction can override willpower, and what to say to an old using friend. They turn the role-play into scripts and decisions.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Telling others about a change can increase accountability, though some research suggests announcing goals may sometimes substitute for action. Disclosure works best paired with a concrete plan.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write a one-line script to an old using friend, such as wanting to meet but only in daylight at a public place. Practicing short scripts makes them available under pressure.

ask: If attraction can override willpower, what does recovery planning need besides willpower?
When does telling old friends you quit protect you, and when might it invite sabotage?

191.title: Session 8 opener: stress and well-being
191.gist: Session 8 introduces stress, types of stressors, and how people respond, with objectives on frustrations, pressures, conflicts, stress tolerance, defense mechanisms, and three stages of stress response. It frames stress management as central to recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The three stages likely echo Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion. Selye showed prolonged stress wears down the body, setting the stage for illness.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Stress is one of the most reliable triggers of relapse in both animal and human studies; reinstatement experiments show stress can restart drug seeking after extinction.

ask: Is stress the cause of relapse or the context in which relapse becomes likely?
How does incarceration itself act as a chronic stressor, and what happens to that stress at release?

terms.d: How much stress a person can handle before functioning breaks down.

192.title: Why drugs raise stress over time
192.gist: The page invites honest self-examination, lists glossary terms, and explains drugs briefly lower stress but leave people more stressed afterward. Recovery itself is a stressful life change, so stress skills are essential.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: George Koob's work on the 'dark side' of addiction describes how repeated use recruits brain stress systems, so baseline distress rises over time and drugs are used just to feel normal.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Holmes and Rahe's life-change research showed even positive changes like marriage count as stress. Release from prison, however welcome, stacks many changes at once.

ask: If recovery itself causes stress, how can a program prepare people without discouraging them?
Why might the glossary terms, which come from psychoanalysis, still be useful in a CBT-oriented program?

terms.d: The cumulative wear on the body from chronic stress.

193.title: Emotional strengths, weaknesses, and goals
193.gist: The text notes some people self-medicate extreme moods with substances, which harms them in the end. Exercise 1 asks for three emotional-health strengths and weaknesses, a main goal, and steps.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Substance use disorders and mood or anxiety disorders often co-occur, and integrated treatment of both is generally recommended over treating one at a time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may list 'getting stressed easily' when the real issue is trauma or undiagnosed depression. Use answers as screening cues for referral, not just goal-setting.

ask: How can you tell when an 'emotional weakness' is actually a treatable disorder?
What does it mean that the sample strengths include asking for help?

terms.d: Having a substance use disorder and another mental health disorder at the same time.

194.title: Stressor versus stress
194.gist: The page separates a stressor, an external demand, from stress, the internal reaction, and names three stressor types: frustrations, pressures, conflicts. Exercise 2 asks for a personal stressor and a reaction that lowers stress.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Lazarus and Folkman's appraisal model explains why stressors don't stress everyone: people judge whether a demand threatens them and whether they can cope. Change the appraisal and stress changes.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Epictetus taught that people are disturbed not by things but by their views of them. The stressor-stress split is that ancient insight restated in clinical terms.

ask: If stress depends on appraisal, what about stressors so severe that almost anyone would be harmed, like solitary confinement?
How would you teach appraisal without implying members are to blame for feeling stressed?

terms.d: An outside demand that requires a response.
A person's judgment of what a situation means and whether they can handle it.

195.title: Frustration: blocked from a goal
195.gist: Frustration is defined as an obstacle between a person and a goal, either external like money or job loss, or internal like guilt, fear, or loneliness. Exercise 3 asks for one of each from members' lives.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The frustration-aggression hypothesis, from Dollard and colleagues in 1939, proposed that blocked goals breed aggression. Later work softened it, but the link helps explain why frustrated members can explode.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Incarceration is a frustration machine: almost every goal meets a rule or wait. Validate that, then ask which internal frustrations they carry regardless of where they live.

ask: Why might internal obstacles be harder to see than external ones?
How does guilt function as both a frustration and a potential motivator?

terms.d: Stress from an obstacle that blocks reaching a goal.

196.title: Pressure to recover fast
196.gist: The page explains pressures as demands to speed up or change, from others' expectations and from oneself, including pressure from sponsors and an inner push to get it right this time. Exercise 4 asks who pushes members to recover quickly.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Perfectionistic pressure to 'get it right this time' links to the abstinence violation effect described by Marlatt: when an all-or-nothing goal breaks, people often abandon it entirely.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Family pressure after release often comes with real stakes: housing, custody, money. Help members distinguish expectations they share from ones imposed on them.

ask: Can pressure from a sponsor be both supportive and harmful? What decides which?
Why might impatience with recovery itself be a relapse risk?

terms.d: After a slip, the all-or-nothing thinking that leads to full relapse.

197.title: Good pressure, bad pressure
197.gist: This page shows pressure can help or harm, contrasting a push to get high with a push to attend a meeting, both stressful now but with opposite later effects. Exercise 5 asks for external and internal pressures.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Selye coined 'eustress' for stress that motivates growth versus 'distress' that harms. The difference often lies in whether the demand serves a person's own goals.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw two arrows for a current pressure: short-term stress now, and likely stress in three months. Comparing futures helps them choose which pressure to give in to.

ask: How do you judge a pressure by its long-term effect when you can't see the future?
Why is peer pressure toward recovery rarely as persuasive as peer pressure toward using?

terms.d: Positive, motivating stress tied to meaningful challenges.

198.title: Conflict: two forces pulling
198.gist: Conflict is defined as opposing forces, internal or external, with internal conflicts between two good options, two bad ones, or a good and a bad one. Members say whether these feel familiar.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Kurt Lewin classified conflicts as approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, and approach-avoidance. The last, such as a party that attracts and threatens, produces the most wavering and stress.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The jail versus community service example will hit home. Ask how members decided when they faced it; their answers reveal how they weigh short versus long-term pain.

ask: Why does an approach-avoidance conflict tend to feel strongest as you get closer to it?
How does ambivalence in MI relate to Lewin's conflict types?

terms.d: Being drawn to and repelled by the same option at once.

199.title: Conflicts with other people
199.gist: External conflicts arise with partners, children, parents, bosses, anyone who wants something different, and the challenge is resolving them without risking sobriety. Exercise 7 asks for an internal and external conflict affecting recovery and how members handle each.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes advised separating positions from interests: what people demand versus why. Many family conflicts soften when underlying interests, like safety or respect, surface.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may say they deal with conflict by avoiding or exploding. Normalize both as common, then ask what the third option looked like the one time it worked.

ask: Which recovery conflicts are worth avoiding, and which must be faced?
How do conflict styles learned in prison help or hurt in families after release?

200.title: What makes stress severe
200.gist: The page explains stress severity depends on the stressor and the person's perception, duration, size, and pile-up of stressors, and notes good events also stress. Anticipated stressors can be prepared for, and stress is a major relapse cause.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale ranked life events by stress, with death of a spouse highest and jail terms high on the list. Later research found the person's appraisal matters more than the event.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members list every change coming at release: housing, job, family, parole, money. Seeing the pile-up on paper explains why the first weeks out are so risky.

ask: Why might anticipating a stressor sometimes make it worse rather than easier?
How does stress pile-up explain relapse soon after release?

201.title: Why the same stressor hits differently
201.gist: Members consider how they cope with anticipated and sudden stressors, then Part 2 explains reactions vary with threat perception, stress tolerance, and supports. Self-doubt makes situations feel more threatening.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bandura's self-efficacy theory predicts this: people who doubt their coping abilities see more threats and avoid more challenges. Building small successes raises efficacy and lowers perceived threat.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Mastery-oriented coping, studied in resilience research, shows people who believe they can influence outcomes tend to recover from setbacks faster.

ask: Is low self-worth a cause of stress, or does chronic stress erode self-worth? How would you know?
How would you build self-efficacy in a setting that limits choices so much?

terms.d: Belief in one's ability to succeed in a specific situation.

202.title: Preparing for the unexpected
202.gist: The page argues preparation, such as calling a sponsor, attending a meeting, or exercising, lowers threats from surprise stressors. Exercises ask about worrying over disasters that never happened and identifying what does not affect stress.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Donald Meichenbaum's stress inoculation training rehearses coping in small doses so the real stressor finds a prepared response, much like a vaccine trains the immune system.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Worrying about disasters that never come is catastrophizing, a cognitive distortion Beck and Burns described. Spotting it is a CBT skill members can use daily.

ask: Why does preparation reduce stress even if the plan is never used?
How could catastrophizing be adaptive in a dangerous environment, and maladaptive after release?

terms.d: Expecting the worst possible outcome and treating it as likely.
Training coping skills through gradual exposure to manageable stress.

203.title: Support as a stress buffer
203.gist: The page explains stress-reduction skills can be learned, and that lacking personal and social supports makes stressors more powerful. Self-help programs act as strong supports; members name their own.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Cohen and Wills' stress-buffering hypothesis proposed social support protects people mainly when stress is high. Studies broadly support the idea, though which kind of support helps varies.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will name people who still use or who share criminal ties. Ask whether each named person supports recovery specifically, not just loyalty.

ask: What separates a supportive person from a merely loyal one in a recovery plan?
How can someone with no positive supports build them, starting from inside a facility?

terms.d: The idea that social support reduces the harm of stress, especially under high stress.

204.title: Rating coping, meeting the defenses
204.gist: Members rate their current ability to handle stress and recall one situation they couldn't handle, then the text compares psychological defenses to an immune system that works mostly outside awareness. Defenses are framed as natural.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Anna Freud's 1936 book on the ego's defense mechanisms systematized these ideas. Later, George Vaillant ranked defenses from immature to mature, showing some protect growth while others block it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Self-ratings of coping are often inflated or deflated by mood and image management. A concrete example in question 3 is more informative than the checkbox.

ask: If defenses work outside awareness, how can a person ever catch their own?
What would a 'mature' defense look like in a prison context?

terms.d: An automatic mental strategy that shields a person from anxiety or painful feelings.

205.title: Old armor that no longer fits
205.gist: The page explains defenses built during addiction once protected people in chaos but can block growth in recovery. Exercise 13 asks members which defenses they've seen in others and which no longer work for them sober.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A strategy adaptive in one setting can be maladaptive in another. Hypervigilance protects on the street or in a unit, but it reads as hostility at a job interview or with family.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking about defenses in others first is a smart entry point: people spot them easily outside themselves. Then turn the mirror gently: 'Which of these did someone ever see in you?'

ask: Which defenses learned in prison will members need to keep, at least for now, and which must go?
How do you honor a defense's past usefulness while asking someone to let it go?

206.title: Repression, insulation, intellectualization
206.gist: The page describes common defenses: repression of painful memories that still drive anxiety, emotional insulation that avoids disappointment but breeds despair, and intellectualization that explains away feelings. Each includes a concrete example.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Repression is the most disputed of these. Memory researchers like Elizabeth Loftus have shown false memories can be created, and evidence that traumatic memories are commonly blocked then recovered is contested. Present it cautiously.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Emotional insulation resembles Martin Seligman's learned helplessness: after repeated uncontrollable failures, people stop trying. Many members have learned this through years of system involvement.

ask: How would you tell intellectualization apart from healthy perspective-taking about a loss?
What responsibility does a counselor have when a member may have repressed a harmful act?

terms.d: Using reasoning to avoid feeling the emotion of a painful event.
Holding back involvement and hope to avoid being disappointed again.

207.title: Regression and refusing to hope
207.gist: The page defines regression as returning to outgrown, less mature ways of coping, such as schoolyard teasing. Exercises ask whether members avoid hoping, and identify that as emotional insulation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: 'Don't get your hopes up' is common among people with long sentences or repeated failures. Don't argue with it; explore its cost by asking what they miss out on by never hoping.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: C. R. Snyder's hope theory defined hope as goals plus pathways plus agency. It treats hope as a learnable thinking skill rather than a feeling, which fits a CBT room.

ask: When is guarding against hope wise, and when does it become self-defeating?
What behaviors in a group might be regression under stress?

terms.d: Reverting to less mature behavior from an earlier life stage under stress.
Snyder's model of hope as having goals, ways to reach them, and belief one can.

208.title: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
208.gist: This page describes three stress stages: alarm, with tension and early defenses; resistance, with intensified rigid coping and dropping meetings; and exhaustion, when resources fail. It shows how unmanaged stress builds toward collapse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome named these stages, originally describing the body's hormonal response to prolonged stress. The manual applies the same arc to psychological coping.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Psychosis is not a typical endpoint of ordinary stress; it usually needs other vulnerabilities. The model is a useful map, but most people under heavy stress show depression, illness, or relapse rather than breaks with reality.

ask: At which stage is intervention cheapest, and what does each stage look like in a reentry client?
Why might dropping recovery meetings be a sign of the resistance stage rather than laziness?

terms.d: Selye's three-stage pattern of response to prolonged stress: alarm, resistance, exhaustion.

209.title: Erik's day of piling stressors
209.gist: Members say whether they've lived the three-stage pattern, then read a story of Erik, who faces a job threat, a lost promotion, and a disastrous lunch, then hears his son skipped school. The story stacks stress in one day.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Lazarus and colleagues found everyday hassles can predict health problems as well as major life events. Erik's day shows small irritations compounding with big threats.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before revealing the rest, ask members to rate Erik's stress from one to ten after each event. Watching the number climb makes accumulation visible.

ask: Which of Erik's stressors are frustrations, pressures, or conflicts?
At what point in this day could one small coping action have changed the outcome?

terms.d: Minor everyday irritations that add up to significant stress.

210.title: Home alone with the worst thoughts
210.gist: Erik's story ends with a flat tire, money fights, suspicion of his wife's affair, and arriving home alone. Members guess what he thinks and feels and how he'll cope.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ending the story with Erik alone is deliberate: isolation plus unchecked rumination is a high-risk moment. Rumination, studied by Susan Nolen-Hoeksema, prolongs and deepens negative mood.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members will project their own coping onto Erik, often predicting he'll drink or confront his wife. Their answers are a window into their own default responses; reflect that back gently.

ask: What does the unconfirmed affair suspicion teach about how uncertain threats amplify stress?
If Erik called you that night, what would your first three moves be?

terms.d: Repetitively dwelling on distress and its causes without moving to solutions.

211.title: From a story to your own stressors
211.gist: The closing questions pivot from a scenario to the member's life: name current stressors, rate how well they are being handled, and plan better responses. It turns a case discussion into a personal stress audit before the session ends.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Talking about a fictional person first lowers defensiveness; the shift to 'your stressors' then borrows the insight members already voiced about someone else. Distanced self-reflection like this tends to make problems feel more workable.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for specific stressors rather than 'everything' or 'being locked up.' Ask each member to pick one stressor they can actually influence this week and one they cannot, and plan differently for each.

ask: Is a member's self-rating of coping effectiveness trustworthy, or does it mostly measure how the group will see them?
Which stressors in a prison setting are truly uncontrollable, and what would acceptance look like there instead of problem solving?

212.title: Session 8 wrap-up
212.gist: A brief summary recaps what the session covered: emotional strengths and weaknesses, emotional health goals, the three stressor types, and coping options. It frames stress coping as a pillar of recovery rather than a side topic.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Summaries work as retrieval cues. Asking members to recall the content before reading the summary strengthens memory far more than rereading it, a finding known as the testing effect.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Before reading the summary aloud, give each member thirty seconds to name one thing from the session they will actually use. Then read it and see what the group missed.

ask: What would change if summaries were written by the members rather than the manual?
How would you check, a week later, whether any of Session 8 transferred to behavior?

213.title: Reclaiming feelings without substances
213.gist: A guided reading affirms that addiction dulled emotional life and that recovery means feeling moods without chemicals, naming feelings, listening, and asking for help. It closes the session on hope and patience rather than skills.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Many people use substances to regulate emotions; when the drug is removed, the raw feelings return with no practiced skills to handle them. That is why emotion identification and help seeking are framed here as recovery tasks.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The reading mentions a Higher Power and faith. For members who are atheist or wary of religion, offer an equivalent frame such as values, community, or purpose so the exercise does not alienate them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Read slowly, with pauses. Afterward ask which single sentence landed or irritated them; irritation is useful data about where resistance lives.

ask: Is 'emotionally healthy' a clear target, or does it hide a cultural standard about how feelings should be shown?
For men raised to hide emotion, what makes asking for help feel safe enough to try?

terms.d: Any substance used to change how one feels, including alcohol, nicotine, and prescribed sedatives.

215.title: Role-play: trust after sobriety
215.gist: Two volunteers act out a couple six months into recovery: lateness triggers the partner's fear of relapse, an argument flares, and a sponsor suggests a meeting. Members then identify the couple's strengths and the problems that could undermine them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Trust lags behind sobriety. The partner's suspicion is a learned response to past lies, not proof of current bad faith; rebuilding it takes repeated, verifiable reliability over time.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Family systems thinking sees the whole household as recovering, which is why the partner also needs support (Al-Anon here). Change in one member unsettles the roles everyone else had adapted to.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to side with John and dismiss Eve as nagging. Swap roles mid-scene so the same person argues both sides; empathy for the partner usually grows fast.

ask: Is a calling-home rule a reasonable trust-building tool or a form of control? Where is the line?
How would this scene change for a member returning home after years of incarceration rather than a month of treatment?

terms.d: A mutual-help group for family members and friends of people with drinking problems.

217.title: Session 8 key terms
217.gist: The glossary defines the three stressor types (frustration, pressure, conflict) and several defense mechanisms such as repression, regression, intellectualization, and emotional insulation. It gives members a shared vocabulary for spotting how they react to stress.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Most of these defenses come from the psychoanalytic tradition, systematized by Anna Freud. Modern research reframes some of them as emotion regulation strategies, such as suppression or avoidance, which can be measured and changed.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Defense mechanisms are hard to observe directly and easy to use as accusations. Use them as self-reflection tools, never as labels the group throws at a member.

ask: Is intellectualizing always a defense, or can explaining a painful event be a healthy way of making meaning?
Which defense do you think is most common in your groups, and how would you tell it apart from a calm temperament?

terms.d: An outside event, person, rule, or demand that requires a response.
Falling back on childish ways of coping under strain.
Holding feelings at a distance from events that actually matter to you.

218.title: Session 9 opens: reducing stress
218.gist: The introduction outlines Session 9's three parts: reviewing stress concepts, restructuring life through organization, priorities, and relationships, and coping strategies like not recovering alone and the Relaxation Response. It moves from understanding stress to doing something about it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The structure mirrors a classic sequence: assess, then change the environment, then build personal coping. Changing the situation is often more effective than coping alone, a point stress researchers make repeatedly.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to rate their stress right now from 0 to 10 and keep the number. Revisit it at the end after the relaxation practice so they experience a change, not just read about one.

ask: How much of an incarcerated person's life can really be 'restructured,' and how should the session adapt for that?
Why might stress management reduce relapse, and what would you want to measure to show it?

terms.d: Herbert Benson's term for a calm bodily state, the opposite of the stress response, brought on by focused, quiet practice.

219.title: Stress versus stressor
219.gist: After listing objectives, the page restarts Part 1 by separating stressors, the outside demands, from stress, the person's inner reaction. It acknowledges members are likely under stress right now and frames the session as practical relief.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating the event from the reaction opens a gap where choice lives. Lazarus and Folkman's appraisal model holds that stress depends on how a person judges the demand and their resources to meet it.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member name one stressor and then describe their stress reaction in body, thought, and action. Seeing these as separate parts makes them easier to target.

ask: If stress is an internal reaction, does that risk blaming people for reacting to genuinely harmful environments?
Where does the event end and the appraisal begin when someone is facing a parole hearing?

terms.d: How a person judges a situation: how threatening it is and whether they can handle it.

220.title: Naming frustrations, pressures, and conflicts
220.gist: Members write one personal stressor of each type, then read that the impact of any stressor depends on its severity, duration, pile-up, and on the person's perception, abilities, and supports. Classification makes vague stress concrete.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Stress is cumulative: several mild stressors stacked together can hit harder than one large one. That is why stress plus perception plus resources, not the event alone, predicts how a person copes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members struggle to tell pressure from conflict. A quick rule: pressure pushes you toward one thing, conflict pulls you between two. Ask a volunteer for an example of each from the yard.

ask: Which of the three types is most likely to trigger use, and why might that differ by person?
How could you strengthen 'external resources' for someone with no family contact?

221.title: Defenses and your stress habits
221.gist: The page recalls that stress-reduction skills and social support guard against relapse and that defense mechanisms bring short relief but block recovery. A checklist then begins, asking members to mark how they typically behave under stress.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Defenses are not character flaws; they are short-term painkillers. The problem is that what eases pain tonight often prevents the problem from being faced at all.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social support is one of the more consistent protective factors in addiction recovery research, though the type of support matters: a network that still uses can raise risk instead of lowering it.

ask: When is denial actually protective, for example in the first days after a devastating loss?
Can a checklist capture coping honestly when members know a counselor will read it?

terms.d: An automatic mental move that shields a person from painful feelings or facts.

222.title: Healthy and unhealthy stress responses
222.gist: The checklist continues with a mix of harmful responses (anger, isolation, avoidance, overwork) and helpful ones (meetings, therapy, exercise, prayer, talking to someone). Members see their own coping pattern laid out side by side.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: After checking, have members circle their top two harmful and top one helpful response. The debrief question is what the helpful one needs to happen more often: time, place, people, or permission.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some items, like working more or explaining things logically, are not clearly good or bad. Their effect depends on whether they solve the problem or help a person avoid it. Invite debate rather than scoring.

ask: Is 'work more' coping or avoidance, and how would you tell in a specific member?
Which healthy responses on this list are actually available inside a facility, and what substitutes exist?

223.title: Order as a relapse shield
223.gist: Part 2 argues that disorganization breeds both stress and relapse chances, so recovery needs structure: scheduled meetings, exercise, sponsor calls, and recreation, without overloading. Time once spent chasing drugs must be deliberately refilled.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral activation and relapse prevention share a point: empty, unstructured time is fertile ground for cravings. Scheduling healthy activities replaces the routine the drug used to provide.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Marlatt's lifestyle balance idea warns that a life full of 'shoulds' and empty of 'wants' builds resentment and a sense of being owed relief. Overloading recovery tasks can backfire for that reason.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members still inside, the schedule is largely set for them. Shift the task to planning the first 72 hours after release, when structure suddenly disappears and risk peaks.

ask: How can a person who has lived by institutional routines for years build self-directed structure without it feeling like another cell?
Where is the tipping point between healthy structure and rigid overcontrol?

terms.d: In relapse prevention, a healthy mix of obligations and genuinely enjoyable activities in daily life.

224.title: Where your time and energy go
224.gist: Members reflect on feeling swamped in early sobriety, name time-wasters that crowd out recovery, and identify time-management problems they need help with. It makes overwhelm a concrete, solvable issue.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Overwhelm often comes from holding every task in your head at once. Writing them down offloads working memory, which itself lowers stress before any task is done.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for one hour of a typical day in detail, minute by minute. Members usually spot a drift pattern, such as idle talk on the tier or TV, that the general question misses.

ask: Is poor time management a skill gap or often a sign of depression or ADHD that deserves screening?
What does 'wasted time' mean to someone whose release date is years away?

225.title: Ranking what recovery needs this week
225.gist: Members learn to sort recovery tasks into must-do this week, should-do if possible, and nice-to-have, then list their non-negotiable Priority 1 goals. Every new activity gets filtered through whether it helps sobriety.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This is a version of triage, the same logic as the Eisenhower urgent-versus-important grid. Its value is permission: lower priorities can slip without guilt, which cuts all-or-nothing thinking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Insist Priority 1 items be small and checkable, like two meetings and one sponsor call, not 'stay sober.' Goals that cannot be checked off cannot build confidence.

ask: What happens to motivation when a member fails a Priority 1 goal in week one, and how should you frame that?
Should sobriety always be priority one, or are there members for whom housing or safety must come first?

226.title: Second priorities, obstacles, solutions
226.gist: The planner continues: members list postponable Priority 2 goals, then anticipate obstacles and solutions for meeting their goals. Planning around barriers before they hit is the core skill.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Implementation intentions, if-then plans studied by Peter Gollwitzer, reliably help people follow through on goals. Pairing each obstacle with a specific response is exactly that format.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Turn each obstacle into one sentence: 'If my ride falls through, then I will call my sponsor by 5 pm.' Have members read one aloud to a partner.

ask: Which obstacles do members typically fail to predict, and why are those blind spots?
How would you tell a realistic solution from a wishful one?

terms.d: A concrete if-then plan linking a likely situation to a chosen response.

227.title: Pressure or support? It depends on you
227.gist: The page argues the same encouragement feels like pressure to someone ambivalent and like support to someone committed. It urges telling former using contacts clearly that you have quit and letting family know so they can help, without making promises.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is ambivalence in action, central to Miller and Rollnick's motivational interviewing. Pushing someone who is undecided tends to strengthen their resistance; the reaction to support tells you their stage of change.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Telling dealers and using friends that you have quit can be risky in some settings and may invite testing or retaliation. Help members plan safe, brief scripts and exit routes, not confrontations.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Skipping promises is wise advice. Families have heard them before; actions over time rebuild credibility better than words.

ask: If a member feels family encouragement as nagging, is that information about the member or about the family?
How do you cut ties with a using network when it overlaps with your neighborhood, family, or only friends?

terms.d: Wanting and not wanting a change at the same time.

228.title: Rating support and rushing into romance
228.gist: Members rate their support system as strong, medium, or weak and name helpful people. The text then warns that early-recovery romance or sex can become a substitute addiction, especially when it mainly feeds dependency needs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Intense new romance activates reward circuits and can numb distress much like a drug. When the relationship falters, the emotional crash can be a direct relapse trigger.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Attachment theory helps here: people with anxious attachment may cling to a new partner for regulation they never learned to provide themselves.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A 'weak' rating can trigger shame. Normalize it as a starting point and ask who could move from zero to one person in the next month.

ask: Is the common advice to avoid relationships in the first year evidence-based, or largely program folklore?
How do you tell genuine connection from dependency in someone's first relationship after release?

229.title: Relationships that drain or sustain
229.gist: The text advises caution about deep emotional involvement in early recovery, especially with someone in crisis, and suggests a sponsor, counselor, or clergy for serious trouble. Members then describe stressful relationship patterns and how to work with people rather than against them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rescuing a partner in crisis can feel like purpose but drains the energy recovery needs. It can also become a way to avoid one's own feelings by managing someone else's.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for one relationship where the member keeps 'fighting the same fight.' Map what each person wants underneath; the struggle often softens once the need is named.

ask: How do you respect a member's autonomy in relationships while still naming a pattern that endangers recovery?
What does 'working with people' look like when the people involved are correctional staff?

230.title: Love or dependency? Mapping your circle
230.gist: Members examine whether intimate ties rest on real care or on meeting their own needs, then read that relationship choices test commitment to sobriety. They begin listing at least three friends and three family members for rating.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social networks spread behavior. Research on social contagion suggests habits such as drinking travel through networks, which is why who you spend time with matters so much in recovery.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The love-or-dependency question invites defensive answers. Ask instead what the member gives in the relationship and what they take; the balance often speaks for itself.

ask: Is it fair to call relationship choices a 'test' of commitment when someone has few alternatives?
How might cultural norms about family loyalty clash with advice to distance from using relatives?

231.title: Grading each person's support
231.gist: Members grade each listed person from definitely supportive to possibly harmful, using guiding questions about whether the person understands addiction, joins self-help, or is in treatment. It turns vague loyalty into an honest risk map.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a social network inventory, a practical relapse prevention tool. Separating 'loves me' from 'helps my sobriety' is often the key insight; the two do not always overlap.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to rate a parent or partner as definitely supportive while describing them using. Ask the guiding questions out loud for that one person and let the member re-rate.

ask: Can someone be both loving and possibly harmful, and how do you help a member hold that?
Should someone in very early recovery count as support or risk, given the scale's questions?

232.title: Final support checks and a wider list
232.gist: The remaining questions ask whether a person is in early recovery, has used with the member, still uses, or recently offered drugs. Members can then extend their list and rate more people.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The question about recent offers to use is the sharpest. Debrief by asking what the member would say the next time that person offers, and rehearse the line once.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw three circles: inner, middle, outer. Place each rated person. Ask which one person to move closer and which one to move out over the next three months.

ask: Why might people with the D rating feel most like home, and what does that suggest about identity in recovery?
How would you adapt this list for someone whose whole family is involved in the justice system?

233.title: Don't recover alone; repair to reconnect
233.gist: Part 3 notes that use often begins socially and ends in isolation, so recovery requires connection. For people who fear anger or rejection, it suggests apologizing, naming the fear, and proving sobriety over time, then asks what members could say to those they hurt.

deeper.label: Connection
