deeper.text: Johann Hari's line that the opposite of addiction is connection popularized this idea, drawing on research like the Rat Park studies, which are suggestive but debated.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shame pushes people toward hiding, guilt toward repair. Framing apology as guilt-driven action helps members move from 'I am bad' to 'I did harm and can make some of it right.'

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Warn against forcing amends on people who do not want contact, including victims. A repair attempt should serve the other person, not the member's relief.

ask: When can an apology do more harm than good to the person receiving it?
How does the Twelve Step idea of amends differ from restorative justice practices?

terms.d: Actions taken to repair harm done to others, beyond simply saying sorry.

234.title: Rebuilding confidence through shared plans
234.gist: Members consider what to say to help others trust them again, then read advice to make recovery social: arrive at meetings with others, plan coffee, movies, exercise, or games with sober peers. Company turns risky situations into supported ones.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A lone person at a game is surrounded by cues to drink and has no one to interrupt the craving. Another person acts as an external brake and a distraction.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies of mutual-help groups suggest much of their benefit comes through changes in social networks, adding sober friends, rather than only the meetings themselves.

ask: What does 'positive things with others' mean for someone whose prior social life revolved entirely around using?
How can a member rebuild confidence in others without over-promising?

235.title: Menu of shared recovery activities
235.gist: Members check recovery activities (AA, NA, group therapy, service) and leisure or exercise options they could do with others, adding their own ideas. It converts 'don't recover alone' into a concrete menu.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A menu lowers the effort of choosing. People are more likely to act when options are already listed than when asked to invent them under stress.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Service activities are often skipped, yet helping others is linked with better outcomes in mutual-help research. Ask who has ever helped someone else stay out of trouble, and how that felt.

ask: Which of these activities would a member on parole actually have access to, and what substitutes fill the gaps?
Why might service to others protect recovery more than receiving help?

236.title: Ordinary life, done together
236.gist: The list extends to recreation (dinner, library, hobbies, games, concerts) and everyday errands like groceries or clothes shopping. Even routine tasks become chances for sober company.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recovery capital, a concept from William White and colleagues, counts these ordinary social resources as assets, alongside housing, work, and health. Sober fun is not a luxury; it is part of what keeps people well.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to pick one routine errand they used to combine with using, like a store run that ended at the dealer, and plan a sober version with a companion.

ask: What makes sober recreation feel boring at first, and how long might that phase last?
How does someone rebuild a sense of fun when pleasure was tied to substances for years?

terms.d: The personal, social, and community resources a person can draw on to start and sustain recovery.

237.title: Benson's Relaxation Response, step by step
237.gist: The page teaches Herbert Benson's 1975 method: a quiet place, a repeated word or focus, a passive attitude toward distractions, and a comfortable seat, followed by muscle relaxation and slow nasal breathing while silently repeating a word. It gives members a portable calming tool.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Benson drew on meditation practices and argued the body has an innate counterpart to the fight-or-flight response. Repetition plus letting go of distractions shifts the nervous system toward rest.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Relaxation and meditation techniques reliably reduce self-reported stress and anxiety in many studies, though effects vary and are often modest. Regular practice matters more than any single session.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Closing eyes can feel unsafe in a correctional or trauma-affected group. Offer eyes open with a soft gaze at the floor, and never touch or walk behind members during practice.

ask: What does Benson's secular repackaging of meditation gain and lose compared with its religious roots?
How would you handle a member who reports panic or flashbacks during relaxation?

terms.d: Noticing distracting thoughts without fighting them, then gently returning to the focus.

238.title: Practice routine and Session 9 recap
238.gist: The method finishes with ten to twenty minutes of practice, a slow return, and once or twice daily practice away from meals. A summary closes Session 9, affirming members now hold practical tools for reducing stress.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run a three-minute version in group, then ask members to rate tension before and after. Seeing a number drop builds belief in the tool more than any explanation.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Twenty minutes twice a day is a lot for most people. A shorter daily habit that actually happens beats an ideal routine that never starts.

ask: How can a relaxation habit be anchored to an existing routine like count time or lights out?
Is relaxation a coping skill or an avoidance strategy when used during a craving?

240.title: Role-play: Friday night without happy hour
240.gist: Volunteers play a man one month sober, shaken after passing his old happy-hour bar, and his wife, who attends Al-Anon and wants him at Friday meetings. Members identify his potential supporters and what he should do.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The scene packs a cue-triggered craving, a lost social ritual, and a mixed family network into one evening. Friday at 5 is a high-risk situation in Marlatt's sense: a predictable time and place tied to past use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have the wife practice holding back her advice and asking first how he is. Contrast the two versions; members feel how unsolicited advice lands as pressure.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The coworkers in recovery show how hidden support often exists outside one's usual circle. Recovery may require crossing social group lines, which takes courage.

ask: Which of Jack's relatives is the trickiest to classify, and why?
How do you replace a social ritual that gave a sense of belonging, not just alcohol?

241.title: Session 10 opens: negative emotions
241.gist: The introduction previews Session 10's two parts: depression, and guilt and fear, including powerlessness, forgiveness, and losing control. Objectives include recognizing depression symptoms, its links with substance use, and that it is treatable.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Negative emotions are among the most common relapse precipitants identified in relapse prevention research. Naming them in sequence gives members a map before the heavy material starts.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Set expectations and safety first: this session may surface suicidal thoughts. Know your facility's protocol and say early that you will check in privately with anyone who seems at risk.

ask: Why might a program group depression, guilt, and fear together, and what is lost by doing so?
How would you screen for depression in a group without singling anyone out?

242.title: Sadness versus depression
242.gist: Part 1 contrasts ordinary sadness after loss with depression, which is deeper and longer, bringing low energy, lost pleasure, sleep changes, and poor concentration. It notes depressed mood during withdrawal is expected.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Clinical depression is defined by persistence and impairment, not by the feeling itself. Distinguishing a normal response to loss from a disorder prevents both overdiagnosis and neglect.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philosophers from the Stoics onward separated grief from despair. Modern debates about removing the bereavement exclusion in DSM-5 revisit that same line.

ask: Where is the line between appropriate sadness about incarceration and a depressive episode?
Should withdrawal-related depression be treated or simply waited out, and who decides?

terms.d: Losing pleasure or interest in things that used to feel good, a core sign of depression.

243.title: Where depression comes from
243.gist: The page explains depression may follow trauma or loss, physical imbalance such as sedative withdrawal, or arise with no clear cause. It defines major depressive disorder and stresses that it is treatable, then asks members about past and childhood episodes.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The manual leans on a brain chemical imbalance explanation. Researchers now see that as an oversimplification; depression likely involves a mix of biology, stress, learning, and social conditions, and antidepressants work for reasons still debated.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking about childhood depression can open trauma. Keep group answers general and invite details in individual sessions.

ask: What does a member gain or lose from believing their depression is 'chemical'?
How might childhood depression in someone with adverse experiences shape later substance use?

terms.d: A diagnosis for persistent low mood or lost interest with other symptoms, lasting at least two weeks and impairing daily life.

244.title: Tracing your own episodes
244.gist: Members describe whether past depression followed a hard event or seemed to come from nowhere, how long it lasted, and what they stopped doing. It builds a personal history of mood.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Noticing what you stopped doing is key. Behavioral activation therapy treats withdrawal from activity as both a symptom and a driver of depression, and rebuilding activity can lift mood.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which dropped activity would be easiest to restart in small form. That gives the reflection a forward step.

ask: How reliable are retrospective reports of depression among people who were using heavily at the time?
Does depression that 'came from nowhere' really lack triggers, or are they just harder to see?

245.title: Signs that sadness has become depression
245.gist: The page compares the two states: sadness is brief and does not disable functioning, while depression lingers for weeks or longer with hopelessness, low energy, worthlessness, excess guilt, and sometimes thoughts of death or suicide. It ends on the message that treatment works.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Substance use disorders and depression often occur together, and both raise suicide risk; the risk is higher when they combine. Periods right after release from incarceration are recognized as especially dangerous.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts when warning signs appear. Research indicates that asking does not plant the idea; it often brings relief and opens the door to help.

ask: How would you tell psychomotor agitation from anxiety or withdrawal in a member?
What makes excessive guilt about small things a depression signal rather than conscience?

terms.d: A stretch of weeks or more when depression symptoms are present most days.

246.title: Depression in the family and the never-ending feeling
246.gist: Members note whether relatives show depression symptoms and whether their own past depression felt like it would never lift, and for how long. Family patterns and the illusion of permanence come into view.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Depression tends to run in families through both genes and shared environment. Seeing it in relatives can reduce shame by showing it is not a personal weakness.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The sense that pain is permanent is a hallmark of depressed thinking, which Beck described as a negative view of self, world, and future. Recalling that past episodes ended is a direct counter to it.

ask: How might growing up with a depressed parent shape a child's coping before any substance use?
Can you use a member's memory of an episode ending as hope without dismissing their current pain?

247.title: Drugs that deepen the low
247.gist: The text explains that depressants can lower mood and stimulant highs end in depressive crashes, feeding a use-to-escape cycle. It describes self-medication and harsh circumstances that breed hopelessness, and asks if members used when sad.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Khantzian's self-medication hypothesis proposes people choose drugs that relieve specific painful states. It is influential, though evidence suggests the relationship between mood and use runs in both directions.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Seligman's learned helplessness work describes how repeated failure to control outcomes leads people to stop trying, which echoes the page's point about harsh circumstances.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Validate the logic of self-medication: it worked in the short run. Then explore what it cost. Shaming the choice shuts down honesty.

ask: If poverty and abuse fuel hopelessness, how much can individual therapy change without structural help?
What does distress tolerance add that the manual's 'learn to tolerate sadness' leaves out?

terms.d: Using substances to ease emotional pain or symptoms without medical guidance.

248.title: Which came first, mood or drug?
248.gist: The page notes withdrawal brings depressive symptoms for most, but people depressed before use tend to have deeper, longer episodes and may need treatment for both. Yes-or-no questions help members sort out the timeline.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Clinicians distinguish substance-induced depression, which usually improves within weeks of abstinence, from independent depression, which persists. Timing of onset is one of the main clues.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Integrated treatment of co-occurring disorders, addressing both at once, is generally recommended over treating them one after another.

ask: Why is it hard to diagnose depression during early abstinence, and how long would you wait?
How should a counselor respond when a member's answers suggest untreated depression but no psychiatrist is available?

terms.d: Having a substance use disorder and another mental health condition at the same time.

249.title: Antidepressants and therapy
249.gist: The page states depression has biological roots from stress, long-term use, or genetics, that antidepressants are not mood-altering and can support sobriety, and that therapy adds psychological and social skills. Members share what they have heard about these medicines.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Antidepressants help many people, with clearer benefits in moderate to severe depression; psychotherapy such as CBT performs comparably for many, and combining them often helps most. Benefits take weeks to appear.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some recovery cultures still discourage any psychiatric medication. The manual's clear stance counters that, but be honest that side effects and stopping symptoms exist and need medical supervision.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect myths: that pills are a crutch, that they make you a zombie, or that they get you high. Gather them on the board and sort them into fact, partly true, and false.

ask: Why might some members distrust prescribed medication inside a correctional system?
Is 'not mood-altering' accurate, given that antidepressants are meant to change mood over time?

250.title: Social roots of depression; guilt begins
250.gist: Members name social situations that can trigger or worsen depression, then Part 2 opens: guilt is a normal, healthy response to harming others, and addiction typically involves broken promises, lying, and stealing that cause harm.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Social defeat, isolation, and loss of status are well-known depression triggers. Incarceration bundles all three, so depression here is often a response to circumstances, not just an inner flaw.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Moral emotions like guilt evolved, many psychologists argue, to repair relationships after harm. They are social signals as much as private feelings.

ask: How would you separate depression caused by prison conditions from depression a member brought in?
If guilt is healthy, why do so many treatment approaches focus on reducing it?

251.title: Numbness, then the guilt flood
251.gist: As addiction progresses, guilt can fade into emotional numbness as part of denial. In recovery, feelings return and some members are hit by a sudden wave of awareness of the harm done. Questions ask whether members knew they were hurting others at the time.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Repeated harm without consequence can blunt moral feelings, a process researchers call moral disengagement (Bandura). Recovery reverses it, which is why guilt often rises as people get better, not worse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Frame the guilt flood as a sign of recovery, not of failure. Members who feel worse at sixty days sober often think something is wrong, and that belief itself is a relapse risk.

ask: What does it mean for responsibility if someone truly did not feel guilt while using?
How do you support someone through a guilt flood without rushing to reassure it away?

terms.d: Mental moves, such as blaming victims or minimizing harm, that switch off guilt about one's own conduct.

252.title: Healthy and unhealthy guilt
252.gist: Members consider whether recovery has made them more aware of the harm they caused and whether guilt has grown, then reflect on when guilt helps and when it becomes unproductive.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to finish two sentences: 'Guilt helps me when it pushes me to...' and 'Guilt hurts me when it makes me...' The contrast usually shows the difference between action and rumination.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In a correctional setting, members may perform guilt for parole boards or staff. Make clear that this reflection is for them, not for an evaluation, if that is truthfully the case.

ask: How can you tell genuine remorse from performed remorse, and does it matter therapeutically?
When does guilt become rumination, and what interrupts that loop?

253.title: When guilt becomes too much
253.gist: Like physical pain, guilt signals that something needs attention. Drugs mute it, and it can return stronger after a high. When guilt, shame, and remorse dominate for long periods, the page calls it a danger sign that needs counseling and group support.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: June Tangney's research separates guilt (focused on the act) from shame (focused on the self). Guilt tends to motivate repair, while shame is linked with hiding, anger, and worse outcomes, including in studies of incarcerated people.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Post-use guilt can itself drive the next use, creating a loop: use, guilt, use to escape guilt. Marlatt's abstinence violation effect describes a similar spiral after a slip.

ask: Is the manual's 'overwhelming guilt' actually describing shame, and does the distinction change your intervention?
How would you help a member convert shame about who they are into guilt about what they did?

terms.d: Feeling that one's whole self is bad, rather than that one did a bad thing.
After a slip, believing 'I've blown it,' which can turn a lapse into full relapse.

254.title: Guilt you inherited as a child
254.gist: Members describe what being overwhelmed by guilt means and its harms. The text explains that children in troubled families often blame themselves for problems they had no power to fix, guilt that persists into adulthood.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Children are naturally egocentric: they tend to see themselves as the cause of events. Taking blame can also feel safer than accepting that the adults around them were unreliable.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Adverse Childhood Experiences research links early household dysfunction with later addiction and mental health problems. It describes risk patterns across populations, not destiny for any individual.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will deny any childhood issue. Do not push; instead ask what a younger sibling in the same house might have felt. Distance makes it safer to see.

ask: How does misplaced childhood guilt differ from appropriate adult guilt for real offenses, and can both coexist?
What risks arise when childhood framing is used to excuse adult harm?

terms.d: Early hardships like abuse, neglect, or a parent's addiction, linked with later health risks.

255.title: How old guilt shows up today
255.gist: The page lists adult signs of childhood guilt: apologizing for nothing or for others, caretaking others' feelings while ignoring one's own, and depression over unchangeable situations. Members then check how they reacted to guilt as children.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Childhood strategies like hiding, acting extra good, or acting out were adaptations that once made sense. Seeing them as survival strategies, not character, makes them easier to update.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which childhood reaction still shows up in the unit today. Acting out under guilt often looks like anger to staff, and naming that link can be eye-opening.

ask: Which of these childhood responses might map onto the criminal thinking patterns you teach in CBI?
Why might people-pleasing be a relapse risk rather than just a personality quirk?

256.title: Facing harm without drowning in it
256.gist: Members note which family member they felt most guilty toward as children. The text turns to adult guilt: recovery means facing the real damage of addiction without being consumed, often through making amends.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Restorative justice frameworks share the manual's logic: acknowledging harm and repairing it can benefit both the person harmed and the person who caused it, when the harmed party chooses to take part.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The page promises a sense of freedom after forgiveness, but forgiveness is not guaranteed. Prepare members for amends that are refused, so the outcome does not become a new source of shame.

ask: Is an amends process ethical when the harmed person may be retraumatized by contact?
How might amends differ for harms tied to crimes versus harms within the family?

257.title: One act you still carry
257.gist: Members name something they did while using that weighs on them, consider whether guilt can be released, and list steps already taken in sobriety to address it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Writing about a specific guilty act can be intense, and disclosure in group may carry legal risk. Remind members not to share details of uncharged crimes and to keep answers private if needed.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Expressive writing about difficult experiences, studied by James Pennebaker, has shown modest benefits for wellbeing in many trials, though results vary across settings.

ask: Should the goal be to get rid of guilt or to carry it in a way that motivates change?
What confidentiality limits apply to these disclosures in your setting, and how do you state them clearly?

258.title: Step One and powerlessness
258.gist: Members consider how far they would go to resolve guilt. The text then introduces Step One of AA, admitting that alcohol was stronger than self-control and life had become unmanageable, and asks whether life felt out of control while using.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Admitting powerlessness can paradoxically restore agency: dropping the fight to control use makes room for choosing abstinence and help. Many members experience it as relief.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Powerlessness language clashes with CBT and criminal justice models that stress personal choice and accountability. Some members, especially those who have felt powerless all their lives, may find it disempowering.

ask: How do you reconcile powerlessness over substances with accountability for crimes committed while using?
Could powerlessness be reframed as limited control under certain conditions, and what would be lost?

terms.d: The first of AA's Twelve Steps: admitting loss of control over alcohol and an unmanageable life.

259.title: What powerlessness means to you now
259.gist: Recognizing powerlessness helps explain past behavior, while healthy guilt should give way to moving forward. Members describe how they are powerless over use, how they hurt others, and their current understanding of the concept.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watch for 'I was powerless, so it was not my fault.' Respond with both truths: control was impaired, and responsibility for repair still belongs to you.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philosophers debate whether addiction is a compulsion or a choice. Positions like Gene Heyman's choice-based view and the brain disease model sit at opposite ends, and many clinicians land somewhere in between.

ask: Does believing in powerlessness change relapse risk, and in which direction?
How would a member from a culture of self-reliance hear this concept?

260.title: Forgiveness: others, maybe them, then yourself
260.gist: The page argues emotional health needs moving beyond past harm through acknowledgment, responsibility, and asking forgiveness, linked to Steps Eight and Nine. It orders the work as forgiving others, possibly being forgiven, and finally forgiving oneself, and asks who could help.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Forgiveness interventions, such as those developed by Robert Enright and Everett Worthington, show benefits for anger and wellbeing in many studies. Effects are clearer for forgiving others than for self-forgiveness.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Self-forgiveness without responsibility can become self-excusing. Researchers suggest genuine self-forgiveness follows acknowledging harm and making efforts to repair it.

ask: Is forgiving others first a sound order, or does it depend on what was done to the person?
What is the difference between forgiving and excusing, and how do you teach that line?

261.title: Courage, time, and the unforgivable
261.gist: Making amends takes time and courage, and as members stop living by guilt and fear, they avoid people less and feel less isolated. They list behaviors they want forgiven and consider whether anything feels unforgivable.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The 'unforgivable' question can expose deep moral injury, including from violence. Do not rush to say everything is forgivable; acknowledge the weight and arrange individual follow-up.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Moral injury, a concept from work with combat veterans, describes lasting distress after violating one's own deepest values. It fits some members' experiences better than guilt alone.

ask: Is it the counselor's role to tell someone an act is forgivable?
How might avoidance of people one harmed maintain both isolation and relapse risk?

terms.d: Deep, lasting distress from doing or witnessing something that violates one's core moral beliefs.

262.title: Giving and receiving forgiveness
262.gist: Members recall forgiving others and being forgiven, how it felt, or what they would want to hear. They then start listing three reasons for guilt today.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Recalling being forgiven builds a model for what self-forgiveness could feel like. People who have never been forgiven may lack that template entirely, which the 'what would you want to hear' prompt tries to supply.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write the exact words they would want from someone they hurt. Then ask whether they could say something similar to themselves.

ask: What happens in a group when one member has never been forgiven by anyone?
Why might forgiving someone else feel threatening to a person's sense of safety?

263.title: Releasing guilt; fears from childhood
263.gist: Members list ways to ease current guilt and three people they will forgive today. Then the page introduces childhood fear: children of unpredictable or abusive parents, or those never made to feel safe, may carry repressed fear into adulthood.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Unpredictability is one of the strongest sources of chronic stress. A child who cannot predict a parent's mood stays on alert, a pattern that can persist as hypervigilance in adults.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Trauma researchers describe how early threat can tune the stress system to react faster and longer. This helps explain why some members feel danger in situations others see as calm.

ask: Is 'forgive three people today' too quick? What are the risks of forced forgiveness?
How does hypervigilance from childhood interact with prison culture, where alertness can be adaptive?

terms.d: A constant state of scanning for threat, often rooted in past danger.

264.title: Remembering childhood fear
264.gist: Members recall times in childhood when they felt scared or unprotected, whether they told anyone, and situations where they shut fear off entirely.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Trauma memories can surface fast. Keep this as private writing, offer a grounding exercise afterward, and avoid asking anyone to read answers aloud.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Many children learn that showing fear brings more danger or ridicule. Shutting it off was protective then; the cost appears later, when fear drives behavior without being noticed.

ask: How would you recognize when this exercise is beyond the scope of a psychoeducational group and needs trauma-focused care?
Why might men in a prison group be especially unlikely to have told anyone about childhood fear?

265.title: Fear that grows up with you
265.gist: Members describe how they acted when afraid as children. The text notes that fear pushed aside in childhood often continues unnoticed in adults, who may feel anxiety without knowing its source, and asks for current greatest fears.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Fear that is not recognized often shows up as something else: irritability, control, aggression, or use. In correctional settings, anger is frequently a mask for fear because fear can look like weakness.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to list current fears, then circle any that, from the outside, look like anger. The overlap usually surprises people.

ask: Which fears are realistic for someone returning home, such as housing or rejection, and should they be soothed or planned for?
How does free-floating anxiety differ from fear, and does the difference change treatment?

terms.d: Ongoing worry about many things that is hard to control and not tied to one specific threat.

266.title: Why hiding feelings feels like control
266.gist: The text explains people in recovery often fear sharing feelings, believing secrecy equals control and expression could lead to chaos, violence, or endless tears, fears it calls usually unrealistic. Members weigh the pros and cons of hiding fear.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gross's research on emotion regulation finds that habitual suppression, hiding feelings outwardly, tends to be linked with worse wellbeing and closeness, while reappraisal tends to fare better.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Honor the advantages column. In prison, hiding feelings can genuinely keep someone safe. The skill is choosing where and with whom to open up, not dropping guard everywhere.

ask: How do you teach emotional openness in an environment where vulnerability can be exploited?
Is the fear of 'going crazy' if feelings come out ever realistic, and how would you respond if it is?

terms.d: Holding back the outward signs of an emotion while still feeling it inside.

267.title: Fear of losing control
267.gist: Members name fears about recovery and how they respond to them. The page then explains that people fear unleashing pent-up emotions, but opening up actually helps them gain control of their lives.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Avoiding an emotion keeps the fear of it alive, much as avoiding a feared object maintains a phobia. Small, safe exposures to feeling show the person that emotions rise and fall on their own.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Linehan's DBT teaches that emotions act like waves: they peak and pass if not fed by action. That idea gives members a concrete picture of control that is not suppression.

ask: How does the legal and family chaos many members face make loss of control a realistic fear rather than a distortion?
What small, safe experiment could a member try to test whether sharing a feeling leads to loss of control?

268.title: Testing the worst-case belief
268.gist: Sentence stems ask members what losing control means to them, their worst fear about it, how revealing fears would feel, and the worst and best outcomes of opening up.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Spelling out the worst case is a cognitive technique: catastrophic predictions often lose power once written down and examined, and pairing them with a best case widens the person's view.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: After writing, ask how likely the worst case really is from 0 to 100 percent, and what they would do if it happened. Coping plans shrink fear more than reassurance.

ask: When is a worst-case prediction accurate, and how should the exercise change then?
Why might the best-case column be harder to fill for some members than the worst?

terms.d: Expecting the worst possible outcome and treating it as likely.

269.title: Releasing control fears; Session 10 recap
269.gist: Members finish stems about the benefits of releasing the fear of losing control. The page stresses that tolerating negative emotions is central to recovery, and summarizes Session 10's work on depression, guilt, powerlessness, fear, and forgiveness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Distress tolerance, the capacity to sit with discomfort without acting impulsively, is linked in research with lower relapse risk. It is a trainable skill, not a fixed trait.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: End with an urge surfing practice: notice a feeling in the body, name its intensity every 30 seconds, and watch it change without doing anything.

ask: Which part of Session 10 is most likely to need individual follow-up, and how would you track that?
Does 'tolerate negative emotions' risk teaching people to accept situations they should change?

terms.d: The ability to endure painful emotions without making them worse through impulsive action.

271.title: Role-play: the payday lapse
271.gist: A couple uses a paycheck plan to protect his recovery from methamphetamine. When she travels, he takes the old route home, enters the bar, meets using friends, and relapses. In version one he can only repeat that he ruins everything.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The story is a textbook chain of seemingly irrelevant decisions, a Marlatt and Gordon idea: small choices like the old road and dinner at the bar move him closer to relapse before he admits any intent.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members stop the story at each decision point and propose a different choice. Seeing several exits makes relapse look preventable rather than sudden.

ask: At which step was Carlos's relapse most avoidable, and why do members usually pick the last step?
What does Carlos's 'I can't do anything right' reveal about shame versus guilt?

terms.d: Small choices that look harmless but set up a high-risk situation for relapse.

272.title: Version two: forgiveness and a plan
272.gist: In the second version the couple discusses the lapse, names Friday as a strong trigger, talks about forgiveness from her and from himself, and looks for solutions. Questions probe what forgiveness means and why he took the old way home.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Version one shows the abstinence violation effect at work; version two shows a lapse treated as a learning event. Marlatt's model holds that how a slip is interpreted shapes whether it becomes a full relapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Run both versions back to back and ask which Carlos is more likely to use again next week. Members usually see that self-blame increases risk.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Forgiveness here is between equals. In couples with abuse or coercion, pressure to forgive can be harmful; the frame should not be used to keep a partner in an unsafe situation.

ask: What is the opposite of forgiveness: resentment, punishment, or something else?
How can a partner forgive a lapse without becoming responsible for preventing the next one?

273.title: Session 11 opens: anger and communication
273.gist: The introduction previews Session 11: the body's anger signals, unhealthy patterns like stuffing, delaying, shifting, and diluting anger, then healthy expression and assertiveness. The aim is handling anger without harming recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anger is a frequent relapse trigger and, in justice-involved groups, often tied to the offense itself. Learning to read it early creates time to choose a response.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle argued that the virtue is not avoiding anger but feeling it at the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right reason. That frame fits this session well.

ask: How does this session overlap with CBI's anger and emotion regulation content, and where do they differ?
Is anger management the right goal, or should it be anger understanding?

274.title: Anger hides like stress does
274.gist: The page notes that people can ignore or repress anger the same way they use defenses against stress and fear, which can be destructive. It begins explaining that anger has strong physical components, many shared with fear.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anger and fear share the body's fight-or-flight system. The same arousal can be labeled either way depending on context and learning, which is why some people only ever notice anger.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members who say they never get angry and others who say they are always angry. Both groups benefit from learning the body signs; one group sees what it misses, the other what comes first.

ask: If anger and fear feel physically similar, what determines which one a person labels?
How might institutional rules against showing anger push members toward repression?

275.title: Your body's anger alarm
275.gist: The page lists physical changes in anger, such as dilated pupils, faster breathing, higher blood sugar, slowed digestion, and sweating, preparing the body to fight. Prolonged anger can harm health. Members begin checking their own body signs.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Chronic hostility has been linked in research with cardiovascular risk, though the size of the effect and its causes are debated.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rank their body signs from earliest to latest. The earliest sign becomes their personal alarm, the moment to step back before anger takes over.

ask: Why would knowing your earliest body cue matter more than knowing the full list?
How might long-term methamphetamine or cocaine use blur the signals listed here?

terms.d: The body's rapid survival reaction to threat, preparing to attack or escape.

276.title: Stuffing anger and the 'no big deal' mask
276.gist: The checklist of anger body signs ends, and the text describes stuffing anger: denying it while still showing physical signs, often in people taught that nice people never get angry. Such phrases hide anger that keeps building.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The idea that held-in anger builds pressure until it bursts is a popular hydraulic model. Research suggests what matters more is rumination; anger that is set aside and not chewed on often fades.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the group for phrases people use to hide anger. List them; members recognize their own and laugh, which lowers defensiveness.

ask: What is the difference between stuffing anger and choosing not to act on it?
How do family and cultural rules about anger, such as machismo or a religious upbringing, shape this pattern?

terms.d: Repeatedly replaying a problem or offense in one's mind, which tends to keep emotions alive.

277.title: Delaying anger until it explodes
277.gist: Members answer whether they were taught anger is bad and whether they used drugs to ease anger. The text explains that ignoring an ongoing problem lets anger build into explosions over small things, while cooling off first is fine if the problem is then addressed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The key distinction is between a time-out, a pause with a plan to return, and avoidance, a pause with no return. Only the first resolves the problem behind the anger.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Brad Bushman's experiments found that venting, such as hitting a punching bag, tends to increase aggression rather than release it. Calming first and then problem solving tends to work better.

ask: Why do small problems trigger big explosions, and what does that say about where the anger came from?
When is waiting genuinely wiser than addressing a conflict now, especially in a facility?

terms.d: Briefly leaving a heated situation to calm down, with an agreed plan to return and talk.

278.title: Cool off, then speak
278.gist: Members check whether ignored anger has led to explosions, read that expressing anger after cooling down avoids making conflict worse, and consider whether they delay, overreact to small problems, or prefer immediate expression.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The last question has no single right answer. Ask what happens when each option goes wrong; immediate expression risks damage, waiting risks never speaking. Help each member find their personal window.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach a simple rule: wait until the body signs drop, but speak within 24 hours. Practice one sentence starting with 'Yesterday when...' to open the later conversation.

ask: What happens when someone is never 'calm enough' to raise an issue?
How could staff-member conflicts be handled with this approach when power is unequal?

279.title: Aiming anger at a safer target
279.gist: The page describes shifting anger from a threatening person, like a boss, to a safer one, like a spouse, often unconsciously, with exaggeration or old grievances. Anger turned inward can become depression and self-hate.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychologists call this displacement. Laboratory work on displaced aggression shows that people provoked by one source often lash out at a later, unrelated target, especially after a minor trigger.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prison makes displacement common: anger at the system or staff lands on cellmates or family on the phone. Ask members who pays for their bad days.

ask: How could a member notice displacement in the moment rather than afterward?
Is the old idea that depression is anger turned inward supported, or just a useful metaphor?

terms.d: Redirecting feelings from their real source to a safer target.

280.title: Stuffing, exploding, and self-directed anger
280.gist: Members identify situations where they stuff feelings and what they do instead, times they exploded at an innocent person after a bad day, and times their anger at themselves frightened others.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The third question may reveal self-harm or suicidal risk. If someone answers yes, check in privately the same day and follow your facility's safety procedures.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to replay one explosion at an innocent person and name the real source. Then draft one sentence they could have said to the actual source, or to a safe listener.

ask: What makes a person 'innocent' in the member's mind, and how often is that line blurry in families?
How would you distinguish anger at oneself from shame?

281.title: Watering down justified anger
281.gist: Through a woman who realizes in therapy that her now-elderly mother abused her yet excuses the abuse, the page shows diluting anger out of guilt. It separates accepting anger from expressing it, so people can choose the wisest outlet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Accepting an emotion means acknowledging it is present and makes sense; expressing it is a separate choice. This split is central to acceptance-based therapies such as ACT and DBT.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Understanding why a parent hurt you and being angry about it can coexist. Literature is full of this double vision, from Kafka's letter to his father to many memoirs of addiction.

ask: Is 'she did the best she could' sometimes wisdom rather than dilution? How do you tell?
Why might anger at a parent feel especially forbidden in some cultures?

282.title: Guilt about being angry
282.gist: Members reflect on comfort with expressing anger, whether they have felt guilty for being angry like the woman in the example, and why awareness of unconscious anger matters.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anger that is not noticed still drives behavior, such as sarcasm, withdrawal, or using. Awareness turns an automatic reaction into a choice, a core principle across CBT and mindfulness approaches.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members carry the opposite problem: anger is the only feeling they allow. Invite them to consider what feeling sits under it, such as hurt or fear.

ask: What makes anger 'unconscious' if the body shows clear signs?
How might guilt about anger be a learned rule from a violent home?

283.title: Case: the paycheck resentment
283.gist: A man in treatment resents that his wife still collects his paycheck but stays silent, isolating and growing depressed. When caught at the payroll office he denies being angry, but later talks openly; the arrangement continues, yet the conflict is spoken.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Resentment, long called a major relapse risk in Twelve Step culture, grows from unspoken grievances replayed over time. Speaking it out loud does not require winning the argument.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members will side with Chen's wish for autonomy. Ask what Ming would need to see to hand the paycheck back; this shifts the anger into a plan.

ask: Is the paycheck arrangement a reasonable safeguard or a shaming restriction, and who should decide when it ends?
Why does Chen's blush matter in the story?

284.title: What Chen can do with his anger
284.gist: Members consider what would happen if Chen kept pretending, and whether he can let go of anger while accepting the paycheck arrangement for now.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anger often eases when a person reframes the restriction from punishment to protection or sees an end point. That is cognitive reappraisal, changing the meaning rather than the situation.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write the paycheck rule as Chen sees it and as Ming sees it, then a third version both could accept with a timeline.

ask: Can someone stop being angry while a situation they dislike stays the same, or is acceptance different from not being angry?
How does this parallel restrictions in probation or parole?

terms.d: Changing how you interpret a situation to change how you feel about it.

285.title: Hurtful ways to express anger
285.gist: Part 2 begins: expressing anger means letting someone know how you feel, not hurting them. Members check past use of blaming and attacking, sarcasm, exaggerations, and yelling or abuse, each with sample lines.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: John Gottman's studies of couples identified criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling as strong predictors of breakups, with contempt among the most corrosive. Sarcasm is a common vehicle for contempt.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Read the examples in a deadpan voice; members often laugh in recognition. Then ask how each line feels to receive, not to say.

ask: Why do words like always and never escalate conflict so reliably?
Is sarcasm ever a healthy release of anger, or always a disguised attack?

terms.d: Treating someone as beneath you, through mockery, sneering, or insults.

286.title: Withdrawal, guilt-tripping, and violence
286.gist: The list continues with pouting and withdrawal, projecting guilt, accusing 'you' statements, and physical violence or threats. Members recall a time they expressed anger this way and what they wanted the other person to feel.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking what the person wanted the other to feel exposes the goal behind anger: often to make the other share the hurt. Naming that goal is the first step to choosing another way to meet it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Grouping violence with pouting on one list may blur important distinctions in risk and responsibility. In a reentry group, violence needs its own safety planning, not just a checkbox.

ask: Is withdrawal always negative, or can stepping away be the healthiest choice?
How might projecting guilt overlap with the criminal thinking error of blaming others?

287.title: Where you learned your anger style
287.gist: Members examine exaggerations they use, whether yelling was common in childhood and still is, whether it is healthy, and whether they have hurt someone with anger and where they learned it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bandura's social learning theory explains that people learn aggression by watching others, especially those close to them, and by seeing it work. The family is often the first classroom.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Intergenerational patterns are not destiny. Many people who grow up with violence do not repeat it, and studying what helped them is as important as the risk itself.

ask: If a member learned violence at home, how do you hold both empathy for the child and accountability for the adult?
What models of healthy anger did your members likely never see, and where could they see one now?

terms.d: Learning behaviors by observing others and their consequences.

288.title: From 'you' statements to rights
288.gist: Members consider why 'you' statements backfire and how it feels to receive negative communication. The page then introduces assertiveness, noting addiction and low self-esteem make it hard, and begins a list of personal rights such as saying no and changing your mind.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Assertiveness sits between passivity and aggression. It respects both your needs and the other person's, which is why it lowers conflict rather than raising it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members equate assertiveness with being disrespected or with snitching. Show how a calm, firm statement can protect status better than an outburst.

ask: Which of these rights are real for someone inside a correctional facility, and how do you discuss that honestly?
Why might people with low self-esteem swing between passive and aggressive rather than land in the middle?

terms.d: Stating your needs and limits directly and respectfully, without attacking.

289.title: Standing up for yourself
289.gist: The rights list ends with asking for help, responding to criticism, complaining about unfair treatment, making time for yourself, and being wrong. Members reflect on how hard it is to stand up for themselves and when they avoid it.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Assertiveness training has a long history in behavior therapy and shows benefits for social anxiety and communication, though much of the research is older and varies in quality.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pick one right from the list and have each member practice a one-sentence version with a partner, such as saying no to an offer to use, using a calm voice and steady eye contact.

ask: Why is the right to be wrong on this list, and what does it protect?
How do assertiveness norms differ across cultures, and where might the model sound rude?

290.title: The 'I feel' statement
290.gist: The page argues negative expression makes people stop listening and get angry too. It explains that feelings come from beliefs, not other people, and teaches 'I feel' statements: name your feeling about a specific incident, without accusing or assuming motives.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The claim that no one makes you feel anything comes from Ellis's REBT: beliefs about events shape emotions. It shifts power back to the speaker.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Taken too far, this can sound like blaming victims for their feelings. Some actions, like abuse, reasonably cause hurt; the point is responsibility for one's response, not denial of harm.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often say 'I feel that you are selfish,' which is a 'you' statement in disguise. Teach a quick test: if you can replace 'I feel' with 'I think,' it is not a feeling.

ask: Do 'I feel' statements work with people who are not trained in them, such as an angry officer?
How does the beliefs-cause-feelings idea fit with the earlier claim that depression has biological roots?

291.title: Writing your own 'I feel' lines
291.gist: After sample statements about lateness, surprise guests, and an empty gas tank, members pick from a wide feelings list and write their own 'I feel ... when ...' statements from real life.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A rich feelings vocabulary matters: studies on emotional granularity suggest people who name feelings precisely regulate them better. Choosing 'disappointed' over 'mad' already changes the conversation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that the list includes positive feelings. Ask members to write at least one positive statement; appreciation spoken this way builds goodwill that later helps hard talks.

ask: Why might some members default to only two or three feelings words?
What does an 'I feel' statement still need, such as a request, to actually solve a problem?

terms.d: The ability to tell apart and name feelings in fine detail.

292.title: More practice and Session 11 recap
292.gist: Remaining blanks let members write more 'I feel' statements, and the summary recaps anger's body signs, unhealthy patterns, and healthy expression as protection for recovery.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pair members and have one read an 'I feel' statement while the other responds only by reflecting it back. The exercise shows how being heard lowers anger on both sides.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication extends this format with observation, feeling, need, and request. The added need and request are often what make the statement actionable.

ask: How would you measure whether members actually use 'I feel' statements outside the group?
Which unhealthy pattern from this session is most common in your groups?

293.title: Role-play: mother, daughter, and a slap
293.gist: A pregnant mother who has been drinking yells insults at her teenage daughter, who fires back about her drinking and warns about fetal alcohol harm; the mother slaps her. After calming down, they reconcile and she resolves to seek support.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The scene shows displacement, labeling, and violence in one exchange, then the repair. It also shows a child taking on a parenting role, a dynamic sometimes called parentification.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Physical violence toward a child is a mandatory reporting issue in real life. Do not act out the slap; describe it, and use the debrief to discuss safety and accountability.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The quick, warm reconciliation may be unrealistic. Repair after hitting a child usually needs more than one talk and may involve outside help.

ask: What would a healthy 'I feel' statement from Christina sound like, given the power imbalance?
How does shame about drinking during pregnancy fuel the mother's anger?

terms.d: Lifelong physical, learning, and behavioral problems caused by alcohol exposure before birth.
When a child takes on adult or parental responsibilities in the family.

295.title: Role-play: sober but always angry
295.gist: A man sober for months but out of meetings and aftercare explodes when his wife returns late, blaming her spending for his stuck job. She cries and tries to calm him, which makes him angrier. Members identify his body signs, the real sources, and her options.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: AA calls this a 'dry drunk': abstinent but without the emotional work, so old irritability and resentment remain. Dropping support often comes before relapse, not after it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The anger is displaced from the boss onto the wife. Ask members to rewrite Juan's outburst as an 'I feel' statement about work; it shows how far the target has drifted.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The question about what Cecilia can do risks making her responsible for his anger. Emphasize her safety and limits, not her job to soothe him.

ask: Why might trying to calm an angry person sometimes increase their anger?
What warning signs here would make you worry about domestic violence risk?

terms.d: Twelve Step term for someone abstinent but still showing the attitudes and moods of active addiction.

297.title: Role-play: jealousy and the surprise night
297.gist: A man in recovery has regained weekend visits with his son. His partner, quietly jealous, plans a surprise evening and is crushed when he arrives with the boy. Version one shows blaming and sarcasm; version two uses 'I feel' statements and leads to a plan including all three.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anger here sits on top of jealousy and disappointment. 'I feel' statements help surface the deeper emotion, which is often easier for the other person to respond to with care.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Blended families face predictable loyalty conflicts. Family therapists note step-relationships take years to settle, so tension early on is normal, not a sign of failure.

ask: Why is jealousy so hard to admit compared with anger?
How does regaining custody or visitation create new relapse risks along with new motivation?

298.title: Debrief: which version works
298.gist: Questions ask in which version Joan truly expresses her feelings, which version lets the couple work things out, and what advantages 'I feel' statements offer.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the two actors how each version felt from inside. Their felt experience is often more persuasive to the group than any explanation.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have the group write a version three where Joan uses an 'I feel' statement but Jim responds defensively. Practicing that harder case is closer to real life.

ask: Does expressing anger well guarantee the other person will respond well, and how do you prepare members for when it does not?
Why is version one more likely in real life even for people who know better?

299.title: Session 12 opens: relapse prevention
299.gist: The introduction previews Session 12: how triggers lead to relapse, types of triggers and how to defuse them, then exercises for avoiding triggers and stopping thoughts before they become relapses.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention model (1985) treats relapse as a process with identifiable steps, not a sudden event. That framing makes it teachable and preventable.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Relapse prevention approaches show benefits across many studies, particularly for reducing the severity of lapses, though effects on total abstinence are more modest.

ask: How does this session's trigger model compare with CBI's relapse prevention content?
What is lost by focusing on triggers rather than on the life conditions that make triggers powerful?

terms.d: A cognitive-behavioral approach that teaches people to anticipate and cope with high-risk situations.

300.title: Stopping use is just the start
300.gist: After objectives on avoiding triggers, visualization, and thought-stopping, Part 1 recaps addiction as compulsion, loss of control, and continued use despite harm, with obsessive thinking and relapse. It warns that a few days clean can falsely feel like a cure.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The 'pink cloud' of early abstinence can bring false confidence. Confidence that outruns skill is a known risk; Bandura's self-efficacy matters most when it is grounded in practice.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Seeing addiction as chronic and relapsing parallels how medicine views conditions like diabetes or hypertension, where management, not a one-time cure, is the goal.

ask: Does the chronic disease framing help or hurt members' motivation?
How would you respond to a member who says, 'I've been locked up three years, I'm obviously done with drugs'?

terms.d: Recovery slang for the euphoria and overconfidence some feel in early sobriety.

301.title: Drug-free versus in recovery
301.gist: Members consider whether being drug-free differs from being in recovery. The text says recovery means changing lifestyle to avoid triggering people, places, and things, with support and work. Members name what is most likely to make them relapse and what they are doing about it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Incarcerated members are often drug-free by circumstance. Ask what they would be doing differently if drugs were freely available tomorrow; the answer shows how much recovery work is underway.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Avoiding people, places, and things is hard when housing options after release are limited to old neighborhoods. Pair the avoidance message with realistic coping plans for unavoidable exposure.

ask: Is forced abstinence in prison an asset for recovery or a misleading test?
How do you help someone predict relapse risk in a world they have not lived in for years?

302.title: The trigger chain
302.gist: After asking if members should do more to prevent relapse, the page defines triggers as people, places, feelings, and things linked with use. It lays out the chain from trigger to thought to craving to relapse, and notes brain changes from use make people vulnerable.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is classical conditioning: repeated pairing of cues with drug effects lets the cue alone produce craving and even bodily responses. Pavlov's dogs and drug cues follow the same logic.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research with brain imaging shows drug cues activate reward and motivation regions in people with addiction. Cue-induced craving can persist long after use stops, which is why time alone does not erase it.

ask: If the chain is automatic, where is the earliest point a person can realistically intervene?
Does describing physical brain changes reduce shame or increase fatalism?

terms.d: Learning in which a neutral cue, paired with a powerful experience, comes to trigger a response on its own.

303.title: Explain the chain in your own words
303.gist: Members describe in their own words how triggers lead to thoughts, thoughts to cravings, and cravings to relapse, then brainstorm ways to break the cycle.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Explaining a process in your own words, called elaboration, deepens understanding far more than recognizing it on a page. It also reveals misconceptions you can correct.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to draw the chain with their own real example at each link. Then have the group find at least two break points per link.

ask: Is the chain really linear, or can craving appear without any noticeable trigger?
What does it mean if a member can explain the chain perfectly but still relapses?

304.title: Internal and external triggers
304.gist: The page separates internal triggers, emotional states tied to use such as happiness, depression, anxiety, or arousal, from external ones like neighborhoods, bars, a dealer's home, paydays, weekends, paraphernalia, and people. Members name one strong trigger of each kind.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Positive emotions are triggers too. Celebration often goes unplanned for because people only prepare for bad days.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name a trigger that is a good feeling, such as getting paid or a release date. Planning for success is a skill most relapse plans skip.

ask: Which internal triggers are hardest to detect because they feel like normal life?
How do external triggers change for someone released to a new city versus the old neighborhood?

terms.d: A feeling or body state linked with past use that can spark cravings.
A person, place, time, or object linked with past use.

305.title: Sensory triggers and the hardest ones
305.gist: The page adds sensory triggers, such as the look of white powder, certain music, smells, and tastes. Members name a strong sensory trigger and the triggers hardest for them in the past and now.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Smell has unusually direct links to brain areas involved in emotion and memory, which may explain why an odor can bring back a scene vividly, as Proust described with his madeleine.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Comparing past and present triggers shows change over time. Point out any trigger that has weakened; it is evidence the member's brain is relearning.

ask: Why might sensory triggers be strongest in early recovery and fade later?
Could some triggers be unavoidable sounds or smells inside the facility itself?

306.title: Identify and avoid
306.gist: The page begins strategies for breaking the trigger chain: first identify personal triggers and when they worsen, then avoid high-risk people, places, and situations whenever possible. Members list one trigger of each type and situations they can avoid.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Stimulus control, a behavioral strategy, reduces exposure to cues so the conditioned response is not set off. It is simple and effective, but works best paired with skills for cues that cannot be avoided.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for avoidable situations that are specific, like a particular corner store, not 'bad places.' Vague answers lead to vague plans.

ask: When does avoidance become a long-term limit on life rather than a temporary safety measure?
What triggers cannot be avoided for most members after release?

terms.d: Changing your surroundings to reduce exposure to cues that prompt unwanted behavior.

307.title: Interrupt and talk about triggers
307.gist: Members name people to avoid. For triggers that cannot be avoided, like certain days or feelings, the page suggests interrupting them with healthy activities such as a Friday meeting. Talking about triggers reduces their power.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naming a trigger aloud moves it from automatic to deliberate processing. Research on affect labeling suggests putting feelings into words can reduce their emotional intensity.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member say one trigger aloud to the group in a single sentence. Ask how intense the urge feels before and after saying it.

ask: Why might talking about triggers increase craving for some people in the short term?
How can a member interrupt a time-of-day trigger, like evenings, when options are limited?

terms.d: Putting a feeling into words, which can lessen its intensity.

308.title: People to call; thought-stopping
308.gist: Members list three people to call when craving. The page introduces thought-stopping: using relaxation and visualization to interrupt drug thoughts before they become cravings, and asks what techniques have and have not worked.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Daniel Wegner's 'white bear' studies showed that trying hard not to think something can make it return more often. Thought-stopping may work better as redirecting attention than as forcing thoughts away.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Alan Marlatt's urge surfing, from mindfulness-based relapse prevention, takes a different route: observe the craving like a wave until it passes, instead of pushing it out.

ask: What does the thought suppression research imply for how you teach thought-stopping?
Why ask what did not work, and how would you use those failures in group?

terms.d: A technique for interrupting unwanted thoughts and shifting attention elsewhere.

309.title: Avoid early, even if it means moving
309.gist: Members reflect on techniques for unavoidable triggers that did and did not work. Part 2 then argues the best time to stop a trigger is before meeting it, which may require major lifestyle changes, even relocating to another town.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on natural experiments, such as studies of Vietnam veterans who used heroin abroad, found that many did not resume use after returning home, a result often cited to show how strongly environment shapes addiction.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Relocation is often blocked for people on parole, who may be required to live in a specific county or with family. Help members plan within those limits rather than prescribing a move.

ask: What does the veteran heroin finding suggest about addiction, and what are its limits?
How would you help a member weigh the costs of moving away, such as losing family support, against the benefits?

310.title: Small decisions, big consequences
310.gist: Members name the easiest way to avoid a trigger. The page stresses that seemingly minor daily choices often matter a lot and suggests asking whether each is good or bad for recovery. Members name a high-risk trigger and the small decisions that would lead them toward it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Tracing backward from a high-risk situation to the small choices that led there is a classic relapse prevention exercise. It reveals decision points that felt innocent at the time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to narrate the decisions as a movie in slow motion, from waking up to arriving at the trigger. Then rewind and change one frame.

ask: Is a single good-or-bad question too simple for complex decisions, such as visiting a using parent who is ill?
Why do people often fail to notice small decisions as decisions at all?

311.title: The mental light switch
311.gist: Members consider different decisions that would avoid their trigger. Then a visualization exercise teaches imagining a large switch they alone control, flipping drug thoughts and cravings from on to off when they start.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Imagery gives an abstract skill a concrete handle, making it easier to recall under stress. The switch also builds a sense of personal control, which supports self-efficacy.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A switch implies cravings can vanish instantly. When they do not, members may feel they failed. Present it as a cue to shift attention and act, not a guaranteed off button.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pair the image with an action: picture the switch, flip it, then immediately do one physical thing, such as standing up, drinking water, or calling someone.

ask: How do you set expectations so a tool that only partly works is still seen as useful?
Could the switch metaphor conflict with mindfulness approaches that teach allowing cravings?

312.title: Replaying a past urge
312.gist: Members describe a real situation in which something triggered the urge to use and how they handled it, setting up a review of what could have been done differently.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reviewing a real past episode, sometimes called a functional analysis or chain analysis, ties abstract skills to the member's own life. Success stories count too; they show what already works.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Invite members to choose an urge they handled well, not only one that ended in use. Starting with a success lowers shame and builds confidence.

ask: Why might people remember urges that led to use more vividly than urges they resisted?
How detailed should a chain analysis be to be useful without becoming exhausting?

terms.d: A step-by-step review of the events, thoughts, and feelings leading to a behavior, used in DBT and CBT.

313.title: Where thought-stopping could fit
313.gist: Members consider how they could have used a thought-stopping technique in that past situation, the best moment to use it, and how things might have turned out differently.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Timing matters: interventions work best early, when craving is mild. As craving intensifies, attention narrows and planning becomes harder, a pattern consistent with research on stress and decision making.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to rate their craving at each step of the replay from 0 to 10. The best intervention point is usually below 4, long before most people act.

ask: If people rarely notice craving below a certain level, how can they learn to catch it earlier?
What is the risk of imagining an ideal outcome that real life would not have delivered?

314.title: Stopping a relapse in progress
314.gist: The page admits avoiding or stopping relapse is very hard and needs groups, counseling, and family support. Relapse is common; stop it quickly, skip self-punishment, take responsibility, and if needed enter a hospital or residential program. A summary closes Session 12.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating a lapse from a relapse, and responding to a lapse without self-condemnation, is central to Marlatt's model. Self-attack fuels the abstinence violation effect and prolongs use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For opioid users after release, a lapse can be fatal because tolerance has dropped. Teach overdose risk and naloxone alongside the relapse plan.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Harm reduction approaches share this realism: the aim is to reduce damage at every stage, not only to prevent the first use.

ask: How do you balance 'relapse is common' with not giving members permission to use?
What would a written 'if I use' plan include for someone on parole who fears reporting a lapse?

terms.d: A single slip or brief return to use, which may or may not become a full relapse.
A medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose, available as a nasal spray.

315.title: Role-play: Friday at the warehouse
315.gist: A warehouse worker new to treatment has long spent Friday paydays at a bar with two coworkers who drink and smoke marijuana. He hasn't told them or tried the union-hall group. In version one they press him to come once more, and he plans to go without using.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Going to the bar but not using is a classic setup, the belief that one can face a high-risk situation untouched. Marlatt would note the decision itself is the relapse risk, not the first drink.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Let the coworkers push hard with 'one last time.' Members who play Marcus learn how quickly resolve weakens under friendly pressure, which makes refusal practice feel necessary.

ask: Why do phrases like 'one last time' work so well on people in early recovery?
How should Marcus decide what to tell coworkers about his treatment, given workplace stigma?

316.title: Version two: choosing the union hall
316.gist: In the second version Marcus, nervous about payday cash and changing his mind, refuses the bar and commits to the support group. Questions ask how he can work with people, build supportive relationships, and plan his recovery.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Commitment is stronger when made in advance and made public. Deciding before the check arrives removes the in-the-moment choice, a strategy behavioral economists call precommitment.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have Marcus's actor plan the payday money before the scene: direct deposit, a set amount for bills, a companion to the meeting. Discuss how each step lowers risk.

ask: What practical money steps could protect a member's first paychecks after release?
How could Marcus stay on good terms with LaTroy and Willie at work without joining them?

terms.d: Locking in a choice ahead of time to limit later temptation.
